sentence.834: title: Malware Analysis: LummaC2 Stealer url: <URL> By SOCRadar Research In our article about Stealer-as-a-Service, as the SOCRadar Research team, we looked at Lumma Stealer, a relatively new and unknown malware.
sentence.835: During our research, we didn’t find much information, so we did threat hunting by monitoring hacker forums with our dark web team.
sentence.836: We added the resulting data to our platform and started our analysis.
sentence.837: LummaC2 is the name of a malicious program classified as a stealer.
sentence.838: It operates by stealing sensitive information from infected devices and installing applications.
sentence.839: After our dark web team discovered LummaC2, we found that it was being sold on underground forums.
sentence.840: Due to its distribution on the web, it can be related to multiple cybercriminals.
sentence.841: According to the promotional material, the LummaC2 is approximately 150-200 KB and can affect operating systems from Windows 7 to Windows 11.
sentence.842: Executive Summary Threat Identifiers Name LummaC2 Threat Type Stealer Detections VirusTotal Symptoms Stealers are designed to stealthily infiltrate the victim’s computer and remain silent.
sentence.843: Thus no particular symptoms are clearly visible on an infected machine.
sentence.844: Distribution Methods Infected email attachments, malicious online advertisements, social engineering, software ‘cracks.’
sentence.845: Damage Stolen passwords and banking information, identity theft, and the victim’s computer added to a botnet.
sentence.846: The LummaC2 stealer begins its operations by obtaining relevant device data, such as OS version and architecture, hardware ID, CPU, RAM, <DATA_OBJECT> resolution, system language, etc.
sentence.847: This malware can exfiltrate <DATA_OBJECT> and extract data from specific applications.
sentence.848: Browsers targeted by LummaC2: Chrome, Chromium, Mozilla Firefox, Microsoft Edge, Brave, Kometa, Opera GX Stable, Opera Neon, Opera Stable, Vivaldi, and others.
sentence.849: This stealer may acquire browsing histories, Internet <DATA_OBJECT>, usernames<FILE_PATH>, personally identifiable details, credit card numbers, and other highly sensitive information from browsers.
sentence.850: LummaC2 also targets multiple cryptocurrencies (e.g., Binance, Electrum, Ethereum, etc.).
sentence.851: In summary, software like LummaC2 on devices can result in severe privacy issues, significant financial losses, and identity theft.

sentence.924: title: FedEx Phishing Campaign Abusing TrustedForm and PAAY url: <URL> Summary Netskope Threat Labs is tracking a phishing campaign that mimics a FedEx package delivery as bait to steal credit card data.
sentence.925: This type of social engineering attack is commonly found in phishing pages, emails, and other scams, where a false sense of urgency is created to urge the victim into doing an action that eventually leads to personal data theft.
sentence.926: This specific phishing campaign is noteworthy because it abuses two cloud services throughout the attack: TrustedForm, a digital certificate service provided by ActiveProspectis, is abused to track victims and collect information about them, and the PAAY 3DS, a cloud-based platform that authenticates payment transactions, is abused to validate the credit card details collected from the victims.
sentence.927: Cybersecurity awareness training, specifically educating users to be wary of fake shipment notifications, is an effective defense against these types of phishing attacks.
sentence.928: Netskope customers also receive protection from the threats discussed in this blog through the Next Generation Secure Web Gateway (SWG).
sentence.930: The attack starts when the victim receives an email or a text message that uses a common social engineering technique, creating a false sense of urgency to get the victim’s attention.
sentence.931: The specific approach here, using a fake shipping notification, is also a common technique used by scammers.
sentence.932: First steps of this FedEx phishing campaign.
sentence.933: Step 1 – Once the victim reaches the page via phishing email or SMS text, they are instructed to click “Confirm” to view a message from “Express.”
sentence.934: This webpage has “FedEx” in the title and uses the same company colors to deceive the user.
sentence.935: The user is also asked to permit push notifications in the browser, which allows the attacker to push malicious ads, as we will demonstrate later in this analysis.
sentence.936: Step 2 – The victim is informed that delivery of a package has been suspended, and that they need to schedule delivery and should enable push notifications to avoid future issues.
sentence.937: Step 3 – Then, the victim is informed that they need to pay a $1.95 customs fee.
sentence.938: The customs fee is just an excuse to collect the victim’s personal and credit card data in the next stage of the attack.
sentence.939: Behind the scenes, once the first page is loaded, the page sends a request to receive a customizable JSON that is used throughout the attack.
sentence.940: The JSON includes the questions, form fields, and second-stage URLs, which will be all used in the next steps.
sentence.941: JSON containing data about the phishing.
sentence.942: Fake questions displayed by the phishing page.
sentence.943: Step 4 – The attacker continues to deceive the victim, in an attempt to add more credibility to the phish, by asking a series of questions to the victim, such as how, where, and when the victim would like to receive the package.
sentence.944: Step 5 – The deception continues by giving the victim a delivery estimate.
sentence.945: As soon as the victim interacts with the questions on step 4, the phishing starts sending requests to the TrustedForm API.
sentence.946: TrustedForm is a digital certificate service provided by ActiveProspect, which provides marketing automation and compliance platforms.
sentence.947: This service can be used to generate a digital certificate that includes information about a lead, such as geolocation, IP address, browser type, operating system, the time spent on the page, and even a web session replay.
sentence.948: We believe that the attacker is creating a TrustedForm certificate to collect more information about victims.
sentence.950: Below is the type of information that would be available in a TrustedForm certificate, as demonstrated in their demo webpage.
sentence.951: Examples of a TrustedForm certificate generated by their demo page.
sentence.952: And finally, the phishing page redirects the victim to the next stage, using a URL parsed from the JSON we demonstrated earlier.
sentence.953: This page returns a second URL, which is used to redirect the user to a third URL.
sentence.954: This is done to add resilience, as the attacker can update the URLs with little effort if the last stage is taken down.
sentence.955: Phishing page redirecting the victim to the next stage.
sentence.956: Second Stage – Stealing Credit Card Data Once the attacker convinces the victim about the allegedly suspended package, they try to steal the victim’s credit card number on a different page.
sentence.957: Phishing trying to steal personal and credit card data.
sentence.958: Step 6 – This page asks for the victim’s personal information, such as the full name, phone number, and email address.
sentence.959: Step 7 – Then, the page asks for credit card details and uses PAAY to assess whether the credit card is valid.
sentence.960: This is done by using their 3DS (3-D Secure) system, which is a protocol designed to add more security and prevent fraud in online purchases.
sentence.961: Once the credit card data is entered in the page, it starts sending requests to the 3DS API, which performs a temporary purchase in the credit card number.
sentence.962: If the credit card is invalid, the phishing does not move forward.
sentence.964: Spreading Adware As demonstrated earlier, the main page asks for permission to show notifications in the browser.
sentence.965: Unsurprisingly, if the victim allows notifications, they are bombarded with ads from the “<DOMAIN>” domain, including ads for fake antivirus software, fake coupons, and free iPads.
sentence.966: Phishing page asking permission to show notifications.
sentence.967: These ads lead to webpages that eventually ask for personal information or try to download malware.
sentence.968: So, even in case the phishing attack fails at any stage, if the victim allows notifications, they will still be targeted with additional scams.
sentence.969: Ads displayed if the victim enabled the notifications in the phishing page.
sentence.970: Conclusions By abusing cloud services, attackers are able to create more elaborate phishing pages that are also more resilient to detection.
sentence.971: This phishing campaign is not only trying to steal data from victims, but also abuses browser notifications to bombard victims with additional scams even if this one is unsuccessful.
sentence.972: Netskope uses ML-based inline, out-of-band phishing detection engines, and threat intelligence systems to block such phishing attempts.
sentence.973: Recommendations Phishing pages from the campaign described in the post are easily recognizable by the URL, as the attacker has made little effort to disguise the URL using typosquatting or other techniques.
sentence.974: We strongly recommend users to never enter their data on pages that promise something, such as the delivery of a supposedly suspended package.
sentence.975: If you are indeed expecting a package, make sure to access the website of the logistics company directly.
sentence.976: Netskope Threat Labs also recommends that organizations review their security policies to ensure that they are adequately protected against these and similar phishing pages and scams: Inspect all <PROTOCOL> and <PROTOCOL> traffic, including all web and cloud traffic, to prevent users from visiting malicious websites.
sentence.977: Netskope customers can configure their Netskope NG-SWG with a URL filtering policy to block known phishing and scam sites, and a threat protection policy to inspect all web content to identify unknown phishing and scam sites using a combination of signatures, threat intelligence, and machine learning.
sentence.978: Use Remote Browser Isolation (RBI) technology to provide additional protection when there is a need to visit websites that fall in categories that can present higher risk, like Newly Observed and Newly Registered Domains.
sentence.979: IOCs Below are the IOCs related to the web pages analyzed in this blog post.

sentence.981: title: Take a “NetWalk” on the Wild Side url: <URL> Executive Summary The NetWalker ransomware, initially known as Mailto, was first detected in August 2019.
sentence.982: Since then, new variants were discovered throughout 2019 and the beginning of 2020, with a strong uptick noticed in March of this year.
sentence.983: NetWalker has noticeably evolved to a more stable and robust ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) model, and our research suggests that the malware operators are targeting and attracting a broader range of technically advanced and enterprising criminal affiliates.
sentence.984: McAfee Advanced Threat Research (ATR) discovered a large sum of bitcoins linked to NetWalker which suggest its extortion efforts are effective and that many victims have had no option other than to succumb to its criminal demands.
sentence.985: We approached our investigation of NetWalker with some possible ideas about the threat actor behind it, only to later disprove our own hypothesis.
sentence.986: We believe the inclusion of our thinking, and the means with which we debunked our own theory, highlight the importance of thorough research and we welcome further discussion on this topic.
sentence.987: We believe it starts valuable discussions and helps avoid duplicate research efforts by others.
sentence.988: We also encourage our peers in the industry to share information with us in case you have more evidence.
sentence.989: McAfee protects its customers against the malware covered in this blog in all its products, including personal antivirus, endpoint and gateway.
sentence.990: To learn more about how McAfee products can defend against these types of attacks, visit our blog on Building Adaptable Security Architecture Against NetWalker.
sentence.991: Check out McAfee Insights to stay on top of NetWalker’s latest developments and intelligence on other cyber threats, all curated by the McAfee ATR team.
sentence.992: Not only that, Insights will also help you prioritize threats, predict if your countermeasures will work and prescribe corrective actions.
sentence.993: Introduction Since 2019, NetWalker ransomware has reached a vast number of different targets, mostly based in western European countries and the US.
sentence.994: Since the end of 2019, the NetWalker gang has indicated a preference for larger organisations rather than individuals.
sentence.995: During the COVID-19 pandemic, the adversaries behind NetWalker clearly stated that hospitals will not be targeted; whether they keep to their word remains to be seen.
sentence.996: The ransomware appends a random extension to infected <DATA_OBJECT> and uses Salsa20 encryption.
sentence.997: It uses some tricks to avoid detection, such as a new defence evasion technique, known as reflective DLL loading, to inject a DLL from memory.
sentence.998: The NetWalker collective, much like those behind Maze, REvil and other ransomware, threatens to publish victims’ data if ransoms are not paid.
sentence.999: As mentioned earlier, NetWalker RaaS prioritizes quality over quantity and is looking for people who are Russian-speaking and have experience with large networks.
sentence.1000: People who already have a foothold in a potential victim’s network and can exfiltrate data with ease are especially sought after.
sentence.1001: This is not surprising, considering that publishing a victims’ data is part of NetWalker’s model.
sentence.1002: The following sections are dedicated to introducing the NetWalker malware and displaying the telemetry status before moving on to the technical malware analysis of the ransomware’s behaviour.
sentence.1003: We will explain how the decryptor works and show some interactions between NetWalker’s operators and their victims.
sentence.1004: After this, we discuss the changes in modus operandi since September 2019, especially regarding payment behaviour.
sentence.1005: Then we show our attempts, unfruitful as they were, at discovering a link between NetWalker and previous, seemingly unrelated ransomware variants.
sentence.1006: Finally, we deliver an overview of IOCs related to NetWalker and its MITRE ATT&CK techniques.
sentence.1007: Telemetry Using McAfee’s billion Insights sensors, we can show the global prevalence of the NetWalker ransomware. Figure 1.
sentence.1008: McAfee MVISION Insights shows global prevalence of the NetWalker ransomware Technical Analysis Ransom note (pre-March 2020)
sentence.1009: Before March 2020, the NetWalker ransom note indicated how to contact the adversary directly using anonymous email account services with random names (such as <EMAIL> and <EMAIL>): Figure 2.
sentence.1010: Example of ransom note prior to March 2020 Ransom Note (Post-March 2020)
sentence.1011: On 12 March 2020, a researcher shared a screenshot of a new NetWalker ransom note in a tweet and we can see that the attackers have changed the contact method significantly.
sentence.1012: Email communication has been dropped completely with victims now required to make contact through the NetWalker Tor interface where, after submitting their user key, they will then be redirected to a chat with NetWalker technical support.
sentence.1013: This change in contact method coincides with underground forum postings where NetWalker revealed it was opening its RaaS up for new affiliates.
sentence.1014: The Tor page was not the only noticeable change we will highlight in this blog.
sentence.1016: Example of ransom note after March 2020 NetWalker Analysis Figure 4. NetWalker behavior NetWalker Resource Analysis (Pre-March 2020)
sentence.1017: The NetWalker malware uses a custom resource type (1337 or 31337) containing its entire configuration.
sentence.1018: This <DATA_OBJECT> is extracted to memory and decrypted using the <ENC_ALGO> algorithm with a hard-coded key in the resource.
sentence.1019: Before 12 March 2020, NetWalker used the email contact process between its support operation and the victims to proceed with payment and send the decryption program.
sentence.1020: To do this, NetWalker used its configuration <DATA_OBJECT> in the resource to set its encryption mode, the name of the ransom note, etc., and email contacts.
sentence.1021: Name <FILENAME> Size 96256 bytes <DATA_OBJECT>-Type EXE SHA 256 <FILE_HASH> Compile time 6 December 2019 Figure 5.
sentence.1022: NetWalker resource from <FILENAME> Once decrypted, the configuration <DATA_OBJECT> reveals several parameters, allowing us to understand how it works (how it constitutes the ransom note, the number of threads allocated for encryption, etc.): mpk Public key mode Encryption mode thr Allocated threads for encryption process spsz Encryption chunk namesz Name length idsz ID length crmask .mailto[email].{ID} mail Contact mail lfile Ransom Note name lend B64 encoded ransom note white Encryption whitelist kill Processes, tasks, service names to terminate unlocker Decryption exclusion list NetWalker Resource Analysis (Post-March 2020)
sentence.1023: When Netwalker changed its contact mode and switched from email to the submission of the user key directly on the web portal of the group’s blog, the configuration <DATA_OBJECT> in the resource also changed.
sentence.1024: We found changes in the configuration <DATA_OBJECT>, such as the disappearance of the contact “mail” and “crmask” fields (previously set as <EMAIL>,<EMAIL>, etc., and .mailto[email].{ID}).
sentence.1025: This field was replaced by “onion1” and “onion2”, and these fields are set with the NetWalker blog URL<FILE_PATH> page (<URL><snip><DOMAIN>/).
sentence.1026: We also noticed that the NetWalker developers complemented their “unlocker” field with some specific values (e.g. “<FILENAME>, system, forti*.exe, <FILENAME>*, etc”).
sentence.1027: Name <DOMAIN> Size 70656 bytes <DATA_OBJECT>-Type EXE SHA 256 <FILE_HASH> Compile time 2 May 2020 Figure 6.
sentence.1028: NetWalker resource from <DOMAIN> Usually, attackers use RC_DATA or a malicious BITMAP.
sentence.1029: The latter can, for example, be a regular Bitmap (open matrix image format used by Windows) that can be used by malware to execute code or as a payload dropper.
sentence.1030: The image’s pixels are an actual binary representation of the payload.
sentence.1031: This process can be summarized as Exe -> Resources -> BMP with embedded data in pixels fetched and decrypted by, e.g. a DLL -> Payload), etc.
sentence.1032: However, in this case, they use this special custom type to increase obfuscation.
sentence.1033: The NetWalker developers chose custom types by using 1337 or 31337 structs, so the resource format does not change.
sentence.1034: However, as we said, several values have changed or been replaced: mpk Public Key mode Encryption mode spsz Encryption chunk thr Allocated threads for encryption process namesz Name length idsz ID length lfile Ransom Note name onion1 Blog URL 1 onion 2 Blog URL 2 white Encryption whitelist kill Processes, tasks, service names to terminate net Network resources encryption unlocker Decryption exclusion list lend B64 encoded ransom note NetWalker Executable Analysis (Post-March 2020)
sentence.1035: The malware sample used for this blog post has the same information: Name c21ecd18f0bbb28112240013ad42dad5c01d20927791239ada5b 61e1c6f5f010 Size 70656 bytes <DATA_OBJECT>-Type EXE SHA 256 c21ecd18f0bbb28112240013ad42dad5c01d20927791239ada5b 61e1c6f5f010 Compile time 2 May 2020
sentence.1036: The unpacked malware is a binary <DATA_OBJECT> of 32 bits that can be found as an EXE <DATA_OBJECT>.
sentence.1038: Information sample of the malware The malware’s first action is to combine all the required functions it needs into one large function, combining the modules already loaded in Windows with additional DLLs as described below.
sentence.1039: Instead of searching for the function in the usual way, the malware makes a CRC32 hash of the name of each function and compares with hardcoded values.
sentence.1040: Additionally, instead of using the function “GetProcAddress”, the malware uses the Process Environment Block (PEB) to make analysis harder. Figure 8.
sentence.1041: Get the module accessing the PEB and using a CRC32
sentence.1042: If the module cannot be discovered, it will load with “LdrLoadDll”, a native function of Windows, to try avoiding hooks in the usual functions, e.g. “LoadLibraryW”: Figure 9.
sentence.1044: Get functions from module, e.g. using a CRC32 hash If the malware fails to get a function, it will go to a “sleep” call and terminate itself.
sentence.1045: Later, the malware extracts the configuration <DATA_OBJECT> from a resource with a custom type and a custom name using the functions “FindResourceA”, “LockResource”, “LoadResource” and “SizeOfResource”.
sentence.1046: The <DATA_OBJECT> extracted in memory is decrypted using the <ENC_ALGO> algorithm with a hardcoded key in the resource.
sentence.1047: The struct of the resource is: 4 bytes ->
sentence.1048: The size of the hardcoded key to decrypt the configuration <DATA_OBJECT>.
sentence.1049: Variable size -> the hardcoded key to decrypt the configuration <DATA_OBJECT>.
sentence.1051: The malware reads the first 4 bytes and reserves memory with the size of the <DATA_OBJECT> and reserves memory of the resource minus 4 bytes and the size of the <DATA_OBJECT>.
sentence.1052: Finally, it decrypts the configuration <DATA_OBJECT>: Figure 11.
sentence.1053: Get configuration <DATA_OBJECT> and decrypt it If the malware fails to get the configuration <DATA_OBJECT>, it will terminate itself.
sentence.1054: After getting the configuration <DATA_OBJECT>, the malware will parse it and save the fields in memory and write in the <DATA_OBJECT> information to encrypt the <DATA_OBJECT> in the machine.
sentence.1055: The malware will try first to write in the <DATA_OBJECT>-hive “HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE” but if it cannot create it, it will use the <DATA_OBJECT>-hive “HKEY_CURRENT_USER”: Figure 12.
sentence.1056: Write in the <DATA_OBJECT> After the writing in the <DATA_OBJECT> has been completed, it will get some privileges using a <DATA_OBJECT> as SE_DEBUG_PRIVILEGE and SE_IMPERSONATE_PRIVILEGE: Figure 13.
sentence.1057: Get some special privileges in the <DATA_OBJECT> Later, the malware creates three threads, one to get information about the machine, such as the operating system version, one to get processes and the last one to get services in the system.
sentence.1058: After this step, it will get the system directory and use “VSSadmin” to delete the Volume Shadow copies of the system.
sentence.1059: Volume Shadow copies can contain copies of the encrypted <DATA_OBJECT> and would be an option to restore from if no backup exists.
sentence.1061: Delete the shadow volumes Later, the malware will enumerate the logical units, prepare the new extension for the future encrypted <DATA_OBJECT>, based on the size that is defined in the ransomware config with a random extension, and encrypt all <DATA_OBJECT> in the fixed type units and remote units with the new extension.
sentence.1063: Crypt the <DATA_OBJECT> After all these steps have been completed, it will create the ransom note on the desktop using the functions “SHGetFolderPathlW” and “CreateFileW”.
sentence.1064: Subsequently, it will write the ransom note from the memory into a new <DATA_OBJECT> with the function “WriteFile”.
sentence.1065: The malware will create the ransom note in the root folder (for example “<FILE_PATH>) of each logical unit.
sentence.1066: Next, it will launch “<FILENAME>” with an argument to the ransom note <DATA_OBJECT> to show the user what happened on the system: Figure 16.
sentence.1067: Creation of the ransom note in the desktop and root units Finally, after the encryption of the <DATA_OBJECT> and creation of the ransom note, the malware creates a bat <DATA_OBJECT> in the %temp% folder of the machine with a temporary name and writes the content to destroy itself using the program “taskkill”.
sentence.1068: The batch script will delete the malware sample with its path using the command “del” and finally delete the bat <DATA_OBJECT> with the command “del %0%”.
sentence.1069: Of course, as the malware uses the “del” command without destroying itself before the deletion, it can be recovered with some forensic tools with luck (the same can also be said for the bat <DATA_OBJECT>).
sentence.1070: This way the malware tries to remove itself from the machine to avoid being detected and analyzed by security researchers: Figure 17.
sentence.1071: Get Temp path and make a temporary <DATA_OBJECT> as a bat and launch it Finally, the malware will finish with “ExitProcess”.
sentence.1072: Decryptor When a NetWalker victim goes through technical support (see an example of this below) and pays the ransom demanded by the group they will be able to download the decryptor to clean up their environment.
sentence.1074: Conversation with NetWalker operators The download is done directly from the NetWalker Tor site, where the payment page switches to a download page certifying that the payment was made and received: Figure 19.
sentence.1075: Decryptor download The decryptor is delivered in a zip archive containing the decryptor executable and a note explaining how to run the program correctly: Figure 20.
sentence.1076: Decryptor delivery The program launches a graphical interface allowing the user to decipher their workstation automatically or manually: Figure 21.
sentence.1077: Decryptor execution At the end of the decryption process, the program indicates the number of decrypted <DATA_OBJECT>, deletes the ransom note if the user has checked that option, and terminates, leaving the user to resume their work peacefully: Figure 22.
sentence.1078: Decryptor has finished the decryption process The decryptor program appears unique and is linked to one victim specifically.
sentence.1079: In our example, it only decrypts the <DATA_OBJECT> belonging to the victim who made the payment from the user key specified in the ransom note.
sentence.1080: Underground Advertising In March 2020, the moniker Bugatti began actively advertising the NetWalker Ransomware-as-a-Service on two popular underground fora.
sentence.1081: Bugatti seems to have joined the underground scene in February 2020 but claims to have been active with NetWalker ransomware since September 2019.
sentence.1082: We have seen NetWalker activity before March but there has been a noticeable uptick in larger victims since their advertisement.
sentence.1083: For a relatively new ransomware it has been well received and respected among other cybercriminals as compared to, for instance, Nemty ransomware.
sentence.1084: The strength of NetWalker’s reputation is such that our current hypothesis is that the individual behind Bugatti is most likely a well-respected and experienced cybercriminal, even though it is a new moniker.
sentence.1086: Bugatti advertising NetWalker on an underground forum Bugatti provides regular updates on the improvements in the ransomware, such as the popular Invoke-ReflectivePEInjection method, also commonly used by Sodinokibi.
sentence.1087: In addition to the improvements in the ransomware, open slots for new affiliates are advertised.
sentence.1088: Bugatti strongly emphasized that they are primarily looking for experienced affiliates that focus on compromising the complete networks of organizations as opposed to end users.
sentence.1089: NetWalker is clearly following in the footsteps of its illustrious targeted ransomware peers like Sodinokibi, Maze and Ryuk.
sentence.1090: One forum message in particular caught our attention as it included screenshots of several partial bitcoin addresses and USD amounts.
sentence.1091: This was most likely done to showcase the financial success of the ransomware.
sentence.1092: We have seen a similar posting in the past with the influential Sodinokibi affiliate Lalartu, so we decided to follow the money once more. Figure 24.
sentence.1093: Bugatti is looking for advanced affiliates and shows samples of BTC payments With the help of CipherTrace software we were able to find the complete BTC addresses from the screenshot and investigate the ledger further: Screenshot 1 3JHTYZhRmMcq7WCKRzFN98vWvAZk792w9J Screenshot 2 39aovzbz5rGoQdKjDm6JiybkSu1uGdVJ2V Screenshot 3 39NRnZtgACDVhhmc7RwmvH9ZDUKTNwwaeB Screenshot 4 3L4AW5kHnUCZBBjg2j1LBFCUN1RsHPLxCs Following the Money In the transactions mentioned in the underground forum post, the ransom amount payed by the victims is presumably shown.
sentence.1094: Since the bitcoin blockchain is a publicly accessible ledger, we can follow the money and see where the ransomware actors are transferring it to.
sentence.1095: In the case of the four posted transactions above, the full amount payed by the victim was transferred to two addresses (these addresses begin with bc1q98 and 1DgLhG respectively).
sentence.1096: It is safe to say that these two bitcoin addresses are under control of the NetWalker actors.
sentence.1097: We then proceeded on to analyze all incoming transactions to these two addresses and we were able to make the following observations: The first incoming transaction occurs on 1 March 2020.
sentence.1098: On 30 March 2020 the first incoming transaction appears where the amount is split between 4 different bitcoin addresses.
sentence.1099: A split like this is typically seen in Ransomware-as-a-Service, where the ransom payment is split between the RaaS operators and the affiliate who caused the infection.
sentence.1100: In this first transaction, the split is 80%, 10% and two 5% portions.
sentence.1101: This split matches the advertisement on the underground forum (80% – 20%).
sentence.1102: The two 5% portions of the ransom payments that are split, seem to be consistently transferred to the two bitcoin addresses we revealed earlier (bc1q98 and 1DgLhG).
sentence.1103: While the beneficiaries of the 5% cuts remain the same, the beneficiary of the 10% cut seems to change over time.
sentence.1104: Based on the forum post we assume these addresses also belong to the NetWalker actors.
sentence.1105: Payments to the bc1q98 and 1DgLhG addresses that are not being split continue up until the end of May.
sentence.1106: Possibly the initial NetWalker operators added a RaaS operation, while continuing to cause NetWalker infections themselves.
sentence.1107: While analyzing the bitcoin addresses that received 80% or more of the transaction amount, we noticed that there are some addresses that receive payments multiple times.
sentence.1108: A possible explanation could be that the address is configured as payout addresses for a certain campaign or affiliate.
sentence.1109: We identified 30 unique bitcoin addresses that seem to be the beneficiary of this larger portion of the ransom transaction.
sentence.1110: Some of these only received one payment but there are several that received multiple payments.
sentence.1111: In the two addresses uncovered by tracing the transactions a total of 641 bitcoin is held on 27 July 2020.
sentence.1112: Which at the current market value of bitcoin is worth well over 7 million USD.
sentence.1113: Amounts Extorted Working under the hypothesis that all the incoming transactions are ransomware payments; we can make the following observations: We found 23 transactions where the ransom payments were not split up and the beneficiaries are the two bitcoin addresses found by following the transactions mentioned in the underground forum post.
sentence.1114: The total amount of bitcoin extorted this way between 1 March 2020 and 27 July 2020 is 677 BTC.
sentence.1115: Additionally, the amount received from remaining transactions following the Ransomware-as-a-Service scheme by these addresses between 1 March 2020 and 27 July 2020 is 188 BTC.
sentence.1116: In the transactions that are split, the largest amount (usually 80% to 90% of the total transaction value) is presumably transferred to the affiliate that caused the infection.
sentence.1117: When we summed up these largest portions, we saw a total of 1723 BTC being transferred to affiliates.
sentence.1118: The total amount of extorted bitcoin that has been uncovered by tracing transactions to these NetWalker related addresses is 2795 BTC between 1 March 2020 and 27 July 2020.
sentence.1119: By using historic bitcoin to USD exchange rates, we estimate a total of 25 million USD was extorted with these NetWalker related transactions.
sentence.1120: Even though we do not have complete visibility into the BTC flow before NetWalker started ramping up, one thing is certain, this quarter alone it has been highly successful at extorting organisations for large amounts of money.
sentence.1121: All this at a time when many sectors are struggling because people are sheltering in place and governments are trying to keep businesses from going bankrupt.
sentence.1122: NetWalker is making millions off the backs of legitimate companies.
sentence.1124: Overview of uncovered bitcoin transactions, highlighting the two identified actor addresses.
sentence.1125: Observed Changes While talking about the impact of NetWalker with our partners, we learned that the change in modus operandi not only affected the way the actors communicate with their victims.
sentence.1126: When there was a change from email communication to a dedicated Tor hidden service, the actors also moved away from using legacy bitcoin addresses to SegWit addresses.
sentence.1127: The benefits of using the newer SegWit addresses include faster transaction time and lower transaction cost.
sentence.1128: The NetWalker advertisement on the underground forum mentions instant and fully automatic payments around the time of this observed change.
sentence.1129: This makes us believe the ransomware actors were professionalizing their operation just before expanding to the Ransomware-as-a-Service model.
sentence.1130: Comparison with Previous Ransomware Given the sudden appearance of NetWalker ransomware and the associated threat actor, it suggests that some prior knowledge on ransomware development or underground presence had to be in place.
sentence.1131: Armed with this hypothesis, we searched for possible links to underground actors and other ransomware strains that might fit the bill.
sentence.1132: We came across one threat actor offering ransomware that caught our attention.
sentence.1133: It was the use of the name NetWalker, in combination with a strong ransomware connection, that sparked our interest.
sentence.1134: Some years ago, a threat actor using the moniker Eriknetwalker was advertising ransomware on several underground forums.
sentence.1135: We found posts from 2016 and the latest public activity was around June 2019, several months before NetWalker ransomware made its appearance.
sentence.1137: Eriknetwalker began advertising their ransomware in 2016 (Google-translated from Russian)
sentence.1138: Based on our underground research, we linked the moniker Eriknetwalker to the development and<FILE_PATH> distribution of Amnesia, Bomber and Scarab ransomware.
sentence.1139: Eriknetwalker stopped advertising ransomware around June 2019.
sentence.1140: Therefore, we decided to perform a comparative analysis between the different ransomware strains linked to Eriknetwalker and some of the earliest versions of NetWalker we could find.
sentence.1141: The goal of this comparative analysis was to identify whether there was an overlap between source codes.
sentence.1142: Such overlap could suggest a stronger link between the current NetWalker version and the other ransomware versions from Eriknetwalker, possibly even explaining the name overlap.
sentence.1143: To execute the analysis, we used several tools one of which was the binary visualization tool Veles, which dynamically translates binary information into an abstract visualization that allows us to identify and compare patterns.
sentence.1144: The different types of ransomware we began analyzing were the variants of Amnesia, Scarab, and NetWalker.
sentence.1146: Flat visualization of binary data of the different ransomware variants Figure 28.
sentence.1147: 3D visualization of binary data of the different ransomware variants Visualizing data in such a manner is a way to use the human brain to quickly identify patterns and be able to draw comparisons between objects.
sentence.1148: In our case, we see that, based on the binary data visualized in Figures 27 and 28, the ransomware binaries do yield differences that we cannot ignore.
sentence.1150: Comparison of source code results Figure 29 shows the results of a source code similarity analysis led on the different variants of ransomware named in the figure itself.
sentence.1151: Interesting enough, Scarab and Amnesia show a higher overlap with Buran and Zeppelin than the early NetWalker samples.
sentence.1152: The percentages shown are the amount of code that is similar between two variants.
sentence.1153: As illustrated in the overview, the September 2019 NetWalker version has a different codebase from the ErikNetWalker-linked ransomware variants.
sentence.1154: This finding disproves our earlier hypothesis that NetWalker is linked to the older Amnesia variants based on code overlap.
sentence.1155: Often, research teams do not publish their results when it disproves their own hypothesis.
sentence.1156: However, for the sake of transparency, we decided to include our research efforts.
sentence.1157: YARA Rules We uploaded a YARA rule to detect almost all the samples observed in the wild to date.
sentence.1158: Indicators of Compromise During our investigation we have observed numerous IoCs linked to NetWalker ransomware.
sentence.1159: To obtain them please visit our McAfee ATR GitHub site, or get the latest NetWalker IoCs and intelligence on many other threats with McAfee Insights.
sentence.1161: The below techniques were based on our research and complemented with research from industry peers.

sentence.1169: Impact Data Encrypted (T1486): NetWalker Ransomware Inhibit System Recovery (T1490): Shadow Copies Deleted Service Stop (T1489) Conclusion Ransomware has evolved into a lucrative business for threat actors, from underground forums selling ransomware, to offering services such as support portals to guide victims through acquiring crypto currency for payment, to the negotiation of the ransom.
sentence.1170: McAfee’s Advanced Threat Research team has analysed the NetWalker ransomware and have been following its evolution from the initial sighting of the Mailto ransomware to its redevelopment into the NetWalker ransomware.
sentence.1171: The recent shift to a business-centric model of Ransomware-as-a-Service is a clear sign that it is stepping up, so it seems that the NetWalker group is following in the footsteps of REvil and other successful RaaS groups.
sentence.1172: The ransomware developers have proven the ability to refocus and capitalize on current world events and develop lures to help ensure the effectiveness of the ransomware, which has allowed them to become selective of their affiliates by limiting access to the ransomware to only those with vetted access to large organizations.
sentence.1173: As development of the ransomware continues, we have witnessed recent shifts in activity that closely follow in the footsteps of other ransomware developments, including threatening victims with the release of confidential information if the ransom is not met.

sentence.1181: title: Malicious OAuth applications used to compromise email servers and spread spam - Microsoft Security Blog url: <URL> Microsoft researchers recently investigated an attack where malicious OAuth applications were deployed on compromised cloud tenants and then used to control Exchange servers and spread spam.
sentence.1182: The investigation revealed that the threat actor launched credential stuffing attacks against high-risk accounts that didn’t have multi-factor authentication (MFA) enabled and leveraged the unsecured administrator accounts to gain initial access.
sentence.1183: The unauthorized access to the cloud tenant enabled the actor to create a malicious OAuth application that added a malicious inbound connector in the email server.
sentence.1184: The actor then used the malicious inbound connector to send spam emails that looked like they originated from the targets’ domain.
sentence.1185: The spam emails were sent as part of a deceptive sweepstakes scheme meant to trick recipients into signing up for recurring paid subscriptions.
sentence.1186: Microsoft has been monitoring the rising popularity of OAuth application abuse.
sentence.1187: One of the first observed malicious usage of OAuth applications in the wild is consent phishing.
sentence.1188: Consent phishing attacks aim to trick users into granting permissions to malicious OAuth apps to gain access to user’s legitimate cloud services (mail servers, <DATA_OBJECT> storage, management APIs, etc.).
sentence.1189: In the past few years, Microsoft has observed that more and more threat actors, including nation-state actors, have been using OAuth applications for different malicious purposes – command-and-control (C2) communication, backdoors, phishing, redirections, and so on.
sentence.1190: This recent attack involved a network of single-tenant applications installed in compromised organizations being used as the actor’s identity platform to perform the attack.
sentence.1191: As soon as the network was revealed, all the related applications were taken down and notifications to customers were sent, including recommended remediation steps.
sentence.1192: This blog presents the technical analysis of this attack vector and the succeeding spam campaign attempted by the threat actor.
sentence.1193: It also provides guidance for defenders on protecting organizations from this threat, and how Microsoft security technologies detect it. Figure 1.
sentence.1195: The time between application deployment and usage varied; there were cases where the actor took months before using the application.
sentence.1196: Initial access For the attack to succeed, the threat actor needed to compromise cloud tenant users with sufficient permissions that would allow the actor to create an application in the cloud environment and give it admin consent.
sentence.1197: The actor performed credential stuffing attacks against their targets, attempting to access users with the global admin role.
sentence.1198: The authentication attempts, which originated from a single IP address, were launched against the Azure Active Directory PowerShell application (app ID: 1b730954-1685-4b74-9bfd-dac224a7b894).
sentence.1199: The same application was later used to deploy the rest of the attack.
sentence.1200: Based on the success ratio of the authentication attempts, it is inferred that the attacker used a dump of compromised <DATA_OBJECT>.
sentence.1201: The investigation also revealed that 86% of the compromised tenants had at least one admin with a real-time high risk score, which means they were flagged by Azure AD Identity Protection to be most likely compromised.
sentence.1202: It is also important to note that all the compromised admins didn’t have MFA enabled, which could have stopped the attack.
sentence.1203: These observations amplify the importance of securing accounts and monitoring for high-risk users, especially those with high privileges.
sentence.1204: Deploying malicious OAuth application Once the threat actor gained access to privileged users, their next step was to set up the malicious application.
sentence.1205: Based on analysis of the event user agent (Swagger-Codegen<FILE_PATH>) and how quickly the deployment of the application was done, it is likely that the actor ran a PowerShell script to perform the following Azure Active Directory (AAD) management activities in all targeted tenants: Register a new single–tenant application with the naming convention of [domain name]_([a-zA-Z]){3} (for example: Contoso_GhY)Add the legacy permission <DOMAIN> which can be used for app-only authentication of Exchange Online PowerShell moduleGrant admin consent to the above permissionGive global admin and Exchange admin roles to the previously registered applicationAdd application <DATA_OBJECT> (key<FILE_PATH>) The threat actor added their own <DATA_OBJECT> to the OAuth application, which enabled them to access the application even if the initially compromised global administrator changed their <DATA_OBJECT>.
sentence.1206: The activities mentioned gave the threat actor control of a highly privileged application.
sentence.1207: It was observed that the threat actor did not always use the application right after it was deployed.
sentence.1208: In some cases, it took weeks or months before the application was utilized.
sentence.1209: Also, in organizations that didn’t monitor for suspicious applications, the applications were deployed for months and used multiple times by the threat actor.
sentence.1210: Modifying Exchange settings The threat actor used the privileged application to authenticate the Exchange Online PowerShell module and modify the Exchange settings of the compromised server.
sentence.1211: There were two modifications which allowed them to perform the next step in the attack chain: Create a new inbound connector Connectors are a collection of instructions that customize the way email flows to and from organizations using Microsoft 365 or Office 365.
sentence.1212: Most organizations using Microsoft 365 and Office 365 don’t need custom connectors for regular mail flow, but some use it when they need to process messages from another messaging system that’s not running Exchange, or if they have a network appliance that performs policy checks and then routes messages to their Exchange server.
sentence.1213: The threat actor set a new inbound connector with the naming convention Ran_([a-zA-Z]){5} (for example Ran_xAFzd).

sentence.1473: title: Threat Assessment: Black Basta Ransomware url: <URL> Executive Summary Black Basta is ransomware as a service (RaaS) that first emerged in April 2022.

sentence.1475: The Black Basta operator(s) use the double extortion technique, meaning that in addition to encrypting <DATA_OBJECT> on the systems of targeted organizations and demanding ransom to make decryption possible, they also maintain a dark web leak site where they threaten to post sensitive information if an organization chooses not to pay ransom.
sentence.1476: Black Basta affiliates have been very active deploying Black Basta and extorting organizations since the ransomware first emerged.
sentence.1477: Although the Black Basta affiliates have only been active for the past couple of months, based on the information posted on their leak site, they have compromised over 75 organizations at the time of this publication.

sentence.1630: title: Hafnium-inspired cyber-attacks neutralized by AI url: <URL> Amidst the ever-changing threat landscape, new tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) seem to emerge daily, creating extreme challenges for security teams.
sentence.1631: The broad range of attack methods utilized by attackers seems to present an insurmountable problem: how do you defend against a playbook that does not yet exist?Faced with the growing number of novel and uncommon attack methods, it is essential for organizations to adopt a security solution able to detect threats based on their anomalies, rather than relying on threat intelligence alone.
sentence.1632: In March 2023, Darktrace observed an emerging trend in the use of an application known as ‘PerfectData Software’ for probable malicious purposes in several Microsoft 365 account takeovers.
sentence.1633: Using its anomaly-based detection, Darktrace DETECT:trade_mark: was able to identify the activity chain surrounding the use of this application, potentially uncovering a novel piece of threat actor tradecraft in the process.
sentence.1634: Microsoft 365 IntrusionsIn recent years, Microsoft’s Software-as-a-Service (SaaS) suite, Microsoft 365, along with its built-in identity and access management (IAM) service, Azure Active Directory (Azure AD), have been heavily targeted by threat actors due to their near-ubiquitous usage across industries.
sentence.1635: Four out of every five Fortune 500 companies, for example, use Microsoft 365 services [1].
sentence.1636: Malicious actors typically gain entry to organizations’ Microsoft 365 environments by abusing either stolen account <DATA_OBJECT> or stolen session <DATA_OBJECT>
sentence.1638: Once inside, actors can access sensitive data within mailboxes or SharePoint repositories, and send out emails or Teams messages.
sentence.1639: This activity can often result in serious financial harm, especially in cases where the malicious actor’s end-goal is to elicit fraudulent transactions.
sentence.1640: Darktrace regularly observes malicious actors behaving in predictable ways once they gain access to customer Microsoft 365 environment.
sentence.1641: One typical example is the creation of new inbox rules and sending deceitful emails intended to convince recipients to carry out subsequent actions, such as following a malicious link or providing sensitive information.
sentence.1642: It is also common for actors to register new applications in Azure AD so that they can be used to conduct follow-up activities, like mass-mailing or data theft.
sentence.1643: The registration of applications in Azure AD therefore seems to be a relatively predictable threat actor behavior [3][4].
sentence.1644: Darktrace DETECT understands that unusual application registrations in Azure AD may constitute a deviation in expected behavior, and therefore a possible indicator of account compromise.
sentence.1645: These registrations of applications in Azure AD are evidenced by creations of, as well as assignments of permissions to, Service Principals in Azure AD.
sentence.1646: Darktrace has detected a growing trend in actors creating and assigning permissions to a Service Principal named ‘PerfectData Software’.
sentence.1647: Further investigation of this Azure AD activity revealed it to be part of an ongoing account takeover.
sentence.1648: ‘PerfectData Software’ Activity Darktrace observed variations of the following pattern of activity relating to an application named ‘PerfectData Software’ within its customer base:Actor signs in to a Microsoft 365 account from an endpoint associated with a Virtual Private Server (VPS) or Virtual Private Network (VPN) serviceActor registers an application called 'PerfectData Software' with Azure AD, and then grants permissions to the applicationActor accesses mailbox data and creates inbox rule In two separate incidents, malicious actors were observed conducting their activities from endpoints associated with VPN services (HideMyAss (HMA) VPN and Surfshark VPN, respectively) and from endpoints within the Autonomous System AS396073 MAJESTIC-HOSTING-01.
sentence.1649: In March 2023, Darktrace observed a malicious actor signing in to a Microsoft 365 account from a Kuwait-based IP address within the Autonomous System, AS198605 AVAST Software s.<FILENAME>.
sentence.1650: This IP address is associated with the VPN service, HMA VPN.
sentence.1651: Over the next couple of days, an actor (likely the same malicious actor) signed in to the account several more times from two different Nigeria-based endpoints, as well as a VPS-related endpoint and a HMA VPN endpoint.
sentence.1652: During their login sessions, the actor performed a variety of actions.
sentence.1653: First, they created and assigned permissions to a Service Principal named ‘PerfectData Software’.
sentence.1654: This Service Principal creation represents the registration of an application called ‘PerfectData Software’ in Azure AD.
sentence.1655: Although the reason for registering this application is unclear, within a few days the actor registered and granted permission to another application, ‘Newsletter Software Supermailer’, and created a new inbox rule names ‘s’ on the mailbox of the hijacked account.
sentence.1656: This inbox rule moved emails meeting certain conditions to a folder named ‘RSS Subscription.
sentence.1657: The ‘Newsletter Software Supermailer’ application was likely registered by the actor to facilitate mass-mailing activity.
sentence.1658: Immediately after these actions, Darktrace detected the actor sending out thousands of malicious emails from the account.
sentence.1659: The emails included an attachment named ‘Credit Transfer <DOMAIN>’, which contained a suspicious link.
sentence.1660: Further investigation revealed that the customer’s network had received several fake invoice emails prior to this initial intrusion activity.
sentence.1661: Additionally, there was an unusually high volume of failed logins to the compromised account around the time of the initial access.
sentence.1662: Figure 1: Advanced Search logs depicting the steps which the actor took after logging in to a user’s Microsoft 365 account.
sentence.1663: In a separate case also observed by Darktrace in March 2023, a malicious actor was observed signing in to a Microsoft 365 account from an endpoint within the Autonomous System, AS397086 LAYER-HOST-HOUSTON.
sentence.1664: The endpoint appears to be related to the VPN service, Surfshark VPN.
sentence.1665: This login was followed by several failed and successful logins from a VPS-related within the Autonomous System, AS396073 MAJESTIC-HOSTING-01.
sentence.1666: The actor was then seen registering and assigning permissions to an application called ‘PerfectData Software’.
sentence.1667: As with the previous example, the motives for this registration are unclear.
sentence.1668: The actor proceeded to log in several more times from a Surfshark VPN endpoint, however, they were not observed carrying out any further suspicious activity.
sentence.1669: Figure 2: Advanced Search logs depicting the steps which the actor took after logging in to a user’s Microsoft 365 account.
sentence.1670: It was not clear in either of these examples, nor in fact any of cases observed by Darktrace, why actors had registered and assigned permissions to an application called ‘PerfectData Software’, and there do not appear to be any open-source intelligence (OSINT) resources or online literature related to the malicious usage of an application by that name.
sentence.1671: That said, there are several websites which appear to provide email migration and data recovery<FILE_PATH> tools under the moniker ‘PerfectData Software’.
sentence.1672: It is unclear whether the use of ‘PerfectData Software’ by malicious actors observed on the networks of Darktrace customers was one of these tools.
sentence.1673: However, given the nature of the tools, it is possible that the actors intended to use them to facilitate the exfiltration of email data from compromises mailboxes.
sentence.1674: If the legitimate software ‘PerfectData’ is the application in question in these incidents, it is likely being purchased and misused by attackers for malicious purposes.
sentence.1675: It is also possible the application referenced in the incidents is a spoof of the legitimate ‘PerfectData’ software designed to masquerade a malicious application as legitimate.
sentence.1676: Darktrace CoverageCases of ‘PerfectData Software’ activity chains detected by Darktrace typically began with an actor signing into an internal user’s Microsoft 365 account from a VPN or VPS-related endpoint.
sentence.1677: These login events, along with the suspicious email and<FILE_PATH> brute-force activity which preceded them, caused the following DETECT models to breach:SaaS / Access / Unusual External Source for SaaS Credential UseSaaS / Access / Suspicious Login AttemptSaaS / Compromise / Login From Rare Following Suspicious Login Attempt(s)SaaS / Email Nexus / Unusual Location for SaaS and Email ActivitySubsequent activities, including inbox rule creations, registration of applications in Azure AD, and mass-mailing activity, resulted in breaches of the following DETECT models.
sentence.1678: SaaS / Admin / OAuth Permission Grant SaaS / Compromise / Unusual Logic Following OAuth Grant SaaS / Admin / New Application Service
sentence.1679: PrincipalIaaS / Admin / Azure Application Administration ActivitiesSaaS / Compliance / New Email RuleSaaS / Compromise / Unusual Login and New Email RuleSaaS / Email Nexus / Suspicious Internal Exchange ActivitySaaS / Email Nexus / Possible Outbound Email SpamSaaS / Compromise / Unusual Login and Outbound Email SpamSaaS / Compromise / Suspicious Login and Suspicious Outbound Email(s)Figure 3: DETECT Model Breaches highlighting unusual login and 'PerfectData Software' registration activity from a malicious actor.
sentence.1680: In cases where Darktrace RESPOND:trade_mark: was enabled in autonomous response mode, ‘PerfectData Software’ activity chains resulted in breaches of the following RESPOND models:• Antigena / SaaS / Antigena Suspicious SaaS Activity Block• Antigena / SaaS / Antigena Significant Compliance Activity BlockIn response to these model breaches, Darktrace RESPOND took immediate action, performing aggressive, inhibitive actions, such as forcing the actor to log out of the SaaS platform, and disabling the user entirely.
sentence.1681: When applied autonomously, these RESPOND actions would seriously impede an attacker’s progress and minimize network disruption.
sentence.1682: Figure 4: A RESPOND model breach created in response to a malicious actor's registration of 'PerfectData Software'In addition, Darktrace Cyber AI Analyst was able to autonomously investigate registrations of the ‘PerfectData Software’ application and summarized its findings into digestible reports.
sentence.1683: Figure 5: A Cyber AI Analyst Incident Event log showing AI Analyst autonomously pivoting off a breach of 'SaaS / Admin / OAuth Permission Grant' to uncover details of an account hijacking.
sentence.1684: Conclusion Due to the widespread adoption of Microsoft 365 services in the workplace and continued emphasis on a remote workforce, account hijackings now pose a more serious threat to organizations around the world than ever before.
sentence.1685: The cases discussed here illustrate the tendency of malicious actors to conduct their activities from endpoints associated with VPN services, while also registering new applications, like PerfectData Software, with malicious intent.
sentence.1686: While it was unclear exactly why the malicious actors were using ‘PerfectData Software’ as part of their account hijacking, it is clear that either the legitimate or spoofed version of the application is becoming an very likely emergent piece of threat actor tradecraft.
sentence.1687: Darktrace DETECT’s anomaly-based approach to threat detection allowed it to recognize that the use of ‘PerfectData Software’ represented a deviation in the SaaS user’s expected behavior.
sentence.1688: While Darktrace RESPOND, when enabled in autonomous response mode, was able to quickly take preventative action against threat actors, blocking the potential use of the application for data exfiltration or other nefarious purposes.

sentence.1692: title: eSentire Threat Intelligence Malware Analysis: BatLoader url: <URL> Since being introduced in February 2022, BatLoader is a malware dropper that has been observed dropping several well-known malware or malicious tools like ISFB, SystemBC RAT, Redline Stealer, and Vidar Stealer.
sentence.1693: Since its MSI installer <DATA_OBJECT> size is 100MB+, BatLoader can easily evade most sandboxes and antivirus tools.
sentence.1694: This malware analysis delves deeper into the technical details of how the BatLoader malware operates and our security recommendations to protect your organization from being exploited.
sentence.1695: Key Takeaways BatLoader delivers additional malware and tools including ISFB, Vidar Stealer, Cobalt Strike, Syncro RMM, and SystemBC RAT via fake <DOMAIN> Threat Response Unit (TRU) observed two different BatLoader campaigns in <DOMAIN> can evade most antivirus detections due to the size of the MSI installers.
