sentence.1855: title: Early Bird Catches the Wormhole: Observations from the StellarParticle Campaign url: <URL> StellarParticle is a campaign tracked by CrowdStrike as related to the SUNSPOT implant from the SolarWinds intrusion in December 2020 and associated with COZY BEAR (aka APT29, “The Dukes”).
sentence.1856: The StellarParticle campaign has continued against multiple organizations, with COZY BEAR using novel tools and techniques to complete their objectives, as identified by CrowdStrike incident responders and the CrowdStrike Intelligence team.
sentence.1857: Browser <DATA_OBJECT> theft and Microsoft Service Principal manipulation are two of the novel techniques and tools leveraged in the StellarParticle campaign and are discussed in this blog.
sentence.1858: Two sophisticated malware families were placed on victim systems in mid-2019: a Linux variant of GoldMax and a new implant dubbed TrailBlazer.
sentence.1859: Supply chain compromises are an increasing threat that impacts a range of sectors, with threat actors leveraging access to support several motivations including financial gain (such as with the Kaseya ransomware attack) and espionage.
sentence.1860: Throughout 2020, an operation attributed to the Foreign Intelligence Service of the Russian Federation (SVR) by the U.S. government was conducted to gain access to the update mechanism of the SolarWinds IT management software and use it to broaden their intelligence collection capabilities.
sentence.1861: This activity is tracked by CrowdStrike as the StellarParticle campaign and is associated with the COZY BEAR adversary group.
sentence.1862: This blog discusses the novel tactics and techniques leveraged in StellarParticle investigations conducted by CrowdStrike.
sentence.1863: These techniques include: Credential hopping for obscuring lateral movement Office 365 (O365) Service Principal and Application hijacking, impersonation and manipulation Stealing browser <DATA_OBJECT> for bypassing multifactor authentication Use of the TrailBlazer implant and the Linux variant of GoldMax malware Credential theft using Get-ADReplAccount Credential Hopping The majority of StellarParticle-related investigations conducted by CrowdStrike have started with the identification of adversary actions within a victim’s O365 environment.
sentence.1864: This has been advantageous to CrowdStrike incident responders in that, through investigating victim O365 environments, they could gain an accurate accounting of time, account and source IP address of adversary victimization of the O365 tenant.
sentence.1865: In multiple engagements, this led CrowdStrike incident responders to identify that the malicious authentications into victim O365 tenants had originated from within the victim’s own network.
sentence.1866: Armed with this information, CrowdStrike investigators were able to identify from which systems in these internal networks the threat actor was making authentications to O365.
sentence.1867: These authentications would typically occur from servers in the environment, leading to natural investigative questions: Why would a user authenticate into O365 from a domain controller or other infrastructure server?
sentence.1868: What <DATA_OBJECT> were used as part of the session from which the O365 authentication occurred?
sentence.1869: This led our responders to identify the occurrence of “credential hopping,” where the threat actor leveraged different <DATA_OBJECT> for each step while moving laterally through the victim’s network.
sentence.1870: While this particular technique is not necessarily unique to the StellarParticle campaign, it indicates a more advanced threat actor and may go unnoticed by a victim.
sentence.1871: Below is an example of how a threat actor performs credential hopping: Gain access to the victim’s network by logging into a public-facing system via Secure Shell (<PROTOCOL>) using a local account <user <PROTOCOL>> acquired during previous credential theft activities.
sentence.1872: Use port forwarding capabilities built into <PROTOCOL> on the public-facing system to establish a Remote Desktop Protocol (<PROTOCOL>) session to an internal server (Server 1) using a domain service account.
sentence.1873: From Server 1, establish another <PROTOCOL> session to a different internal server (Server 2) using a domain administrator’s account.
sentence.1874: Log in to O365 as a user with privileged access to cloud resources.
sentence.1876: Example of “credential hopping” technique This technique could be hard to identify in environments where defenders have little visibility into identity usage.
sentence.1877: In the example shown in Figure 1, the threat actor leveraged a service interactively, which should generate detections for defenders to investigate.
sentence.1878: However, the threat actor could have easily used a second domain administrator account or any other combination of accounts that would not be easily detected.
sentence.1879: A solution such as CrowdStrike Falcon:registered: Identity Threat Detection would help identify these anomalous logons — and especially infrequent destinations for accounts.
sentence.1880: (Read how CrowdStrike incident responders leverage the module in investigations in this blog: <DATA_OBJECT>, Authentications and Hygiene: Supercharging Incident Response with Falcon Identity Threat Detection.)
sentence.1881: But how had the threat actor succeeded in authenticating into victim O365 tenants, when multifactor authentication (MFA) had been enabled for every O365 user account at each victim organization investigated by CrowdStrike? <DATA_OBJECT> Theft to Bypass MFA Even though the victims required MFA to access cloud resources from all locations, including on premises, the threat actor managed to bypass MFA through the theft of Chrome browser <DATA_OBJECT>.
sentence.1882: The threat actor accomplished this by using administrative accounts to connect via <PROTOCOL> to targeted users, and then copy their Chrome profile directories as well as data protection API (DPAPI) data.
sentence.1883: In Windows, Chrome <DATA_OBJECT> and saved passwords are encrypted using DPAPI.
sentence.1884: The user-specific encryption keys for DPAPI are stored under <FILE_PATH><user>\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Protect\. To leverage these encryption keys, the threat actor must first decrypt them, either by using the user account’s Windows <DATA_OBJECT>, or, in Active Directory environments, by using a DPAPI domain backup key that is stored on domain controllers.
sentence.1885: Once the threat actor had a Chrome <DATA_OBJECT> <DATA_OBJECT> from a user that had already passed an MFA challenge recently (for example, a timeout was 24 hours), they decrypted the <DATA_OBJECT> <DATA_OBJECT> using the user’s DPAPI key.
sentence.1886: The <DATA_OBJECT> were then added to a new session using a “<DATA_OBJECT> Editor” Chrome extension that the threat actor installed on victim systems and removed after using.
sentence.1887: Shellbags, Falcon Telemetry and <PROTOCOL> Bitmap Cache From a forensic standpoint, the use of the <DATA_OBJECT> Editor Chrome extension would have been challenging to identify, due to the threat actor’s penchant for strict operational security.
sentence.1888: This activity was identified via a NewScriptWritten event within Falcon when a JavaScript <DATA_OBJECT> was written to disk by a threat actor-initiated Chrome process.
sentence.1889: This event captured the unique extension ID associated with the extension, thereby allowing CrowdStrike incident responders to validate via the Chrome Store that the JavaScript <DATA_OBJECT> was associated with the “<DATA_OBJECT> Editor” plugin.
sentence.1890: This extension permitted bypassing MFA requirements, as the <DATA_OBJECT>, replayed through the <DATA_OBJECT> Editor extension, allowed the threat actor to hijack the already MFA-approved session of a targeted user.
sentence.1891: Shellbags were also instrumental in identifying the <DATA_OBJECT> theft activity.
sentence.1892: This artifact very clearly showed the threat actor accessing targeted users’ machines in sequence and browsing to the Chrome and DPAPI directories one after another.
sentence.1893: Parsing Shellbags for an administrative account leveraged by the threat actor resulted in entries similar to the below.
sentence.1895: Shellbag artifacts showing targeting of Chrome directories CrowdStrike identified forensic evidence that showed the entire attack path: browsing to a target user’s Chrome and DPAPI directories via administrative share, installing the <DATA_OBJECT> Editor extension, and using Chrome to impersonate the targeted user in the victim’s cloud tenants.
sentence.1896: The decryption of the <DATA_OBJECT> is believed to have taken place offline after exfiltrating the data via the <DATA_OBJECT> in the threat actor’s <PROTOCOL> session.
sentence.1898: Representation of lateral movement to <DATA_OBJECT> theft to O365 authentication CrowdStrike identified a similar TTP where the threat actor connected via <PROTOCOL> to a user’s workstation with the workstation owner’s account (e.g., connecting via <PROTOCOL> to user1-pc using the account user1).
sentence.1899: In cases where the user had only locked their <DATA_OBJECT> and not signed out, the threat actor was able to take over the user’s Windows session, as the <PROTOCOL> session would connect to the existing session of the same user.
sentence.1900: By examining <PROTOCOL> Bitmap Cache <DATA_OBJECT>, CrowdStrike was able to demonstrate that the threat actor had opened Chrome and exported all of the user’s saved passwords as plaintext in a CSV <DATA_OBJECT> during these sessions.
sentence.1901: Figure 4. <PROTOCOL> Bitmap Cache reconstruction showing exportation of Chrome passwords In addition, the threat actor visited sensitive websites that the user had access to, which in one instance allowed them to browse and download a victim’s customer list.
sentence.1902: After this, the threat actor navigated to the user’s Chrome history page and deleted the specific history items related to threat actor activity, leaving the rest of the user’s Chrome history intact.
sentence.1903: O365 Delegated Administrator Abuse CrowdStrike also identified a connection between StellarParticle-related campaigns and the abuse of Microsoft Cloud Solution Partners’ O365 tenants.
sentence.1904: This threat actor abused access to accounts in the Cloud Solution Partner’s environment with legitimate delegated administrative privileges to then gain access to several customers’ O365 environments.
sentence.1905: By analyzing Azure AD sign-ins, CrowdStrike was able to use known indicators of compromise (IOCs) to identify several threat actor logins to customer environments.
sentence.1906: These cross-tenant sign-ins were identified by looking for values in the resourceTenantId attribute that did not match the Cloud Solution Partner’s own Azure tenant ID.
sentence.1907: CrowdStrike also identified a limitation within Microsoft’s Delegated Administration capabilities for Microsoft Cloud Solution Partners.
sentence.1908: While a normal O365 administrator can be provided dozens of specific administrative roles to limit the privileges granted, this same degree of customization cannot be applied to Microsoft Cloud Solution Partners that use the delegated administrator functionality in O365.
sentence.1909: For Microsoft Cloud Solution Partners, there are only two substantial administrative options today when managing a customer’s environment, Admin agent or Helpdesk agent.2
sentence.1910: The Helpdesk agent role provides very limited access that is equivalent to a <DATA_OBJECT> admin role, whereas the Admin agent role provides broad access more equivalent to global administrator.
sentence.1911: This limitation is scheduled to be resolved in 2022 via Microsoft’s scheduled feature, Granular Delegated Admin Privileges (GDAP).3 User Access Logging (UAL)
sentence.1912: The Windows User Access Logging (UAL) database is an extremely powerful artifact that has played an instrumental role in the investigation of StellarParticle-linked cases.
sentence.1913: In particular, UAL has helped our responders identify earlier malicious account usage that ultimately led to the identification of the aforementioned TrailBlazer implant and Linux version of the GoldMax variant.
sentence.1914: The UAL database is available by default on Server editions of Windows starting with Server 2012.
sentence.1915: This database stores historical information on user access to various services (or in Windows parlance, Roles) on the server for up to three years (three years minus one day) by default.
sentence.1916: UAL contains information on the type of service accessed, the user that accessed the service and the source IP address from which the access occurred.
sentence.1917: One of the most useful roles recorded by UAL is the <DATA_OBJECT> Server role, which includes <PROTOCOL> access, though other role types can also be very helpful.
sentence.1918: An overview of UAL, what information it contains and how it can be leveraged in forensic investigations can be found here.
sentence.1919: In multiple StellarParticle-related cases, because the threat actor used the same set of accounts during their operations in the environment, CrowdStrike was able to identify previous malicious activity going back multiple years, based solely on UAL data.
sentence.1920: Even though it’s only available on Server 2012 and up, UAL can still be used to trace evidence of threat actor activity on legacy systems as long as the activity on the legacy system involves some (deliberate or unintentional) access to a 2012+ system.
sentence.1921: For example, in addition to tracking <PROTOCOL> activity, UAL databases on Domain Controllers track Active Directory access.
sentence.1922: This allowed CrowdStrike to demonstrate that a given user account was also authenticating to Active Directory from a given source IP address two years prior.
sentence.1923: Because the user account was known to have recently been abused by the threat actor, and the source IP of the system in question was not one that account would typically be active on, the investigation led to the source system and ultimately resulted in the timeline of malicious activity being pushed back by years, with additional compromised systems even being discovered still running unique malware from that time period.
sentence.1924: TrailBlazer and GoldMax Throughout StellarParticle-related investigations, CrowdStrike has identified two sophisticated malware families that were placed on victim systems in the mid-2019 timeframe: a Linux variant of GoldMax and a completely new family CrowdStrike refers to as TrailBlazer.
sentence.1925: TrailBlazer Attempted to blend in with a <DATA_OBJECT> name that matched the system name it resided on Configured for WMI persistence (generally uncommon in 2019) Used likely compromised infrastructure for C2 Masquerades its command-and-control (C2) traffic as legitimate Google Notifications <PROTOCOL> requests TrailBlazer is a sophisticated malware family that provides modular functionality and a very low prevalence.
sentence.1926: The malware shares high-level functionality with other malware families.
sentence.1927: In particular, the use of random identifier strings for C2 operations and result codes, and attempts to hide C2 communications in seemingly legitimate web traffic, were previously observed tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs) in GoldMax and SUNBURST.
sentence.1928: TrailBlazer persists on a compromised host using WMI event subscriptions4 — a technique also used by SeaDuke — although this persistence mechanism is not exclusive to COZY BEAR.5 WMI event filter SELECT * FROM __
sentence.1932: SystemUpTime < 480 WMI Event consumer (CommandLineTemplate) <FILE_PATH> <DATA_OBJECT> (x86)\Common <DATA_OBJECT>\Adobe\<FILENAME>.exe Filter to consumer binding CommandLineEventConsumer.
sentence.1934: TrailBlazer WMI Persistence In the obfuscated example above, TrailBlazer (<FILENAME>.exe) would be executed when the system’s uptime was between 180 and 480 seconds.
sentence.1935: GoldMax (Linux variant) Attempted to blend in with a <DATA_OBJECT> name that matched the system name it resided on Configured for persistence via a crontab entry with a @reboot line Used likely compromised infrastructure for C2 GoldMax was first observed during post-exploitation activity in the campaign leveraging the SolarWinds supply chain attacks.
sentence.1936: Previously identified samples of GoldMax were built for the Windows platform, with the earliest identified timestamp indicating a compilation in May 2020, but a recent CrowdStrike investigation discovered a GoldMax variant built for the Linux platform that the threat actor deployed in mid-2019.
sentence.1937: This variant extends the backdoor’s known history and shows that the threat actor has used the malware in post-exploitation activity targeting other platforms than Windows.
sentence.1938: The 2019 Linux variant of the GoldMax backdoor is almost identical in functionality and implementation to the previously identified May 2020 Windows variant.
sentence.1939: The very few additions to the backdoor between 2019 and 2020 likely reflect its maturity and longstanding evasion of detections.
sentence.1940: It is likely GoldMax has been used as a long-term persistence backdoor during StellarParticle-related compromises, which would be consistent with the few changes made to the malware to modify existing functions or support additional functionality.
sentence.1941: Persistence was established via a crontab entry for a non-root user.
sentence.1942: With the binary named to masquerade as a legitimate <DATA_OBJECT> on the system and placed in a hidden directory, a crontab entry was created with a @reboot line so the GoldMax binary would execute again upon system reboot.
sentence.1943: Additionally, the threat actor used the nohup command to ignore any hangup signals, and the process will continue to run even if the terminal session was terminated.
sentence.1945: Crontab entry for GoldMax persistence Enumeration Tools<FILE_PATH> Directory Structure Throughout our StellarParticle investigations, CrowdStrike identified what appeared to be a VBScript-based Active Directory enumeration toolkit.
sentence.1946: While the script’s contents have not been recovered to date, CrowdStrike has observed identical artifacts across multiple StellarParticle engagements that suggest the same or similar tool was used.
sentence.1947: In each instance the tool was used, Shellbags data indicated that directories with random names of a consistent length were navigated to by the same user that ran the tool.
sentence.1948: After two levels of randomly named directories, Shellbags proved the existence of subdirectories named after the FQDNs for the victims’ various domains.
sentence.1949: In addition, the randomly named directories are typically created in a previously existing directory that’s one level off of the root of the C drive.
sentence.1950: The randomly named directories have a consistent length where the first directory is six characters and the next directory is three characters.
sentence.1951: To date, the names of the directories have always been formed from lowercase alphanumeric characters.
sentence.1952: For example, Shellbags indicated that directories matching the naming patterns below were browsed to (where “XX” is a previously existing directory on the system): <FILE_PATH>]{6} <FILE_PATH>]{6}\[a-z0-9]{3} <FILE_PATH>]{6}\[a-z0-9]{3}\domain.
sentence.1954: In each case, immediately prior to the creation of the directories referenced above, there was evidence of execution of a VBScript <DATA_OBJECT> by the same user that browsed to the directories.
sentence.1955: This evidence typically came from a UserAssist entry for <FILENAME>, as well as RecentApps entries for <FILENAME> (that would also include the VBScript filename).
sentence.1956: In addition, the Jump List for <FILENAME> contained evidence of the VBScript <DATA_OBJECT>.
sentence.1957: The name of the VBScript <DATA_OBJECT> varied across engagements and was generally designed to look fairly innocuous and blend in.
sentence.1959: Due to the subdirectories that are named after the FQDNs for victim domains, CrowdStrike assesses with moderate confidence that the scripts represent an AD enumeration tool used by the adversary.
sentence.1960: Internal Wiki Access Across multiple StellarParticle investigations, CrowdStrike identified unique reconnaissance activities performed by the threat actor: access of victims’ internal knowledge repositories.6 Wikis are commonly used across industries to facilitate knowledge sharing and as a source of reference for a variety of topics.
sentence.1961: While operating in the victim’s internal network, the threat actor accessed sensitive information specific to the products and services that the victim organization provided.
sentence.1962: This information included items such as product<FILE_PATH> architecture and design documents, vulnerabilities and step-by-step instructions to perform various tasks.
sentence.1963: Additionally, the threat actor viewed pages related to internal business operations such as development schedules and points of contact.
sentence.1964: In some instances these points of contact were subsequently targeted for further data collection.
sentence.1965: The threat actor’s wiki access could be considered an extension of “Credential Hopping” described earlier.
sentence.1966: The threat actor established <PROTOCOL> sessions to internal servers using privileged accounts and then accessed the wiki using a different set of <DATA_OBJECT>.
sentence.1967: CrowdStrike observed the threat actor accessing the wiki as users who would be considered “non-privileged” from an Active Directory perspective but had access to sensitive data specific to the victim’s products or services.
sentence.1968: At this time, the malicious access of internal wikis is an information gathering technique that CrowdStrike has only observed in StellarParticle investigations.
sentence.1969: CrowdStrike was able to identify the wiki access primarily through forensic analysis of the internal systems used by the threat actor.
sentence.1970: Given the threat actor’s penchant for clearing browser data, organizations should not rely upon the availability of these artifacts for future investigations.
sentence.1971: CrowdStrike recommends the following best practices for internal information repositories: Enable detailed access logging Ensure logs are centralized and stored for at least 180 days Create detections for anomalous activity such as access from an unusual location like a server subnet Enable MFA on the repository site, or provide access via Single Sign On (SSO) behind MFA O365 Built-in Service Principal Hijacking The threat actor connected via Remote Desktop from a Domain Controller to a vCenter server and opened a PowerShell console, then used the PowerShell command -ep bypass to circumvent the execution policy.
sentence.1972: Using the Windows Azure Active Directory PowerShell Module, the threat actor connected to the victim’s O365 tenant and began performing enumeration queries.
sentence.1973: These queries were recorded in text-based logs that existed under the path <FILE_PATH><user>\AppData\Local\Microsoft\Office365\Powershell\. Similar logs (for Azure AD instead of O365) can be found under the path:
sentence.1974: <FILE_PATH><user>\AppData\Local\Microsoft\AzureAD\Powershell\. While the logs didn’t include what data was returned by the queries, they did provide some insight such as the user account used to connect to the victim’s O365 tenant (which was not the same as the user the threat actor used to <PROTOCOL> to the vCenter server).
sentence.1975: The logs contained commands issued and the count of the results returned for a specific command.
sentence.1976: The commands included enumeration queries such as: ListAccountSkus ListPartnerContracts ListServicePrincipals ListServicePrincipalCredentials ListRoles ListRoleMembers ListUsers ListDomains GetRoleMember GetPartnerInformation GetCompanyInformation In this case, however, the most significant and concerning log entry was one that indicated the command AddServicePrincipalCredentials was executed.
sentence.1977: By taking the timestamp that the command was executed via the PowerShell logs on the local system, CrowdStrike analyzed the configuration settings in the victim’s O365 tenant and discovered that a new secret had been added to a built-in Microsoft Azure AD Enterprise Application, Microsoft StaffHub Service Principal, which had Application level permissions.
sentence.1978: Further, the newly added secret was set to remain valid for more than a decade.
sentence.1979: This data was acquired by exporting the secrets and certificates details for each Azure AD Enterprise Application.
sentence.1980: The Service Principal (now renamed to Microsoft Teams Shifts) had the following permissions at the time the configuration settings were collected: Member.
sentence.1995: All CrowdStrike was unable to find Microsoft documentation, but based on open-source research,7 this application likely had the following permissions around the time of registration: Mail.
sentence.1999: All The most notable permissions above are the Mail.
sentence.2003: These permissions would allow the threat actor to use the Microsoft Staffhub service principal to read all mail and SharePoint<FILE_PATH> <DATA_OBJECT> in the organization, as well as create new accounts and assign administrator privileges to any account in the organization.
sentence.2004: By running the commands from within the victim’s environment, MFA requirements were bypassed due to conditional access policies not covering Service Principal sign-ins at this point of time.8 However, as explained earlier, the threat actor managed to continue to access the victim’s cloud environment even when the victim enforced MFA for all connections regardless of source.
sentence.2005: While the bulk of the evidence for this activity came from the text-based O365 PowerShell logs, the <DOMAIN> <DATA_OBJECT> hive for the user that was running the PowerShell cmdlets also included information on the accounts that were used to authenticate to the cloud.
sentence.2006: This information was stored under the <DATA_OBJECT> path.
sentence.2007: Below is an example of the <DATA_OBJECT> data: Figure 6.
sentence.2008: Example <DATA_OBJECT> entry showing target O365 email accounts The same WSMan connection string was also located in the user’s <DOMAIN> <DATA_OBJECT> hive under the path: Figure 7.
sentence.2009: WSMan connection string <DATA_OBJECT> location While not strictly related to the O365 PowerShell activity, the Windows Event Log Microsoft-Windows-WinRM%<DOMAIN> also included information on connection attempts made to external O365 tenants.
sentence.2010: This information was logged under Event ID 6.
sentence.2011: Below is an example of what the event included: Figure 8.
sentence.2012: Windows Event Log entry showing connection to O365 tenants O365 Company Service Principal Manipulation
sentence.2013: The threat actor also deployed several layers of persistence utilizing both pre-existing and threat actor-created Service Principals with the ultimate goal of gaining global access to email.
sentence.2014: Attacker-created Service Principal First, the threat actor used a compromised O365 administrator account to create a new Service Principal with a generic name.
sentence.2015: This Service Principal was granted company administrator privileges.
sentence.2016: From there, the threat actor added a credential to this Service Principal so that they could access the Service Principal directly, without use of an O365 user account.
sentence.2017: These actions were recorded in Unified Audit Logs with the following three operation names: Add service principal Add member to role Add service principal <DATA_OBJECT>.
sentence.2018: Update Service Principal Company-Created Service Principal Hijacking Next, the threat actor utilized the threat actor-created Service Principal to take control of a second Service Principal.
sentence.2019: This was done by adding <DATA_OBJECT> to this second Service Principal, which was legitimately created by the company.
sentence.2020: This now compromised company-created Service Principal had <DOMAIN> graph permissions consented on behalf of all users within the tenant.
sentence.2021: This action was recorded by just one operation type in Unified Audit Logs.
sentence.2022: This operation type is named Add service principal <DATA_OBJECT>.
sentence.2024: Read Service Principal Abuse Finally, the threat actor utilized the compromised Service Principal with the assigned <DOMAIN> permissions to then read emails of several different users in the company’s environment.
sentence.2025: CrowdStrike was able to use the Unified Audit Logs’ (UAL) MailItemsAccessed operation events to see the exact emails the threat actor viewed, as the majority of the users in the tenant were assigned O365 E5 licenses.
sentence.2026: When performing analysis on the UAL, CrowdStrike used the ClientAppId value within the MailItemsAccessed operation and cross-correlated with the Application ID of the compromised service principal to see what activities were performed by the threat actor.
sentence.2027: O365 Application Impersonation Another consistent TTP identified during StellarParticle investigations has been the abuse of the ApplicationImpersonation9 role.
sentence.2028: When this role was assigned to a particular user that was controlled by the threat actor, it allowed the threat actor to impersonate any user within the O365 environment.
sentence.2029: These impersonated events are not logged verbosely by the Unified Audit Logs and can be difficult to detect.
sentence.2030: While the assignment of these ApplicationImpersonation roles were not logged in the Unified Audit Logs, CrowdStrike was able to identify this persistence mechanism via the management role configuration settings, which can be exported with the Exchange PowerShell command: Get-ManagementRoleAssignment -Role ApplicationImpersonation.
sentence.2031: CrowdStrike then analyzed the exported configuration settings and identified several users (not service accounts) that the threat actor likely gave direct ApplicationImpersonation roles during the known periods of compromise.
sentence.2032: Remote Tasklist The threat actor attempted to remotely list running processes on systems using <FILENAME>.
sentence.2033: As tasklist uses WMI “under the hood,” this activity was captured by Falcon as SuspiciousWmiQuery events that included the query and the source system.
sentence.2034: Additionally, the failed (not successful) process listing resulted in a DCOM error that was logged in the <DOMAIN> event log under Event ID 10028.
sentence.2035: A sample of the information included with this event is below: Figure 9.
sentence.2036: Event ID 10028 showing failed execution of remote tasklist This remote process listing was consistently used by the threat actor targeting the same or similar lists of remote systems, and the owners of the targeted systems also happened to be the individuals with cloud access that the threat actor was interested in.
sentence.2037: While unproven, it’s possible the threat actor was running tasklist remotely on these systems specifically to see which of the target systems was running Google Chrome.
sentence.2038: This is because a current or recent Chrome session to the victim’s cloud tenants would be potentially beneficial in the hijacking of sessions that the threat actor performed in order to access the victim’s cloud resources.
sentence.2040: In one instance, after being evicted from a victim environment, the threat actor began probing external services as a means to regain access, initially focusing on (S)<PROTOCOL> servers that were internet-accessible.
sentence.2041: Logs on the servers indicated that the threat actor attempted to log in with multiple valid accounts and in several cases was successful.
sentence.2042: There was little to no activity during the (S)<PROTOCOL> sessions.
sentence.2043: This likely was an exercise in attempting to identify misconfigured (S)<PROTOCOL> accounts that also had shell access, similar to what’s described in the Credential Hopping section earlier.
sentence.2044: Some of the accounts used were not in the victim’s Active Directory, as these were accounts for customers of the victim and stored in a separate <PROTOCOL> database.
sentence.2045: However, the threat actor had knowledge of these accounts and used them on the correct systems, which further confirmed that the threat actor had advanced knowledge of the victim’s environment.
sentence.2046: After confirming the <PROTOCOL> accounts did not provide shell access into the environment, the threat actor began attempting to connect into the environment via VPN.
sentence.2047: The threat actor attempted to log in to the VPN using several user accounts but was prevented from connecting, either due to not having the correct <DATA_OBJECT>, or due to having the correct <DATA_OBJECT> but not getting past the recently implemented MFA requirement.
sentence.2048: Eventually, the threat actor attempted an account that they had the correct <DATA_OBJECT> for but that had not been set up with MFA.
sentence.2049: This resulted in a prompt being displayed to the threat actor that included an MFA setup link.
sentence.2050: The threat actor subsequently set up MFA for the account and successfully connected to the victim’s network via VPN.
sentence.2051: TA Masquerading of System Names During the attempted and successful VPN authentications described above, the threat actor ensured the hostname of their system matched the naming convention of hostnames in the victim’s environment.
sentence.2052: This again showed a strong knowledge of the victim’s internal environment on the part of the threat actor.
sentence.2053: Not only did the masqueraded hostnames follow the correct naming convention from a broad perspective, they were also valid in terms of what would be expected for the user account the threat actor leveraged (i.e., in terms of the site name and asset type indicated in the hostname).
sentence.2054: This masqueraded hostname technique has been observed at multiple StellarParticle-related investigations.
sentence.2056: In one example, the threat actor connected into the victim’s environment via a VPN endpoint that did not have MFA enabled.
sentence.2057: Once connected to the VPN, the threat actor connected via Remote Desktop to a Domain Controller and copied the DSInternals10 PowerShell module to the system.
sentence.2058: The threat actor subsequently ran the DSInternals command Get-ADReplAccount targeting two of the victim’s domains.
sentence.2059: This command uses the Microsoft Directory Replication Service (MS-DRSR) protocol and specifically the IDL_DRSGetNCChanges method to return account information from Active Directory such as the current NTLM <DATA_OBJECT> hashes and previous <DATA_OBJECT> hashes used for enforcing <DATA_OBJECT> reuse restrictions.

sentence.2066: Get-ADReplAccount example output When executing the Get-ADReplAccount command, the threat actor specified the AD context to be targeted via the NamingContext parameter.
sentence.2067: This was necessary, as the threat actor was targeting multiple domains.
sentence.2068: The resulting output of each command was redirected to a text <DATA_OBJECT> and compressed as zip archives before exfiltration.
sentence.2069: The fact that Get-ADReplAccount command includes not only the current NTLM hashes but also the hash history (i.e., hashes of previous passwords used by a user account) meant that the threat actor also had the ability to discover accounts that either reused the same passwords or used similar passwords when the account <DATA_OBJECT> was changed.
sentence.2070: Credential Refresh On some investigations, the dwell time of the threat actor spanned years.
sentence.2071: Given this extended period, it is logical to assume that some <DATA_OBJECT> obtained by the threat actor would be rotated during normal business operations.
sentence.2072: To combat this, the threat actor periodically “refreshed” their credential set by performing credential theft activities in an already compromised environment.
sentence.2073: At one victim, CrowdStrike identified multiple instances of domain credential theft months apart, each time with a different credential theft technique.
sentence.2074: One of the credential theft techniques identified by CrowdStrike was the use of a PowerShell script to execute Mimikatz in-memory.
sentence.2075: While in-memory Mimikatz is not particularly unique, the script executed by the threat actor was heavily obfuscated and encrypted the output using AES256.
sentence.2076: CrowdStrike was able to reconstruct the PowerShell script from the PowerShell Operational event log as the script’s execution was logged automatically due to the use of specific keywords.
sentence.2077: CrowdStrike recommends that organizations upgrade PowerShell on their systems, as this functionality is only available with PowerShell version 5 and above.
sentence.2078: In addition to refreshing the threat actor’s <DATA_OBJECT>, the threat actor would also refresh their understanding of the victim’s AD environment.
sentence.2079: Around the time when the threat actor executed Get-ADReplAccount, the threat actor also executed a renamed version of AdFind to output domain reconnaissance information.
sentence.2080: In this instance, AdFind was renamed to masquerade as a legitimate Windows binary.
sentence.2081: The usage of renamed AdFind is consistent with other industry reporting on this campaign.
sentence.2082: In addition to using scripted commands, operators were repeatedly observed manually executing several standard PowerShell cmdlets to enumerate network information from AD, including Get-ADUser and Get-ADGroupMember to query specific members in the directory.
sentence.2083: This information provided the adversary with a list of accounts possessing particular privileges — in this case, the ability to make VPN connections — that would be subject to later credential stealing attempts and leveraged to access the victim at a later time.
sentence.2085: In some cases, the threat actor was able to quickly return to the environment and essentially pick up where they left off, even though the organization had performed an enterprise-wide <DATA_OBJECT> reset, including a reset of all service accounts and the double-reset of the krbtgt account.
sentence.2086: CrowdStrike determined that in these cases, administrative users had “reset” their own <DATA_OBJECT> to the same <DATA_OBJECT> they previously used, essentially nullifying the impact of the enterprise-wide reset.
sentence.2087: This was possible even though the customer’s Active Directory was configured to require new passwords to be different from the previous five passwords for a given account.
sentence.2088: Unfortunately, this check only applies when a user is changing their <DATA_OBJECT> via the “<DATA_OBJECT> change” method — but if a “<DATA_OBJECT> reset” is performed (changing the <DATA_OBJECT> without knowing the previous <DATA_OBJECT>), this check is bypassed for an administrative user or a Windows account that has the Reset <DATA_OBJECT> permission on a user’s account object.12 Since the Get-ADReplAccount cmdlet described above included the NTHashHistory values (i.e., previous <DATA_OBJECT> hashes) for user accounts, CrowdStrike was able to verify that some administrative accounts indeed had the exact same <DATA_OBJECT> hash showing up multiple times in the <DATA_OBJECT> history, as well as in the current NTHash value.
sentence.2089: Close Out The StellarParticle campaign, associated with the COZY BEAR adversary group, demonstrates this threat actor’s extensive knowledge of Windows and Linux operating systems, Microsoft Azure, O365, and Active Directory, and their patience and covert skill set to stay undetected for months — and in some cases, years.

sentence.2111: title: 3CXDesktopApp Backdoored in a Suspected Lazarus Campaign url: <URL> Introduction The attack involved a compromised version of the 3CX VoIP desktop client, which was used to target 3CX’s customers.
sentence.2112: The compromised 3CX application is a private automatic branch exchange (PABX) software and is available for Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, IOS and Chrome.
sentence.2113: Currently, there are reports of attacks for both Windows and macOS.
sentence.2114: The Qualys Threat Research Unit (TRU) is tracking a supply chain compromise in a popular VOIP desktop client by 3CX that is attributed to DPRK nation-state adversaries.
sentence.2115: The attack was reported in late March 2023 and is an ongoing investigation.
sentence.2116: Executive Summary The North Korean state-sponsored group Labyrinth Chollima have been identified as the perpetrators behind the supply chain compromise of 3CXDesktopApp beta 18.12.407 and final 18.12.416 applications.
sentence.2117: The affected applications are signed and have valid signatures.
sentence.2118: The adversary infrastructure on GitHub used for staging the attack has now been taken down.
sentence.2119: This means that newer infections will not occur.
sentence.2120: However, the attack’s potential impact was significant, as the software is widely used by businesses around the world.
sentence.2121: To mitigate the risk, affected users are recommended to immediately uninstall the application and perform a full system scan to detect and remove any associated malware.
sentence.2122: This threat is being tracked as by MITRE as <CVE> Fig.1 Campaign flow Technical Summary Once the affected version of 3CX is installed or updated, it drops a compromised <FILENAME> as well as <FILENAME>, which contains embedded shellcode.
sentence.2123: When 3CXDesktopApp starts, it sideloads the compromised <FILENAME>, which in turn decodes the embedded shellcode from <FILENAME> and loads it.
sentence.2124: The shellcode accesses a GitHub repository and brings down icon <DATA_OBJECT> which contain encrypted C2 strings that the shellcode then decrypts and communicates to.
sentence.2125: The adversary has also deployed a previously unseen info stealer in the later stages of the attack and we have provided an analysis for it in later sections.
sentence.2126: This info stealer gathers system information and browser data from Chrome, Edge, Brave, and Firefox.
sentence.2127: This info stealer was likely meant to identify interesting targets for the operators.
sentence.2128: Existing customers of Qualys can follow the steps in the Detection and Protection sections to identify potential impacts.
sentence.2129: We also recommended that customers implement robust security measures, such as regular vulnerability assessments, patch management regular auditing of vendors.
sentence.2130: Overall, this supply chain attack highlights the importance of ensuring the security and integrity of the supply chain, as well as the need for businesses to remain vigilant and proactive in their security measures.

sentence.2181: Conclusion Supply chain compromises are a growing concern for businesses, as they can lead to serious security breaches and financial losses.
sentence.2182: The attack was a multi-stage chain where attackers compromised a version of the 3CX VoIP desktop client, which was then used to target the company’s customers.
sentence.2183: This is reminiscent of the SolarWinds campaign that we examined back in December 2022.
sentence.2184: Organizations should take immediate steps to stop using the vulnerable version of the software, apply patches and monitor for anomalous behavior in 3CX processes.
sentence.2185: It is also essential to enable behavioral monitoring to detect the presence of such attacks within the system.

sentence.2192: title: Not just an infostealer: Gopuram backdoor deployed through 3CX supply chain attack url: <URL> On March 29, Crowdstrike published a report about a supply chain attack conducted via 3CXDesktopApp, a popular VoIP program.
sentence.2193: Since then, the security community has started analyzing the attack and sharing their findings.
sentence.2194: The following has been discovered so far:
sentence.2195: The infection is spread via 3CXDesktopApp MSI installers.
sentence.2196: An installer for macOS has also been trojanized.
sentence.2197: The malicious installation package contains an infected dll library that decrypts a shellcode from the <FILENAME> library’s overlay and executes it.
sentence.2198: The decrypted payload extracts C2 server URLs from icons stored in a GitHub repository (the repository is removed).
sentence.2199: The payload connects to one of the C2 servers, downloads an infostealer and starts it.
sentence.2200: The infostealer collects system information and browser history, then sends it to the C2 server.
sentence.2201: As we reviewed available reports on the 3CX attack, we began wondering if the compromise concluded with the infostealer or further implants followed.
sentence.2202: To answer that question, we decided to review the telemetry we had on the campaign.
sentence.2203: On one of the machines, we observed a DLL named <FILENAME>, which was loaded into the infected <FILENAME> process.
sentence.2204: Interestingly enough, we opened an investigation into a case linked to that DLL on March 21, about a week before the supply chain attack was discovered.
sentence.2205: A DLL with that name was used in recent deployments of a backdoor that we dubbed “Gopuram” and had been tracking internally since 2020.
sentence.2206: Three years ago, we were investigating an infection of a cryptocurrency company located in Southeast Asia.
sentence.2207: During the investigation, we found that Gopuram coexisted on victim machines with AppleJeus, a backdoor attributed to the Korean-speaking threat actor Lazarus.
sentence.2208: Over the years, we observed few victims compromised with Gopuram, but the number of infections began to increase in March 2023.
sentence.2209: As it turned out, the increase was directly related to the 3CX supply chain attack.
sentence.2210: We found out that the threat actor specifically targeted cryptocurrency companies, dropping the following <DATA_OBJECT> on infected machines: <FILE_PATH>, a malicious library (<ENC_ALGO>: <FILE_HASH>); <FILE_PATH><machine hardware profile GUID>.<DOMAIN>-ms, an encrypted shellcode payload.
sentence.2211: Once dropped, <FILENAME> becomes loaded on every startup by the IKEEXT service via DLL hijacking.
sentence.2212: We further saw DLLs with the names <FILENAME> and <FILENAME> being sideloaded into <FILENAME> and <FILENAME>, respectively.
sentence.2213: The <FILENAME> library is responsible for decrypting and executing the shellcode stored in the <FILE_PATH> directory.
sentence.2214: The decryption is notably performed through the CryptUnprotectData API function that uses a different encryption key internally on every machine.
sentence.2215: This makes it difficult for researchers to decrypt the payload from the <DATA_OBJECT> without physical access to the victim machines.
sentence.2216: Snippet of the loading function using CryptUnprotectData The component loaded by the library is Gopuram’s main module.
sentence.2217: As mentioned above, its name in the export directory is <FILENAME>.
sentence.2218: The job of the main module is to connect to a C2 server and request commands.
sentence.2219: The backdoor implements commands that allow the attackers to interact with the victim’s <DATA_OBJECT> system and create processes on the infected machine.
sentence.2220: Gopuram was additionally observed to launch in-memory modules.
sentence.2221: Just like the implants used in the 3CX campaign, Gopuram’s modules are DLL <DATA_OBJECT> that include an export function named DllGetClassObject.

sentence.2234: The discovery of the new Gopuram infections allowed us to attribute the 3CX campaign to the Lazarus threat actor with medium to high confidence.
sentence.2235: Our attribution is based on the following facts: While investigating an attack on a Southeast Asian cryptocurrency company in 2020, we found Gopuram coexisting on the same machine with the AppleJeus backdoor, which is attributed to Lazarus.
sentence.2236: The Gopuram backdoor has been observed in attacks on cryptocurrency companies, which is aligned with the interests of the Lazarus threat actor.
sentence.2237: While looking for additional implants that used the same loader shellcode as the 3CX implants, we discovered a sample on a multiscanner service (<ENC_ALGO>: <FILE_HASH>) loading a payload that uses the <DOMAIN> C2 server.

sentence.2244: These four facts allow us to conclude that Lazarus is likely the threat actor deploying the Gopuram backdoor.
sentence.2245: As for the victims in our telemetry, installations of the infected 3CX software are located all over the world, with the highest infection figures observed in Brazil, Germany, Italy and France.
sentence.2246: As the Gopuram backdoor has been deployed to less than ten infected machines, it indicates that attackers used Gopuram with surgical precision.
sentence.2247: We additionally observed that the attackers have a specific interest in cryptocurrency companies.

sentence.2305: [T1074.001] and remotely [T1074.002] for exfiltration Exfiltration over C2 channel [T1041] MitigationsNetwork Defense-in-Depth Proper network defense-in-depth and adherence to information security best practices can assist in mitigating the threat and reducing the risk.
sentence.2306: The following guidance may assist organizations in developing network defense procedures.
sentence.2307: Patch and Vulnerability Management Install vendor-provided and verified patches on all systems for critical vulnerabilities, prioritizing timely patching of internet-connected servers and software processing internet data—such as web browsers, browser plugins, and document readers.
sentence.2308: Ensure proper migrating steps or compensating controls are implemented for vulnerabilities that cannot be patched in a timely manner.
sentence.2309: Maintain up-to-date antivirus signatures and engines.
sentence.2310: Routinely audit configuration and patch management programs to ensure the ability to track and mitigate emerging threats.
sentence.2311: Implementing a rigorous configuration and patch management program will hamper sophisticated cyber threat actors’ operations and protect resources and information systems.
sentence.2312: Review the articles in the References section for more information on Chinese APT exploitation of common vulnerabilities.
sentence.2313: Protect <DATA_OBJECT> Strengthen credential requirements, regularly change passwords, and implement multi-factor authentication to protect individual accounts, particularly for webmail and VPN access and for accounts that access critical systems.
sentence.2314: Do not reuse passwords for multiple accounts.
sentence.2315: Audit all remote authentications from trusted networks or service providers.
sentence.2316: Detect mismatches by correlating <DATA_OBJECT> used within internal networks with those employed on external-facing systems.
sentence.2317: Log use of system administrator commands such as net, ipconfig, and ping.
sentence.2319: Network Hygiene and Monitoring Actively scan and monitor internet-accessible applications for unauthorized access, modification, and anomalous activities.
sentence.2320: Actively monitor server disk use and audit for significant changes.
sentence.2321: Log Domain Name Service (<PROTOCOL>) queries and consider blocking all outbound <PROTOCOL> requests that do not originate from approved <PROTOCOL> servers.
sentence.2323: Develop and monitor the network and system baselines to allow for the identification of anomalous activity.
sentence.2325: Identify and suspend access of users exhibiting unusual activity.
sentence.2326: Use allowlist or baseline comparison to monitor Windows event logs and network traffic to detect when a user maps a privileged administrative share on a Windows system.
sentence.2327: Leverage multi-sourced threat-reputation services for <DATA_OBJECT>, <PROTOCOL>, URLs, IP addresses, and email addresses.
sentence.2328: Network device management interfaces—such as Telnet, Secure Shell (<PROTOCOL>), Winbox, and <PROTOCOL>—should be turned off for wide area network (WAN) interfaces and secured with strong passwords and encryption when enabled.
sentence.2329: When possible, segment critical information on air-gapped systems.

sentence.2346: Targeted malware attacks in Colombia url: <URL> ESET researchers uncover attacks targeting Colombian government institutions and private companies, especially from the energy and metallurgical industries
sentence.2347: In 2020 ESET saw several attacks targeting Colombian entities exclusively.
sentence.2348: These attacks are still ongoing at the time of writing and are focused on both government institutions and private companies.
sentence.2349: For the latter, the most targeted sectors are energy and metallurgical.
sentence.2350: The attackers rely on the use of remote access trojans, most likely to spy on their victims.
sentence.2351: They have a large network infrastructure for command and control: ESET observed at least 24 different IP addresses in use in the second half of 2020.
sentence.2352: These are probably compromised devices that act as proxies for their C&C servers.
sentence.2353: This, combined with the use of dynamic <PROTOCOL> services, means that their infrastructure never stays still.
sentence.2354: We have seen at least 70 domain names active in this timeframe
sentence.2355: and they register new ones on a regular basis.
sentence.2356: The attackers The attacks we saw in 2020 share some TTPs with previous reports about groups targeting Colombia, but also differ in many ways, thus making attribution difficult.
sentence.2357: One of those reports was published in February 2019, by QiAnXin researchers.
sentence.2358: The operations described in that blogpost are connected to an APT group active since at least April 2018.
sentence.2359: We have found some similarities between those attacks and the ones that we describe in this article: We saw a malicious sample included in IoCs of QiAnXin’s report and a sample from the new campaign in the same government organization.
sentence.2360: These <DATA_OBJECT> have fewer than a dozen sightings each.
sentence.2361: Some of the phishing emails from the current campaign were sent from IP addresses corresponding to a range that belongs to Powerhouse Management, a VPN service.
sentence.2362: The same IP address range was used for emails sent in the earlier campaign.
sentence.2363: The phishing emails have similar topics and pretend to come from some of the same entities – for example, the Office of the Attorney General (Fiscalia General de la Nacion) or the National Directorate of Taxes and Customs (DIAN).
sentence.2364: Some of the C&C servers in Operation Spalax use <DOMAIN> and <DOMAIN> subdomains, along with IP addresses that belong to Powerhouse Management.
sentence.2365: This also happened in the earlier campaign.
sentence.2366: However, there are differences in the attachments used for phishing emails, the remote access trojans (RATs) used and in most of the operator’s C&C infrastructure.
sentence.2367: There is also this report from Trend Micro, from July 2019.
sentence.2368: There are similarities between the phishing emails and parts of the network infrastructure in that campaign and the one we describe here.
sentence.2369: The attacks described in that article were connected to cybercrime, not espionage.
sentence.2370: While we have not seen any payload delivered by the attackers other than RATs, some of the targets in the current campaign (such as a lottery agency) don’t make much sense for spying activities.
sentence.2371: These threat actors show perfect usage of the Spanish language in the emails they send, they only target Colombian entities, and they use premade malware and don’t develop any themselves.
sentence.2372: Attack overview Targets are approached with emails that lead to the download of malicious <DATA_OBJECT>.
sentence.2373: In most cases, these emails have a PDF document attached, which contains a link that the user must click to download the malware.
sentence.2374: The downloaded <DATA_OBJECT> are regular RAR archives that have an executable <DATA_OBJECT> inside.
sentence.2375: These archives are hosted in legitimate <DATA_OBJECT> hosting services such as OneDrive or MediaFire.
sentence.2376: The target has to manually extract the <DATA_OBJECT> and execute it for the malware to run.
sentence.2377: We’ve found a variety of packers used for these executables, but their purpose is always to have a remote access trojan running on the victimized computer, usually by decrypting the payload and injecting it into legitimate processes.
sentence.2378: An overview of a typical attack is shown in Figure 1.
sentence.2379: We have seen the attackers use three different RATs: Remcos, njRAT and AsyncRAT. Figure 1.
sentence.2380: Overview of the attack Phishing emails The attackers use various topics for their emails, but in most cases they are not specially crafted for their victims.
sentence.2381: On the contrary, most of these emails have generic topics that could be reused for different targets.
sentence.2382: We found phishing emails with these topics: A notification about a driving infraction A notification to take a mandatory COVID-19 test A notification to attend a court hearing An open investigation against the recipient for misuse of public funds A notification of an embargo of bank accounts The email shown in Figure 2 pretends to be a notification about a driving infraction for a value of around US$250.
sentence.2383: There is a PDF <DATA_OBJECT> attached that promises a photo of the infraction, as well as information about time and place of the incident.
sentence.2384: The sender has been spoofed to make the email look like it is coming from SIMIT (a system for paying transit violations in Colombia).
sentence.2386: Example of a phishing email The pdf <DATA_OBJECT> only contains an external link that has been shortened with the acortaurl service, as shown in Figure 3.
sentence.2388: After the shortened link is expanded, a RAR archive is downloaded from: <URL>
sentence.2390: PDF attached to phishing email Figure 4 shows part of the email’s header.
sentence.2391: The spoofed sender is <EMAIL> but we can see that the real sender is IP address <IPv4>, which is connected with the domain name <DOMAIN>, as found in historic <PROTOCOL> data.
sentence.2392: It’s not a coincidence that the same domain name is used for contacting the C&C server in the malicious sample contained in the RAR archive.
sentence.2393: This IP address belongs to Powerhouse Management, a VPN service provider.
sentence.2395: Header of a phishing email In more recent emails, the shortened link in the PDF <DATA_OBJECT> resolves to <URL> (a legitimate site) when visited from outside of Colombia.
sentence.2396: Also, in some cases the GetResponse service has been used to send the email.
sentence.2397: This is probably done to track whether the victim has clicked on the link.
sentence.2398: In these cases there is no attachment: a link to the GetResponse platform leads to the download of malware.
sentence.2399: You can see the other emails in the following gallery (click to enlarge): Figures 5 to 13.

sentence.2401: In the following sections, we describe the various droppers we have seen.
sentence.2402: NSIS installers The dropper that is most commonly used by these attackers comes as a <DATA_OBJECT> that was compiled with NSIS (Nullsoft Scriptable Install System).
sentence.2403: To try to evade detection, this installer contains several benign <DATA_OBJECT> that are written to disk (they are not part of NSIS binaries and they are not used at all by the installer) and two <DATA_OBJECT> that are malicious: an encrypted RAT executable and a DLL <DATA_OBJECT> that decrypts and runs the trojan.

sentence.2425: This, along with a complete analysis of the dropper, was described earlier this year by Sophos in their RATicate article.
sentence.2426: There is also an article by Lab52 describing one of the NSIS installers used in Operation Spalax, which they attribute to APT-C-36.
sentence.2427: In the vast majority of cases these NSIS droppers decrypt and run the Remcos RAT, but we have also seen cases where the payload is njRAT.
sentence.2428: These will be described later in the Payloads section.
sentence.2429: Agent Tesla packers We have seen several droppers that are different variants of a packer that uses steganography and is known to be used in Agent Tesla samples.
sentence.2430: Interestingly, the attackers use various payloads, but none of them are Agent Tesla.
sentence.2431: Even though there are differences in all the samples regarding the layers of encryption, obfuscation or anti-analysis used, we can summarize the actions taken by the droppers as follows: The dropper reads a string (or binary data) from its resource section and decrypts it.
sentence.2432: The result is a DLL that will be loaded and called in the same address space.
sentence.2433: The DLL reads pixels from an image contained in the first binary and decrypts another executable.
sentence.2434: This one is loaded and executed in the same address space.
sentence.2435: This new executable is packed with CyaX. It reads data from its own resource section and decrypts a payload.
sentence.2436: There are anti-analysis checks; if they pass, the payload can be injected into a new process or loaded in the same process space.
sentence.2437: The initial dropper is coded in C#.
sentence.2438: In all the samples that we have seen, the code for the dropper was hiding in non-malicious code, probably copied from other apps.
sentence.2439: The benign code is not executed; it’s there to evade detection.
sentence.2440: In Figure 16 we see an example of the resources contained in one of these droppers.
sentence.2441: The text in green (only shown partially) is a string that will be decrypted to generate the next stage to be executed and the image that we see below the green text will be decrypted by the second stage malware.
sentence.2442: The algorithm used for decryption of the string varies from sample to sample, but sometimes the resource is just an unencrypted binary.
sentence.2444: Resources contained in Agent Tesla’s packer
sentence.2445: The method to be executed in the DLL is always named StartGame or StartUpdate.
sentence.2446: It reads the image from the first executable, and stores every pixel as three numbers according to its red, green and blue components.
sentence.2447: Then it decrypts the array by doing a single-byte <ENC_ALGO> operation, cycling through the key.
sentence.2448: After that, the array is gzip-decompressed and executed.
sentence.2449: Part of the code for the mentioned operations is shown in Figure 17. Figure 17.
sentence.2450: Code to decrypt and run the third-stage malware The third stage is in charge of decrypting and running the payload.
sentence.2451: The .NET packer known as CyaX is used to perform this task.
sentence.2452: The version of the packer used by the attackers is v4, although they used v2 in some cases.
sentence.2453: Figure 18 shows the hardcoded configuration for one of their samples.
sentence.2456: The decryption of the payload is based on <ENC_ALGO> operations and is the same as the algorithm previously shown but with an extra step: the payload is XORed with its first 16 bytes as a key.
sentence.2457: Once it’s decrypted, it can be run in the same address space or injected into a different process, depending on the configuration.
sentence.2458: This packer supports various anti-analysis operations such as disabling Windows Defender, checking for security products, and detecting virtual environments and sandboxes.
sentence.2459: The majority of the payloads for these droppers are njRAT, but we have also seen AsyncRAT.
sentence.2460: We saw Remcos in one of these droppers, but the code in the packer was different.
sentence.2461: Part of the main routine for the injection of the payload is shown in Figure 19. Figure 19.
sentence.2462: Code for the last stage of a dropper We have noticed that the configuration is contained in different variables.
sentence.2463: Values like #startup_method# or #bind# mean that the configuration was not set for those options.
sentence.2464: The payload is read from an encrypted resource and XORed with a hardcoded <DATA_OBJECT>.
sentence.2465: The shellcode that performs the injection is contained in an array and is dynamically loaded.
sentence.2466: There are no anti-analysis checks or protection mechanisms.
sentence.2468: droppers For some of their droppers, the attackers have used an AutoIt packer that comes heavily obfuscated.
sentence.2469: Unlike the cases that were previously described, in this case the first-stage malware performs the injection and execution of the payload.
sentence.2470: It does so by using two shellcodes contained in the compiled AutoIt script: one to decrypt the payload and another to inject it into some process.
sentence.2471: The payload is constructed by concatenating several strings, as shown in Figure 20.
sentence.2472: By inspecting the last two characters, we can see that the string is in reverse order.
sentence.2474: Concatenation of the payload The routine that decrypts the payload contains a small shellcode that is loaded with VirtualAlloc and executed.
sentence.2475: The decryption done by the shellcode is based on a single-byte <ENC_ALGO> algorithm.
sentence.2476: The code that loads the shellcode is shown in Figure 21. Figure 21.
sentence.2477: Execution of shellcode to decrypt the payload We can see that the shellcode is stored encrypted.
sentence.2478: In fact, before deobfuscating the script, all strings were encrypted with this same <ENC_ALGO>-based algorithm.
sentence.2479: The decryption routine used is shown in Figure 22. Figure 22.
sentence.2480: Routine to decrypt strings Once the payload is decrypted, a shellcode with RunPE code is used to perform the injection.
sentence.2481: The shellcode is concatenated in the same manner as the payload and executed like the previous shellcode.
sentence.2482: To achieve persistence, a VBS script is created to execute a copy of the dropper (which is renamed to <FILENAME>).
sentence.2483: Then an Internet Shortcut (.url) <DATA_OBJECT> is created in the Startup folder to execute the script.
sentence.2484: The code that generates these <DATA_OBJECT> is shown in Figure 23. Figure 23.
sentence.2486: droppers The dropper contains code that is not executed.
sentence.2487: It can: Check for VMware and VirtualBox Delete the dropper executable Run the dropper continuously Download and execute <DATA_OBJECT> Terminate if a “Program Manager” window is found Read a binary from its resource section, write it to disk and execute it Modify the security descriptor (ACL) for the injected process For more information see this analysis by Morphisec where similar AutoIt droppers were used with Frenchy shellcode.
sentence.2488: Payloads The payloads used in Operation Spalax are remote access trojans.
sentence.2489: These provide several capabilities not only for remote control, but also for spying on targets: keylogging, <DATA_OBJECT> capture, <DATA_OBJECT> hijacking, exfiltration of <DATA_OBJECT>, and the ability to download and execute other malware, to name a few.
sentence.2490: These RATs were not developed by the attackers.
sentence.2491: They are: Remcos, sold online njRAT, leaked in underground forums AsyncRAT, open source There is not a one-to-one relationship between droppers and payloads, as we have seen different types of droppers running the same payload and also a single type of dropper connected to different payloads.
sentence.2492: However, we can state that NSIS droppers mostly drop Remcos, while Agent Tesla and AutoIt packers typically drop njRAT.
sentence.2493: Remcos is a tool for remote control and surveillance.
sentence.2494: It can be purchased with a six-month license that includes updates and support.
sentence.2495: There is also a free version with limited functionalities.
sentence.2496: While the tool can be used for legitimate purposes, it is also used by criminals to spy on their victims.
sentence.2497: Most of the Remcos samples used by this group are v2.5.0 Pro, but we have also seen all versions that were released since September 2019, which may indicate that the attackers bought a license after that month and have been actively using the different updates that they received during their six month license period.
sentence.2498: Regarding njRAT, this group mostly uses v0.7.3 (also known as the Lime version).
sentence.2499: That version includes functionalities such as DDoS or ransomware encryption, but only spy features such as keylogging are used by the attackers.
sentence.2500: For a more complete description of this version, refer to this 2018 article by Zscaler.
sentence.2501: Another njRAT version used by the attackers is v0.7d (the “green edition”) which is a simpler version focused on spying capabilities: keylogging, taking screenshots, access to webcam and microphone, uploading and downloading <DATA_OBJECT>, and executing other binaries.
sentence.2502: The final type of payload that we will mention is AsyncRAT.
sentence.2503: In all cases we have observed v0.5.7B, which can be found on GitHub, has been used.
sentence.2504: The functionalities in this RAT are similar to those in the previously mentioned RATs, which allow attackers to spy on their victims.
sentence.2505: Network infrastructure During our research we saw approximately 70 different domain names used for C&C in the second half of 2020.
sentence.2506: This amounts to at least 24 IP addresses.
sentence.2507: By pivoting on passive <PROTOCOL> data for IP addresses and known domain names, we found that the attackers have used at least 160 additional domain names since 2019.
sentence.2508: This corresponds to at least 40 further IP addresses.
sentence.2509: They’ve managed to operate at such scale by using Dynamic <PROTOCOL> services.
sentence.2510: This means that they have a pool of domain names (and also register new ones on a regular basis) that are dynamically assigned to IP addresses.
sentence.2511: This way a domain name can be related to several IP addresses over a period of time and IP addresses can be related to many domain names.
sentence.2512: Most of the domain names we have seen were registered with Duck <PROTOCOL>, but they have also used <PROTOCOL> Exit for <DOMAIN> and <DOMAIN> subdomains.
sentence.2513: Regarding IP addresses, almost all of them are in Colombia.
sentence.2514: Most are IP addresses related to Colombian ISPs: 60% of them are Telmex and 30% EPM Telecomunicaciones (Tigo).
sentence.2515: As it is highly unlikely that the criminals own so many residential IP addresses, it is possible that they use some victims as proxies, or some vulnerable devices to forward communication to their real C&C servers.
sentence.2516: Finally, a subset of the IP addresses belongs to Powerhouse Management, a VPN service provider.
sentence.2517: They are used in conjunction with <PROTOCOL> Exit subdomains.
sentence.2518: Similar findings can be found in this analysis by Lab52. Conclusion Targeted malware attacks against Colombian entities have been scaled up since the campaigns that were described last year.
sentence.2519: The landscape has changed from a campaign that had a handful of C&C servers and domain names to a campaign with very large and fast-changing infrastructure with hundreds of domain names used since 2019.
sentence.2520: Even though TTPs have seen changes, not only in how malware is delivered in phishing emails but also in the RATs used, one aspect that remains the same is that the attacks are still targeted and focused on Colombian entities, both in the public and private sectors.
sentence.2521: It should be expected that these attacks will continue in the region for a long time, so we will keep monitoring these activities.
sentence.2522: A comprehensive list of Indicators of Compromise (IoCs) and samples can be found in our GitHub repository.
sentence.2523: For any inquiries, or to make sample submissions related to the subject, contact us at <EMAIL>.
