sentence.2590: title: LAPSUS$: Recent techniques, tactics and procedures url: <URL> Authored by: David Brown, Michael Matthews and Rob Smallridge tl;dr This post describes the techniques, tactics and procedures we observed during recent LAPSUS$ incidents.
sentence.2591: Our findings can be summarised as below: Access and scraping of corporate Microsoft SharePoint sites in order to identify any <DATA_OBJECT> which may be stored in technical documentation.
sentence.2592: Access to local <DATA_OBJECT> managers and databases to obtain further <DATA_OBJECT> and escalate privileges.
sentence.2593: Living of the land – tools such as RVTools to shut down servers and ADExplorer to perform reconnaissance.
sentence.2594: Cloning of git repositories and extraction of sensitive API Keys.
sentence.2595: Using compromised <DATA_OBJECT> to access corporate VPNs.
sentence.2596: Disruption or destruction to victim infrastructure to hinder analysis and consume defensive resource.
sentence.2597: Summary LAPSUS$ first appeared publicly in December 2021, however, NCC Group first observed LAPSUS$ months prior during an incident response engagement.
sentence.2598: We believe the group has also operated prior to this date, though perhaps not under the “LAPSUS$” banner.
sentence.2599: Over the last 5 months, LAPSUS$ has gained large notoriety with some successful breaches of some large enterprises including, Microsoft, Nvidia, Okta & Samsung.
sentence.2600: Little is still known about this group with motivations appearing to be for reputation, money and “for the lulz”.
sentence.2601: Notifications or responsibility of victims by LAPSUS$ are commonly reported via their telegram channel and in one case a victim’s <PROTOCOL> records were reconfigured to LAPSUS$ controlled domains<FILE_PATH>
sentence.2602: However, not all victims or breaches appear to actively be announced via their telegram channel, nor are some victims approached with a ransom.
sentence.2603: This distinguishes themselves from more traditional ransomware groups who have a clear modus operandi and are clearly financially focused.
sentence.2604: The result of this is that LAPSUS$ are less predictable which may be why they have seen recent success.
sentence.2605: This serves as a reminder for defenders for defence in depth and the need to anticipate different tactics that threat actors may use.
sentence.2606: It is also worth mentioning the brazen behaviour of this threat actor and their emboldened attempts at Social Engineering by offering payment for insiders to provide valid <DATA_OBJECT>.
sentence.2607: This tactic is potentially in response to greater home working due to the pandemic which means there is a far larger proportion of employees with VPN access and as such a greater pool of potential employees willing to sell their <DATA_OBJECT>.
sentence.2608: To combat this, organisations need to ensure they have extensive VPN logging capabilities, robust helpdesk ticketing as well as methods to help identify anomalies in VPN access.
sentence.2609: It is notable that the majority of LAPSUS$ actions exploit the human element as opposed to technical deficiencies or vulnerabilities.
sentence.2610: Although potentially viewed as unsophisticated or basic these techniques have been successful, so it is vital that organisations factor in controls and mitigations to address them.
sentence.2611: Initial access Threat Intelligence shows that LAPSUS$ utilise multiple methods to gain Initial access.
sentence.2612: The main source of initial access is believed to occur via stolen authentication <DATA_OBJECT> which would grant the attacker access to a specific application.
sentence.2613: These <DATA_OBJECT> are usually in the form of Single sign-on (SSO) applications which would allow the attacker to pivot into other corporate applications ultimately bypassing controls such as multi-factor authentication (MFA).
sentence.2614: Credential access and Privilege escalation Credential Harvesting and privileged escalation are key components of the LAPSUS$ breaches we have seen, with rapid escalation in privileges the LAPSUS$ group have been seen to elevate from a standard user account to an administrative user within a couple of days.
sentence.2615: In the investigations conducted by NCC Group, little to no malware is used.
sentence.2616: In one case NCC Group observed LAPSUS$ using nothing more than the legitimate Sysinternals tool ADExplorer, which was used to conduct reconnaissance on the victim’s environment.
sentence.2617: Access to corporate VPNs is a primary focus for this group as it allows the threat actor to directly access key infrastructure which they require to complete their objectives.
sentence.2618: In our incident response cases, we saw the threat actor leveraging compromised employee email accounts to email helpdesk systems requesting access <DATA_OBJECT> or support to get access to the corporate VPN.
sentence.2619: Lateral Movement In one incident LAPSUS$ were observed to sporadically move through the victim environment via <PROTOCOL> in an attempt to access resources deeper in the victim environment.
sentence.2620: In some instances, victim controlled hostnames were revealed including the host “VULTR-GUEST” which refers to infrastructure hosted on the private cloud service, Vultr[3].
sentence.2621: Exfiltration LAPSUS$’s action on objectives appears to focus on data exfiltration of sensitive information as well as destruction or disruption.
sentence.2622: In one particular incident the threat actor is observed to utilise the free <DATA_OBJECT> drop service “<DOMAIN>”.
sentence.2623: Impact NCC Group has observed disruption and destruction to client environments by LAPSUS$ such as shutting down virtual machines from within on-premises VMware ESXi infrastructure, to the extreme of mass deletion of virtual machines, storage, and configurations in cloud environments making it harder for the victim to recover and for the investigation team to conduct their analysis activities.
sentence.2624: The theft of data reported appears to heavily be focused on application source code or proprietary technical information.
sentence.2625: With a targeting of internal source code management or repository servers.
sentence.2626: These git repositories can contain not only commercially sensitive intellectual property, but also in some cases may include additional API keys to sensitive applications including administrative or cloud applications.
sentence.2627: Recommendations Ensure that Cloud computing environments have sufficient logging enabled.
sentence.2628: Ensure that cloud administrative access is configured to prevent unauthorised access to resources and that API keys are not overly permissive to the permissions they require.
sentence.2629: Utilise MFA for user authentication on both cloud and remote access solutions to help reduce the risk of unauthorised access.
sentence.2630: Ensure logging is in place to record MFA device enrolmentSecurity controls such as Conditional Access can help restrict or prevent unauthorised access based on criteria such as geographical location.
sentence.2631: Implement activities to detect and investigate anomalies in VPN access.
sentence.2632: Ensure a system is in place to record all helpdesk queries.
sentence.2633: Avoid using SMS as an MFA vector to avoid the risk of SIM swapping.
sentence.2634: Securing source code environments to ensure that users can only access the relevant repositories.
sentence.2635: Secret Scanning[1][2] on source code repositories should be conducted to ensure that sensitive API <DATA_OBJECT> are not stored in source code.
sentence.2636: GitHub and Gitlab offer detection mechanisms for thisRemote Desktop services or Gateways used as a primary or secondary remote access solution should be removed from any corporate environment in favour for alternative solutions such as secured VPNs, or other Remote Desktop applications which mitigate common attack techniques such as brute force or exploitation and can offer additional security controls such as MFA and Conditional Access.
sentence.2637: Centralise logging including cloud applications (SIEM solution).Offline or immutable backups of servers should be taken to ensure that in the event of a data disruption or destruction attack, services can be restored.
sentence.2638: Reduce MFA <DATA_OBJECT><FILE_PATH> <DATA_OBJECT> validity timesEnsure principle of least privilege for user accounts is being adhered to.
sentence.2639: Social engineering awareness training for all staff.

sentence.2646: title: Detecting Credential Stealing Attacks Through Active In-Network Defense url: <URL> Executive Summary Today, enterprises tend to use multiple layers of security defenses, ranging from perimeter defense on network entry points to host based security solutions deployed at the end user’s machines to counter the ever-increasing threats.
sentence.2647: This includes inline traffic filtering and management security solutions deployed at access and distribution layers in the network, as well as out of band solutions like NAC, SIEM or User Behavior Analysis to provide identity-based network access and gain more visibility into the user’s access to critical network resources.
sentence.2648: However, layered security defenses face the major and recurring challenge of detecting newer exploitation techniques as they heavily rely on known behaviors.
sentence.2649: Additionally, yet another significant challenge facing the enterprise network is detecting post-exploitation activities, after perimeter security is compromised.
sentence.2650: Post initial compromise, to be able to execute meaningful attacks, attackers would need to steal <DATA_OBJECT> to move laterally inside the network, access critical network assets and eventually exfiltrate data.
sentence.2651: They will use several sophisticated techniques to perform internal reconnaissance and remote code execution on critical resources, which range from using legitimate operating system tools to discover network assets to using novel code execution techniques on the target.
sentence.2652: Consequently, differentiating between the legitimate and malicious use of Windows’ internal tools and services becomes a high priority for enterprise networks.
sentence.2653: To tackle this long-standing problem of detecting lateral movement, enterprise networks must formulate active in-network defense strategies to effectively prevent attackers from accessing critical network resources.
sentence.2654: Network Deception is one such defensive approach which could potentially prove to be an effective solution to detect credential theft attacks.
sentence.2655: Detecting credential stealing attacks with deception essentially requires building the necessary infrastructure by placing the decoy systems within the same network as production assets and configuring them with decoy contents to lure the attackers towards the decoy machines and services.
sentence.2656: Accurately configuring and tuning the deceptive network can deflect the attacker’s lateral movement path towards the deceptive services, consequently allowing the attackers to engage with the deceptive network, helping enterprises protect production assets.
sentence.2657: MITRE Shield, a knowledge base maintained by MITRE for active defense techniques highlights many of the methods in adversary engagement.
sentence.2658: Some of the techniques described by MITRE Shield Matrix with respect to network deception are as below: MITRE Shield Description ATT&CK Technique Decoy Account – DTE0010 A decoy account is created for defensive or deceptive purposes.
sentence.2659: The decoy account can be used to make a system, service, or software look more realistic or to entice an action Account Discovery, Reconnaissance Decoy <DATA_OBJECT> – DTE0012 Seed a target system with <DATA_OBJECT> (such as username<FILE_PATH>, browser <DATA_OBJECT>, and other forms of authentication data) Credential Access, Privilege Escalation Decoy Diversity – DTE0013 deployment of decoy systems with varying Operating Systems and software configurations Reconnaissance Decoy Network – DTE0014 Multiple computing resources that can be used for defensive or deceptive purposes Initial Access Decoy Personna – DTE0015 Used to establish background information about a user.
sentence.2660: In order to have the adversary believe they are operating against real targets Initial Access, Discovery, Reconnaissance Decoy System – DTE0017 Computing resources presented to the adversary in support of active defense Reconnaissance Over the course of this paper, we will discuss some of the widely adapted credential theft attacks executed by adversaries after the initial compromise and then move on to discuss defense techniques against the above MITRE Shield attacks and how to use them effectively to detect deceptive credential usage in the network.
sentence.2661: Network Deception – An Active in-network defensive approach Most of the targeted attacks involve stealing <DATA_OBJECT> from the system at a certain point in time as attackers would use them to pivot to other systems in the network.
sentence.2662: Some of the credential stealing techniques like Golden Ticket attacks have been found to be used in multiple ransomwares armed with lateral movement capabilities.
sentence.2663: Active in-network defense strategies described by the MITRE Shield matrix are significant and play a critical role in detecting credential abuse in the network.
sentence.2664: Network Deception uses these active defense techniques to build the deceptive network infrastructure which could potentially lead to redirecting an attacker’s lateral movement path and engaging them to the decoy services without touching the critical production systems.
sentence.2665: It involves placing decoy systems, decoy <DATA_OBJECT> and decoy contents all throughout the production network essentially converting it into a trap, playing a crucial role in mitigating the attacks.
sentence.2666: McAfee Protection McAfee MVISION Endpoint Security has the capabilities to protect against credential theft attacks like credential extraction from LSASS process memory via ATP rule 511.
sentence.2667: More details on configuring policies and a demo are available here.
sentence.2668: McAfee MVISION Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) has the capabilities to detect credential access from tools like Mimikatz.
sentence.2669: With McAfee MVISION EDR and ENS integration with Attivo’s network and endpoint deception sensor, McAfee can manage its agents and receive alerts for detections in ePO and EDR.
sentence.2670: Lateral Movement – Introduction Lateral movement refers to the tools and techniques used by attackers to progressively expand their foothold within an enterprise network after gaining initial access.
sentence.2671: As shown in the figure below, lateral movement activity comprises of several stages starting from credential theft, target enumeration and discovery, privilege escalation, gaining access to network resources and eventually remote code execution on the target before exfiltrating data to accomplish a successful attack.
sentence.2672: Once inside the network, attackers will deploy a range of techniques at each stage of lateral movement to achieve their end goal.
sentence.2673: One of the primary challenges an attacker will face while moving laterally inside a network is to hide their activities in plain sight by generating a minimum volume of legitimate looking logs to be able to remain undetected.
sentence.2674: To achieve this, an attacker might choose to embed the tool within a malicious executable or use the operating system’s internal legitimate tools and services to perform its lateral movement operations, consequently making this network traffic harder to distinguish.
sentence.2675: As per the Verizon DBIR report 2020, over 80% of data breaches involve credential theft attacks.
sentence.2676: Credential theft is one of the primary tasks attackers need to perform post-exploitation and after gaining initial control of the target machine.
sentence.2677: It will usually be the first step towards lateral movement strategies which will allow attackers to elevate their privileges and acquire access to other network resources.
sentence.2678: As indicated earlier, attackers have long been abusing Windows legitimate features like <PROTOCOL>, RPC over <PROTOCOL>, Windows Management Instrumentation, Windows Remote Management, and many other features to perform lateral movement activities.
sentence.2679: Figure 1 below highlights where lateral movement falls within the attack chain and its different stages.
sentence.2680: To remain stealthier, these activities would span a period ranging from many weeks to months.
sentence.2681: Figure 1 – Stages of Lateral movement To be able to distinguish between the admissible and malicious use of these inbuilt services, it is extremely critical for organizations to deploy advanced Threat Detection solutions.
sentence.2682: Over the course of this blog, we will discuss various credential theft techniques used by adversaries during lateral movement.
sentence.2683: We will also discuss an approach that can be used to effectively detect these techniques inside the network.
sentence.2684: Credential Theft Attacks Attackers use a variety of tools and techniques to execute credential theft attacks.
sentence.2685: Many of these tools are open source and readily available on the internet.
sentence.2686: Operating systems like Windows implement Single Sign
sentence.2687: On (SSO) functionality, which require the user’s <DATA_OBJECT> to be stored in memory, thereby allowing the OS to seamlessly access network resource without repeatedly asking the user to re-enter those <DATA_OBJECT>.
sentence.2688: Additionally, user <DATA_OBJECT> are stored in memory in a variety of formats like NTLM hashes, reversibly encrypted plaintext, <PROTOCOL> tickets, PINs, etc., which can be used to authenticate to services depending upon the supported authentication mechanism.
sentence.2689: These <DATA_OBJECT> can be acquired by attackers from memory by parsing appropriate credential storage structures or using the Windows credential enumeration APIs.
sentence.2690: Consequently, these attacks pose major security concerns, especially in the domain environment if the attacker gains access to privileged <DATA_OBJECT> which can then be reused to access critical network resources.
sentence.2691: In the following sections, we discuss some of the widely adapted credential stealing techniques used by malware, with respect to the Windows operating system.
sentence.2692: Similar credential stealing techniques can also be used with other operating systems as well.
sentence.2693: Stealing <DATA_OBJECT> from LSASS Process Memory The Local Security Authority Subsystem Service (LSASS) process manages and stores the <DATA_OBJECT> of all the users with active Windows sessions.
sentence.2694: These <DATA_OBJECT> stored in the LSASS process memory will allow users to access other network resource such as <DATA_OBJECT> shares, email servers and other remote services without asking them for the <DATA_OBJECT> again.
sentence.2695: LSASS process memory stores the <DATA_OBJECT> in many formats including reversibly encrypted plaintext, NTLM hashes, <PROTOCOL> Tickets (Ticket Granting Tickets, etc.).
sentence.2696: These <DATA_OBJECT> are generated and stored in the memory of the LSASS process when a user initiates the interactive logon to the machine such as console logon or <PROTOCOL>, runs a scheduled task or uses remote administration tools.
sentence.2697: The encryption and decryption of <DATA_OBJECT> is done using LsaProtectMemory and LsaUnProtectMemory respectively and hence a decryption tool using these APIs will be able to decrypt LSASS memory buffers and extract them.
sentence.2698: However, malware would need to execute with local administrator privileges and enable “SeDebugPrivilege” on the current process to be able access the LSASS process memory.
sentence.2699: Below is a code snapshot from one of the famous credential harvesting tools, Mimikatz, enabling the required privileges on the calling thread before dumping the <DATA_OBJECT>.
sentence.2700: Figure 2 – Checking for required privileges We can see that the NTLM hash of the user’s <DATA_OBJECT> is revealed, and this can be brute forced offline as shown below.
sentence.2701: Many Windows services, such as <PROTOCOL>, support NTLM authentication and NTLM hashes can be used directly for authentication eliminating the need for the clear text passwords.
sentence.2702: Figure 3 – Cracking NTLM Hashes offline Attackers avoid using freely available tools like Mimikatz directly on the target machine to harvest <DATA_OBJECT> since they are easily detected by AVs.
sentence.2703: Instead, they use recompiled clones of it with minimal functionality to avoid noise.
sentence.2704: Below is one such instance where malware embeds recompiled Mimikatz code with the minimal required functionality.
sentence.2705: Figure 4 – Credential extraction tool embedded inside malicious executable Detection can also be avoided by using several “living off the land’ mechanisms, available in many post-exploitation frameworks, to execute the credential harvesting tools directly from memory using Reflective PE injection, where the binary is never written to the disk.
sentence.2706: Yet another approach is to dump the LSASS process memory using process dumping tools, exfiltrate the dump and extract the <DATA_OBJECT> offline.
sentence.2707: Microsoft has documented multiple ways to configure additional LSASS process protection which can prevent <DATA_OBJECT> being compromised.
sentence.2708: Stealing <DATA_OBJECT> from Security Accounts Manager (SAM) Database The SAM database is a <DATA_OBJECT> on a local hard drive that stores the <DATA_OBJECT> for all local accounts on the Windows computer.
sentence.2709: NT hashes for all the accounts on the local machine, including the local administrator credential hash, are stored in the SAM database.
sentence.2710: The SAM database <DATA_OBJECT> is in %SystemRoot%system32<FILE_PATH> and the hashes of the <DATA_OBJECT> are within the <DATA_OBJECT> <REGKEY>
sentence.2711: Attackers need to acquire elevated privileges to be able to access the <DATA_OBJECT> from the SAM database.
sentence.2712: The example below demonstrates how the <DATA_OBJECT> from the SAM database can be revealed through a simple Meterpreter session.
sentence.2713: Figure 5 – Dumping SAM database Stealing <DATA_OBJECT> from Windows Credential Manager (CredMan) Windows Credential Manager stores the Web and <PROTOCOL><FILE_PATH> <DATA_OBJECT> of users if they choose to save them on the Windows machine, thereby preventing the authentication mechanism from asking for those passwords again on subsequent logins.
sentence.2714: These <DATA_OBJECT> are encrypted with Windows Data Protection APIs (DPAPI) CryptProtectData, either using the current user’s logon session or a generated master key, and then saved on the local hard drive.
sentence.2715: Consequently, any process running in the context of the logged in user will be able to decrypt the <DATA_OBJECT> using CryptUnProtectData DPAPI.
sentence.2716: In the domain environment, these <DATA_OBJECT> can be used by attackers to pivot to other systems in the network.
sentence.2717: Data Protection APIs provide the cryptographic functionalities that can be used to securely store <DATA_OBJECT> and keys.
sentence.2718: These APIs are used by several other Windows components like browsers (IE<FILE_PATH>), certificates and many other applications as well.
sentence.2719: Below is one example of how credential dumping tools like Mimikatz can be used to dump stored Chrome <DATA_OBJECT>.
sentence.2720: Figure 6 – Dumping browser <DATA_OBJECT> DPAPI can be abused in multiple ways.
sentence.2721: In the Active Directory domain joined environment, if other users have logged into the compromised machine, provided a malware is running with escalated privileges, it can extract other user’s master keys from the LSASS memory which can then be used to decrypt their secrets.
sentence.2722: Below is a screenshot of how the master key can be extracted by using the credential dumping tool.
sentence.2723: Figure 7 – Extracting DPAPI Master Key Malware also tends to use multiple variants of credential enumeration APIs available within Windows.
sentence.2724: These APIs can extract <DATA_OBJECT> from Windows Credential Manager.
sentence.2725: Below is one instance of the malware using CredEnumerateW API to retrieve <DATA_OBJECT> and then search for terminal services passwords which It would use to pivot to other systems.
sentence.2726: Figure 8 – Extracting <DATA_OBJECT> using Windows API Stealing Service Account <DATA_OBJECT> Through Kerberoasting In the domain joined environment, the <PROTOCOL> protocol has a significant role to play with respect to authentication and requesting access to services and applications.
sentence.2727: It provides Single-Sign-On functionality for accessing multiple shared resources within the enterprise network.
sentence.2728: The <PROTOCOL> authentication mechanism in Active Directory involves multiple requests and responses like Ticket Granting Ticket (TGT) and Ticket Granting Service (TGS) supported by a Key Distribution Server (KDC), usually a Domain Controller.
sentence.2729: Upon successful authentication, a user will be able to access the respective services.
sentence.2730: Attackers gaining access to a system joined in the domain would usually look for high value assets like Active Directory Controller, Database server, SharePoint server, Web Server, etc., and these services are registered in the domain with the specific Service Principal Name (SPN) values, which is a unique identifier of the Service Account in the domain.
sentence.2731: These SPN values are used by <PROTOCOL> to map the instance with the logon account allowing the client to authenticate to the respective service.
sentence.2732: Well known SPN values are listed out here.
sentence.2733: Once the attacker is authenticated with any domain user <DATA_OBJECT> and has information about the SPN values of the services within the domain, they can initiate the <PROTOCOL> Ticket Granting Service request (TGS – REQ) to the Key Distribution Server with the specified SPN value.
sentence.2734: Details on how the SPN values are registered and used in <PROTOCOL> authentication is documented here.
sentence.2735: TGS response from the KDC will have the <PROTOCOL> Ticket encrypted with the hash of the service account.
sentence.2736: This ticket can be extracted from the memory and can be brute forced offline to acquire service account <DATA_OBJECT>, allowing a domain user to gain admin level access to the service.
sentence.2737: Kerberoasting is a well-documented attack technique listed in MITRE ATT&CK and it essentially abuses the <PROTOCOL> authentication allowing adversaries to request the TGS Tickets for the valid service accounts and brute force the ticket offline to extract the plain text <DATA_OBJECT> of the service accounts, consequently enabling them to elevate their privileges from domain user to domain admin.
sentence.2738: As an initial step to this lateral movement technique, the attacker would perform an internal reconnaissance to gain information about the services registered in the domain and get SPN values.
sentence.2739: A simple PowerShell command after importing the Active Directory PowerShell module, as shown below, can initiate the <PROTOCOL> query to get information about all the user accounts from the Domain Controller with the SPN value set. Figure 9 – PowerShell command to generate <PROTOCOL> query Attackers can specifically choose to scan the domain for MSSQL service with the registered SPN value used for <PROTOCOL> authentication.
sentence.2740: PowerShell scripts like GetUserSPNs can scan all the user SPNs in the domain or MSSQL service registered in the domain with Discover-PSMSSQLServers or Invoke-Kerberoast scripts.
sentence.2741: Following is an example output from the script:
sentence.2742: Figure 10 – Kerberoasting PowerShell script output Once an attacker has the SPN value of the SQL service, a <PROTOCOL> Ticket Granting Service Ticket request (TGS-REQ) can be initiated to the domain controller with the SPN value.
sentence.2743: This can be done by a couple of PowerShell commands generating KRB-TGS-REQ as shown below: Figure 11 – <PROTOCOL> TGS request Consequently, the Domain Controller sends the TGS-RESP with the ticket of the service account which will be cached in the memory and can be extracted by dumping tools like Mimikatz as a .kirbi document.
sentence.2744: This can be brute forced offline by tgsrespcrack, allowing the attacker to gain unrestricted access to the service with elevated privileges.
sentence.2745: Stealing <DATA_OBJECT> from Active Directory Domain Service (<DOMAIN>) <DATA_OBJECT> As indicted earlier, once an attacker has penetrated the domain network, it will be natural to progress towards targeting critical assets, such as the Active Directory controller.
sentence.2746: The Active Directory Database Services AD DS <DOMAIN> <DATA_OBJECT> is one of the most overlooked attack vectors in the domain environment but can have significant impact if the attacker is able to gain the domain administrative rights leading to complete domain compromise.
sentence.2747: The <DOMAIN> <DATA_OBJECT> is the authoritative store of <DATA_OBJECT> for all the users in the domain joined environment, storing all the information about the users, groups and memberships, including <DATA_OBJECT> (NT Hashes) of all the users in the domain with historical passwords and user’s DPAPI backup master keys.
sentence.2748: An Attacker with domain admin rights can gain access to the Domain Controller’s <DATA_OBJECT> system and acquire <DATA_OBJECT> like hashes, <PROTOCOL> tickets and other reversibly encrypted passwords of all the users joined in the domain by dumping and exfiltrating the <DOMAIN> <DATA_OBJECT>.
sentence.2749: These <DATA_OBJECT> can then be used by the attacker to further access resources by using attack techniques like PTH within the network since the <DATA_OBJECT> used across other shared resource could be same.
sentence.2750: Multiple techniques can be used to dump the <DOMAIN> <DATA_OBJECT> from the Domain Controller locally as well as remotely and extract the NTLM hashes<FILE_PATH> backup keys for all the domain joined users.
sentence.2751: One of the techniques is to use the Volume Shadow Copy Service using the vssadmin command line utility and then extract the <DOMAIN> <DATA_OBJECT> from the volume shadow copy as shown below.
sentence.2752: Figure 12 – Dumping Volume shadow copy for C drive Sensitive data on Active Directory is encrypted with the Boot Key (Syskey) stored in the SYSTEM <DATA_OBJECT> hive and dumping the SYSTEM <DATA_OBJECT> hive is a prerequisite as well to be able to extract all the <DATA_OBJECT>.
sentence.2753: Publicly available Active Directory auditing frameworks like DSInternals provide PowerShell cmdlets to extract the Syskey from the SYSTEM <DATA_OBJECT> hive and extract all the <DATA_OBJECT> from the <DOMAIN> <DATA_OBJECT>.
sentence.2754: <DOMAIN> can also give access to the powerful service account within the Active Directory Domain, KRBTGT (Key Distribution Centre Service account).
sentence.2755: Acquiring the NTLM hash of this account can enable the attacker to execute a Golden Ticket attack leading to complete domain compromise with unrestricted access to any service on the domain joined system.
sentence.2756: Stealing <DATA_OBJECT> Through a DCSync Attack – From Domain user to Domain Admin A DCSync attack is a method of credential acquisition which allows an attacker to impersonate the Domain Controller and can consequently replicate all the Active Directory objects to the impersonating client remotely, without requiring the user to logon to the DC or dumping the <DOMAIN> <DATA_OBJECT>.
sentence.2757: By impersonating the Domain Controller, the attacker could acquire the NTLM hash of the KRBTGT service account, enabling them to gain access to all the shared resources and applications in the domain joined environment.
sentence.2758: To be able to execute this credential stealing technique, an attacker would have to compromise the user account with the required permissions, specifically DS-Replication-Get-Changes and DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All, as shown below.
sentence.2759: Figure 13 – User with privileges Once the attacker compromises the user account with the required privileges, Pass-The-Hash attacks can be executed to spawn a command shell with the forged logon session.
sentence.2760: Credential dumping tools like Mimikatz do this by enumerating all the user logon sessions and replacing the user <DATA_OBJECT> with the stolen usernames and NTLM hashes provided, in the current logon session.
sentence.2761: Behind the scenes, this is executed by duplicating the current process’s access <DATA_OBJECT>, replacing the user <DATA_OBJECT> pointed by duplicated access <DATA_OBJECT> and subsequently using the modified access <DATA_OBJECT> to start a new process with the stolen <DATA_OBJECT> which will be used for network authentication.
sentence.2762: This is as shown below for example user “DCPrivUser”.
sentence.2763: Figure 14 – Pass-the-Hash attack Further, as indicated below, any subsequent NTLM authentication from the logon session will use the stolen <DATA_OBJECT> to authenticate to domain joined systems like the Active Directory Controller.
sentence.2764: Attackers can now initiate the AD user objects Replication request to the Domain Controller using Directory Replication Services Remote Protocol (DRSUAPI).
sentence.2765: DRSUAPI is the RPC protocol used for replication of AD objects.
sentence.2766: With DCERPC bind request to DRSUAPI, an RPC call to DSGetNCChanges will replicate all the user AD objects to the impersonating client.
sentence.2767: Attackers would usually target the KRBTGT account since acquiring the NTLM hash of this account will enable them to execute a Golden Ticket attack resulting in unrestricted access to domain services and applications.
sentence.2768: Figure 15 – DCSync Attack As indicated earlier, with the NTLM hash of the KRBTGT account, adversaries can initiate a Golden Ticket attack (Pass-the-Ticket) by injecting the forged <PROTOCOL> tickets into the current session which can be used to authenticate to any service with the client that supports pass the ticket (for instance, <FILENAME> connection to DB server, PsExec, etc.)
sentence.2769: Figure 16 – Golden ticket with forged <PROTOCOL> ticket Detecting Credential Stealing Attacks with Network Deception
sentence.2770: The credential theft techniques we discussed in the previous sections are just the tip of the iceberg.
sentence.2771: Adversaries can use many other sophisticated credential stealing techniques to take advantage of system misconfigurations and legitimate administrative tools and protocols and, at the same time, remain undetected for a longer period.
sentence.2772: With many other event management solutions with SIEMs, used in conjunction with other network security solutions, it becomes a challenge for administrators to distinguish malicious use of legitimate tools and services from lateral movement.
sentence.2773: Perimeter solutions have their limitations in terms of visibility once the attacker crosses the network boundary and is inside the domain environment.
sentence.2774: It is extremely critical for organizations to protect and monitor critical network assets like the Domain Controller, Database server, Exchange Servers, build systems and other applications or services, as compromising these systems will result in significant damages.
sentence.2775: Therefore, enterprise networks must deploy a solution to detect credential stealing attacks as they can be used to pivot to other systems on the network and move laterally once an attacker establishes an attack path to a high value target.
sentence.2776: If the deployment of a solution within the critical zones of the network can detect the use of stolen <DATA_OBJECT> before adversaries can reach their target, the critical assets could still be prevented from being compromised.
sentence.2777: Network Deception is one such deployment within the domain environment where, using the MITRE Shield techniques like decoy systems and network, decoy <DATA_OBJECT>, decoy accounts, decoy contents, could potentially help detect lateral movement early in the adversary’s attack path to the target asset and at the same time, report significantly low false detection rates.
sentence.2778: The idea of deception originates from the decades old honeypot systems but, unlike those, relies more on forging trust and giving adversaries what they are looking for.
sentence.2779: With its inbuilt proactiveness it is configured to lure attackers towards deceptive systems.
sentence.2780: As shown in the figure below, Network Deception consists of authentic looking decoy systems placed within the domain network, specifically in the network where the critical assets are placed.
sentence.2781: These decoy systems (could be virtual machines) are the full-fledged OS with configured applications or services and could be replicating the crucial services like Domain Controller, Exchange or DB server and other decoy machines that could lead to those systems.
sentence.2782: The image below highlights the key foundational aspects of the Network Deception Figure 17 – Network Deception Key Aspects of Network Deception As visualized in the figure above, Network Deception comprises the following key basic facts with respect to the deployment in the domain joined environment: As a part of deployment, decoy<FILE_PATH> machines are planted within the network alongside production systems and critical assets.
sentence.2783: These decoy systems could be real systems or virtual systems with production grade operating systems with the required setup to make them blend well with real systems.
sentence.2784: As one of the key aspects, deceptive machines are configured to lure attackers towards the decoy services instead of the production services, thereby deflecting or misleading the attacker’s lateral movement path to the target asset.
sentence.2785: Many of the decoy machines could replicate critical services like Domain Controller, DB servers, Exchange<FILE_PATH> servers and other critical services or applications within the data center.
sentence.2786: Any legitimate domain user should not be generating traffic to or communicating with the configured decoy machines unless there are some misconfigurations in the network, which need to be corrected.
sentence.2787: Basic Decoy Network Setup Since credential theft plays an important role in a successful targeted attack, deception essentially focuses on planting fake <DATA_OBJECT> on the production and decoy endpoints at multiple places within the OS and monitoring the use of these <DATA_OBJECT> to pivot to other systems.
sentence.2788: With respect to the network setup, the following are the key aspects, however this list is not exhaustive, and much more could be added: Replicating critical network assets and services with decoy machines: Replicating critical network services like Active Directory, DB services, etc., will make more sense since these are the most targeted systems in the network.
sentence.2789: The decoy Active Directory should be configured with deceptive AD objects (users, groups, SPNs, etc.).
sentence.2790: with deceptive contents for other replicated services.
sentence.2791: Planting authentic looking decoy machines in the production network: As indicated earlier, these decoy machines could be real or virtual machines with the production grade OS placed alongside production systems in the critical infrastructure to blend in well.
sentence.2792: These decoy machines should be joined to the decoy AD and configured with deceptive user accounts to monitor successful logon attempts to the systems.
sentence.2793: Injecting deceptive <DATA_OBJECT> on production endpoints: Production endpoints should be injected with deceptive <DATA_OBJECT> at multiple places like LSASS process memory, Credential Manager, browser <DATA_OBJECT>, etc., to increase the possibility of these <DATA_OBJECT> being picked up and used to pivot to decoy systems in the network.
sentence.2794: These endpoints could be public facing machines or their replicas as well.
sentence.2795: Decoy Machine runs client applications pointing to decoy services: Decoy machines may run the client with deceptive <DATA_OBJECT> and configured to point to the decoy services.
sentence.2796: These could be DB<FILE_PATH> clients and any other replicated decoy services.
sentence.2797: Mark decoy systems as “NO LANDING ZONE”: One of the key deployment aspects of deception is to mark all the decoy systems and services as “NO LANDING ZONE”, essentially meaning no legitimate domain users should be accessing decoys and any attempts to access these systems should be closely monitored.
sentence.2798: Some of the other setup required for effective deployment of deception is as summarized below: Figure 18 – Deceptive network setup – Basic requirements Basic Decoy Systems Setup To detect the use of deceptive <DATA_OBJECT>, setting up decoy machines is an essential part of the solution as well.
sentence.2799: Primarily, decoy machines should enable the access attackers are looking to have during the lateral movement phase.
sentence.2800: Decoys should also be configured to enable relevant auditing services to be able to generate events.
sentence.2801: For instance, the following enables the account logon events to be audited: Decoy machines must be setup to run the log collector agent that can collect the access logs generated and forward them to the correlation server.
sentence.2802: However, in the domain joined environment, it is also essential to tune the decoy machines to forward only the relevant logs to the correlation server to minimize false positives.
sentence.2803: The below highlights some of the auditing required to be enabled on the decoy systems for effective correlation.
sentence.2804: Figure 19 – Basic decoy setup Illustrating and Achieving Network Deception
sentence.2805: The following sections describe some examples of how deception can be achieved in the domain network, along with a visualization of how credential theft can be detected.
sentence.2806: Network Deception – Example 1: Injecting NETONLY <DATA_OBJECT> into LSASS process memory LSASS process memory is one of the prime targets for attackers, as well as malware armed with lateral movement capabilities since it caches a variety of <DATA_OBJECT>.
sentence.2807: Credential extraction from the LSASS process requires opening a read handle to the process itself which is closely monitored by EDR products but there are stealthier ways around it.
sentence.2808: One of the primary tasks towards achieving credential-based deception is to stage the deceptive <DATA_OBJECT> in LSASS process memory.
sentence.2809: This can be accomplished on the production and decoy systems by executing a trivial credential injection code which uses the CreateProcessWithLogonW Windows API with the specified crafted <DATA_OBJECT>.
sentence.2810: CreateProcessWithLogonW creates the new logon session using the caller process access <DATA_OBJECT> and spawns the process specified as a parameter in the security context of the specified deceptive <DATA_OBJECT> and it will be staged in the LSASS memory until the process runs in the background.
sentence.2811: The below shows the example code calling the API with the specified <DATA_OBJECT> which is also visible when <DATA_OBJECT> are extracted with Mimikatz.
sentence.2812: Figure 20 – Injecting <DATA_OBJECT> into LSASS memory One of the parameters to CreateProcessWithLogonW is “dwLogonFlags” which should be specified as LOGON_NETCREDENTIALS_ONLY as shown in the code above.
sentence.2813: This ensures the specified <DATA_OBJECT> are used only on the network and not for local logons.
sentence.2814: Additionally, NETONLY <DATA_OBJECT> used to create a logon session are not validated by the system.
sentence.2815: Below is a code snapshot from credential extraction tool Mimikatz, using a similar approach to forge a logon session and replacing the <DATA_OBJECT> with the supplied ones while executing Pass-the-Hash attacks.
sentence.2816: Figure 21 – Mimikatz code for PTH attack Network Deception – Example 2: Configure deceptive hostnames for decoy VMs Attackers or malware moving laterally inside the network might do a recon for interesting hostnames via nbtstat<FILE_PATH>
sentence.2817: To deflect the lateral movement path, decoy systems can be configured with real looking hostnames that match the production systems.
sentence.2818: These hostnames will then be visible on NetBIOS scans as shown below.
sentence.2819: Figure 22 – Deceptive host names pointing to decoy machines
sentence.2820: These decoy systems can also run the relevant client applications pointing to the decoy services, with authentication directed to the decoy Domain Controller in the network.
sentence.2821: Detection of this attack path happens much earlier, however the decoy network setup keeps the adversaries engaged, helping admins to study their Tools and Techniques. Figure 23 – Decoy machines running clients pointing to decoy services A similar deception setup can also be done for the browsers where saved <DATA_OBJECT> can point to the decoy applications and services within the domain.
sentence.2822: For instance, Chrome saves the <DATA_OBJECT> in the SQLite format on the disk which can be decrypted using DPAPI as discussed earlier sections.
sentence.2823: The below examples demonstrate deceptive browser <DATA_OBJECT> which can lure adversaries towards the decoy services.
sentence.2825: In addition to some of the techniques discussed above, and many others highlighted in the previous sections, setting up deception involves much more advanced configuration of decoy systems to minimize false positives and needs to be tuned to the environment to accurately identify malicious activities.
sentence.2826: Deception can also be configured to address multiple other phases of lateral movement activity including reconnaissance and target discovery, essentially redirecting the adversaries and giving them a path to the target.
sentence.2827: Below is a high-level visualization of how the decoy network can look like the domain environment.
sentence.2828: Figure 25 – Deception network setup On the occasion where one of the domain-joined or public facing systems is compromised, authentication would be attempted to other domain joined systems in the network.
sentence.2829: If an authentication is attempted and any of the decoy systems are accessed and logged on, the use of these planted deceptive <DATA_OBJECT> should be a red flag and something which must be investigated.
sentence.2830: The visualization below shows the flow and an event being sent to an administrator on accessing one of the decoy systems.
sentence.2831: Figure 26 – Deceptive <DATA_OBJECT> usage for authentication in the domain One such example event of successfully logging on to the decoy system is as shown below: Figure 27 – Alert send to administrator on using deceptive <DATA_OBJECT> MITRE ATT&CK Techniques: Credential theft attacks discussed here are mapped by MITRE as below: Technique ID Technique Name Description T1003.001 LSASS Process Memory Attackers may attempt to access LSASS process memory to extract <DATA_OBJECT> as it stores a variety of <DATA_OBJECT>.
sentence.2832: Administrative privileges are required to access the process memory.
sentence.2833: T1003.002 SAM Database Accessing <DATA_OBJECT> from SAM database requires SYSTEM level privileges.
sentence.2834: Stores <DATA_OBJECT> for all the local user accounts on the machine.
sentence.2835: T1003.003 <DOMAIN> <DATA_OBJECT> Contains <DATA_OBJECT> for all the domain users.
sentence.2836: <DATA_OBJECT> is present on the DC and domain admin privileges are required to access this <DATA_OBJECT>.
sentence.2837: T1003.006 DCSync Attacker can extract the <DATA_OBJECT> from the DC by impersonating the domain controller and use DRSUAPI protocol to replicate <DATA_OBJECT> from DC.
sentence.2838: T1558.001 Golden Ticket Attackers acquiring <DATA_OBJECT> for KRBTGT account can forge the <PROTOCOL> ticket called Golden Ticket, allowing them to get unrestricted access to any system in the domain T1558.002 Silver Ticket Allows attacker to get admin level access to the service accounts by abusing <PROTOCOL> authentication T1558.003 Kerberoasting Allows attackers to extract the <PROTOCOL> tickets for service accounts from memory and brute force offline to get <DATA_OBJECT> Conclusion As credential theft attacks play a significant role in an attacker’s lateral movement, so as in-network defense for the defenders.
sentence.2839: With attackers’ lateral movement tactics evolving and getting more stealthier, defenders will have to adapt to innovative ways of defending the critical network assets.
sentence.2840: In–network defense strategies like Deception could prove to be a promising and forward-looking approach towards detecting and mitigating data theft attacks.
sentence.2841: Strategic planting of decoy systems within the production network, inserting decoy <DATA_OBJECT> and decoy contents on calculative selection of endpoints and decoy systems and accurately setting up the logging and correlation via SIEMs for monitoring the use of decoy contents, could certainly detect and mitigate the attacks early in the lateral movement life cycle.
sentence.2842: Endpoint solutions like User Entity Behavior Analytics (UEBA) and Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) could also play a significant role in building the deception infrastructure.
sentence.2843: For instance, one of the ways UEBA solutions could prove useful is to baseline user behavior and monitor access to credential stores on the system.
sentence.2844: UEBA<FILE_PATH> could raise the red flag on injection of forged <PROTOCOL> tickets in the memory.
sentence.2845: This can provide user level visibility to a greater extent when integrated with SIEM, playing a crucial role in mitigating credential theft attacks.

sentence.2847: title: Understanding <PROTOCOL> attacks: Identifying and patching vulnerabilities | Snyk url: <URL> The Domain Name System (<PROTOCOL>) translates domain names into IP addresses.
sentence.2848: Every device and website has an IP address that other devices, websites, and online services use to communicate with it.
sentence.2849: IP addresses are a string of numbers usually formatted as 000.000.000.000.
sentence.2850: However, we use domain names since people can’t easily remember these numbers.
sentence.2851: When we want to visit Google, we simply type the domain name into our browser’s address bar, and the <PROTOCOL> service translates the user-entered domain name “<DOMAIN>” into the corresponding IP address that a computer uses.
sentence.2852: <PROTOCOL> is a fundamental component of the internet infrastructure, as any communication must start with a <PROTOCOL> name resolution.
sentence.2853: If the <PROTOCOL> becomes unavailable, internet programs will no longer function.
sentence.2854: <PROTOCOL> attacks refer to any attack that targets the stability and security of the <PROTOCOL> infrastructure.
sentence.2855: They commonly aim to render the <PROTOCOL> unavailable or intercept and alter the answers provided by the <PROTOCOL>, directing unsuspecting users to malicious websites.
sentence.2856: <PROTOCOL> infrastructure contains two components — authoritative and recursive <PROTOCOL> servers — and both are open to attack.
sentence.2857: Below, we’ll explore the most common attacks against <PROTOCOL> and review mitigation strategies to avoid them.
sentence.2858: Crash course in <PROTOCOL> attacksThere are several types of <PROTOCOL> attacks, each function differently, have unique impacts, and require specific countermeasures.
sentence.2859: SpoofingDNS spoofing occurs when threat actors alter the legitimate <PROTOCOL> server records to redirect users to fraudulent websites instead of their intended destination.
sentence.2860: When unsuspecting users reach the fraudulent website, the website prompts them to enter sensitive information, such as login details or credit card information.
sentence.2861: Threat actors use this technique to steal the victim’s sensitive data or plant malware — like ransomware or keyloggers — on their victim’s device.
sentence.2862: Attackers execute <PROTOCOL> spoofing attacks using two methods:Intercepting the communications between the target device and the <PROTOCOL> server and redirecting users’ requests to a malicious websiteDirectly attacking the legitimate <PROTOCOL> server and forcing it to return malicious IP addressesTo counter this attack, we should:Update and patch the <PROTOCOL> server software regularly.
sentence.2863: Check the website for the secure connection (padlock) symbol.
sentence.2864: This symbol appears next to the address bar of the web browser.
sentence.2865: If there’s no padlock, this may indicate threat actors have mirrored the website for malicious purposes.
sentence.2866: Enable the Domain Name System Security Extensions (DNSSEC) on the domain.
sentence.2867: These extensions add a layer of security by attaching a digital certificate signature to <PROTOCOL> information.
sentence.2868: Cache poisoningIn this attack, the threat actor injects false <PROTOCOL> information into the <PROTOCOL> cache to force it to return incorrect information and direct users to malicious websites.
sentence.2869: For example, when a user requests to visit <DOMAIN>, the poisoned <PROTOCOL> server returns the IP address of another website that could contain an exploit kit or phishing page.
sentence.2870: <PROTOCOL> cache poisoning and spoofing are often used interchangeably in cybersecurity.
sentence.2871: However, they are different in terms of their function and order of appearance.
sentence.2872: In <PROTOCOL> poisoning, threat actors replace the <PROTOCOL> records to redirect unsuspecting users to malicious destinations.
sentence.2873: Then, <PROTOCOL> spoofing redirects unsuspecting users to the malicious website using a poisoned cache.
sentence.2874: To prevent a <PROTOCOL> poisoning attack, we should:Use DNSSEC, which uses public key cryptography.
sentence.2875: This ensures that only a legitimate <PROTOCOL> nameserver answers a request with the correct <PROTOCOL> information.
sentence.2876: Prevent local <PROTOCOL> servers from answering internet-based <PROTOCOL> queries — unless our <PROTOCOL> nameserver is registered with <DOMAIN><FILE_PATH> flooding is an attack by which malicious actors try to overwhelm <PROTOCOL> servers with false <PROTOCOL> requests to prevent them from serving legitimate requests.
sentence.2877: There are two types of <PROTOCOL> flood attacks: denial of service (DoS) flooding and distributed denial of service (DDoS) flooding.
sentence.2878: DoS flood attackIn a DoS flood attack, the attacker uses one computer to flood a remote <PROTOCOL> server with false traffic.
sentence.2879: This technique is no longer effective because modern <PROTOCOL> servers have advanced technical specifications that one device cannot disrupt.
sentence.2880: DDoS <PROTOCOL> flood attackThe DDoS <PROTOCOL> flood is the most effective attack mechanism wherein attackers use many devices to target one <PROTOCOL> server.
sentence.2881: This action consumes the target <PROTOCOL> memory and CPU resources, eventually taking the server offline.
sentence.2882: In cybersecurity, a bot can refer to any computing device, for example, a laptop, workstation, or internet of things (IoT) device infected with malware and under a threat actor’s control.
sentence.2883: A collection of these bots is called a botnet.
sentence.2884: Attackers commonly use networks of botnets containing thousands or millions of compromised devices that run malicious scripts.
sentence.2885: The attacker orchestrates the attack by directing all devices to send traffic simultaneously to one server, generating a DoS status.
sentence.2886: <PROTOCOL> floods are considered relatively modern, made widely possible by the increasing numbers of IoT devices worldwide.
sentence.2887: Many IoT devices have poor security configurations, making them easy targets for hackers to control.
sentence.2888: To prevent DDoS and DoS flood attacks, we should:Use a DDoS mitigation service to prevent outside attackers from overwhelming our <PROTOCOL> servers with false requests.
sentence.2889: Use one dedicated server as the authoritative name server and another as the <PROTOCOL> resolver.
sentence.2890: This enables one component to remain operational if the second fails.
sentence.2892: Small and medium-sized organizations often use one server for multiple purposes, such as hosting applications and running the <PROTOCOL> service.
sentence.2893: However, if the attacker accesses one application hosted on the server, they can compromise and alter the <PROTOCOL> settings.
sentence.2894: NXDomainLike a <PROTOCOL> flood attack, the NXDomain attack overwhelms the target <PROTOCOL> server with many requests for invalid records (nonexistent domain names).
sentence.2895: To execute this attack, attackers use a <PROTOCOL> proxy server that automatically sends a massive number of <PROTOCOL> requests to the targeted authoritative <PROTOCOL> server.
sentence.2896: The authoritative server consumes resources (fills the server cache) in resolving these invalid requests, making it respond slowly to legitimate requests — and eventually stop responding altogether.
sentence.2897: To prevent the <PROTOCOL> NXD flood attack, we should:Conduct regular <PROTOCOL> audits.
sentence.2898: Blocklist suspicious domain names and servers.
sentence.2899: Temporarily blocklist a client’s IP address if it sends too many NXDomain requests.
sentence.2900: Increase the Time to Live (TTL) on current <PROTOCOL> records to ensure that they’ll remain for an extended time in external <PROTOCOL> caches.
sentence.2901: These records don’t need to be updated regularly.
sentence.2902: Amplification attacksThis is another DDoS attack that aims to prevent the target <PROTOCOL> server from serving legitimate <PROTOCOL> queries.
sentence.2903: In this attack, threat actors exploit open <PROTOCOL> servers to send multiple responses to the target server.
sentence.2904: Threat actors initiate this attack by sending numerous <PROTOCOL> requests to the open <PROTOCOL> server using the target IP address as the source address.
sentence.2905: The open <PROTOCOL> server returns the response to the requester (in this example, the target spoofed IP address).
sentence.2906: Sending many <PROTOCOL> responses eventually crashes the target server by consuming its network bandwidth and making it unresponsive to legitimate requests.
sentence.2907: Attackers commonly leverage botnets, especially on IoT devices, to generate spoofed <PROTOCOL> requests to overwhelm the target servers or organization network with <PROTOCOL> responses.
sentence.2908: To prevent this attack, we should:Enforce source IP verifications on all network devices.
sentence.2909: Prevent <PROTOCOL> authoritative name servers from functioning as recursive servers.
sentence.2910: Enforce response rate limiting (RRL) settings on all <PROTOCOL> servers.
sentence.2911: Configure open <PROTOCOL> resolvers to only respond to queries from a trusted source.
sentence.2912: HijackingIn this attack, threat actors manipulate <PROTOCOL> response queries to direct unsuspecting users to fraudulent or malicious websites.
sentence.2913: This attack occurs by:Installing malware, such as a trojan horse, on the victim’s computer to incorrectly resolve <PROTOCOL> queries and lead the unsuspecting user to malicious sitesCompromising the target router and changing its <PROTOCOL> settings.
sentence.2914: This affects all users connected to the router.
sentence.2915: Intercepting the communications between the legitimate <PROTOCOL> server and user device — as in the case of a man-in-the-middle attack — and manipulating <PROTOCOL> responses to lead the unsuspecting user to malicious sitesTargeting the <PROTOCOL> server directly and then changing its <PROTOCOL> settings to lead unsuspecting users to different URLsAlthough
sentence.2916: this attack is malicious, some internet service providers (ISPs) use this technique to direct users to other websites.
sentence.2917: For example, some ISPs use it to display advertisements based on a user’s browsing history.
sentence.2918: RebindingIn this attack, the threat actor infects the target router with malware to control it remotely.
sentence.2919: The attack begins by executing malicious JavaScript code on a user’s browser to infect the router.
sentence.2920: Many people don’t protect their router using a complex <DATA_OBJECT> — or just safeguard it using the default factory <DATA_OBJECT>.
sentence.2921: This leaves them vulnerable to rebinding attacks.
sentence.2922: A good first step toward guarding against rebinding attacks is to protect the router with a strong <DATA_OBJECT>.
sentence.2923: We should also:Change the default router username and <DATA_OBJECT> to something difficult to guess.
sentence.2924: Keep the <PROTOCOL> server and all client operating systems and installed applications up to date.
sentence.2925: Tunneling This <PROTOCOL> attack routes unsuspecting user traffic to the attacker’s server.
sentence.2926: This attack is typical among ransomware operators for facilitating communication with the Command and Control Center (C&C) and exfiltrating data from the target device.
sentence.2927: <PROTOCOL> tunneling evades detection by security tools like firewalls.
sentence.2928: Threat actors send stolen data from the target network in small chunks and deliver them as a series of <PROTOCOL> queries and responses to avoid detection.
sentence.2929: A <PROTOCOL> tunneling attack works as follows:The attacker has a server with a domain name pointing to it.
sentence.2931: The attacker infects a computer with malware.
sentence.2932: The infected computer might sit behind a company firewall but can use the <PROTOCOL> resolver.
sentence.2933: Now, the <PROTOCOL> resolver can communicate with the remote attacker’s C&C server.
sentence.2934: By doing this, each infected device and the remote attacker’s server have created a covert channel that can be used to exfiltrate data from the victim device or deliver more malware, such as ransomware, to the target device.
sentence.2935: To prevent this attack, we should:Use advanced security solutions, including next-generation firewalls on network perimeters and network detection and response (NDR), to monitor all interactions within our IT environment.
sentence.2936: This enables us to detect APT and ransomware operators and halt communications with attackers’ servers.
sentence.2937: Configure all devices within an organization’s network to send all their <PROTOCOL> queries to an internal <PROTOCOL> server that blocks suspicious domain names.
sentence.2938: Phantom domainIn this attack, the threat actor sets up numerous phantom domain names and requests the target <PROTOCOL> server to resolve them.
sentence.2939: These domains (commonly a large number of sub-domain names) respond very slowly or never.
sentence.2940: After a while, the target <PROTOCOL> server consumes its server cache while waiting for the attacker domain’s responses and eventually becomes unresponsive.
sentence.2941: To prevent this attack, we should:Increase the number of recursive <PROTOCOL> servers.
sentence.2942: Limit the number of successive recursive <PROTOCOL> requests on each <PROTOCOL> server.
sentence.2943: ConclusionThe <PROTOCOL> service is a critical component of internet infrastructure.
sentence.2944: It’s responsible for translating users’ domain names into IP addresses that other servers can understand.
sentence.2945: However, it was not made for security.
sentence.2946: With the widespread use of the internet and the growing number of cyberattacks, cybercriminals have become increasingly interested in <PROTOCOL> attacks.
sentence.2947: Any attack against the <PROTOCOL> service prevents all internet programs from functioning correctly.
sentence.2948: Cybercriminals know this and have developed many ways to attack <PROTOCOL> services for malicious purposes.
sentence.2949: There are several different techniques to attack the <PROTOCOL> service, which we can group into two main categories:Attacks that aim to make the <PROTOCOL> service unavailableAttacks that aim to manipulate the <PROTOCOL> records to lead unaware users to malicious destinationsAs this article has demonstrated, each type of <PROTOCOL> attack requires a different set of countermeasures to mitigate it.
sentence.2950: However, generally speaking, the keys to preventing <PROTOCOL> attacks include keeping the DNC server software up to date, using a dedicated <PROTOCOL> server to provide the <PROTOCOL> service, increasing the number of recursive <PROTOCOL> servers, and checking for vulnerabilities to mitigate DDoS attacks.

sentence.3028: title: LockBit 2.0: How This RaaS Operates and How to Protect Against It url: <URL> Executive Summary LockBit 2.0 is ransomware as a service (RaaS) that first emerged in June 2021 as an upgrade to its predecessor LockBit (aka ABCD Ransomware), which was first observed in September 2019.
sentence.3029: Since its inception, the LockBit 2.0 RaaS attracted affiliates via recruitment campaigns in underground forums, and thus became particularly prolific during the third quarter of calendar year 2021.
sentence.3030: The LockBit 2.0 operators claimed to have the fastest encryption software of any active ransomware strain as of June 2021, claiming accordingly that this added to its effectiveness and ability to disrupt the ransomware landscape.
sentence.3031: While several top-tier RaaS affiliate programs, such as Babuk, DarkSide and REvil (aka Sodinokibi) disappeared from the underground in 2021, LockBit 2.0 continued to operate and gradually became one of the most active ransomware operations.
sentence.3032: While Conti was recognized as being the most prolific ransomware deployed in 2021 per our 2022 Unit 42 Ransomware Threat Report, LockBit 2.0 is the most impactful and widely deployed ransomware variant we have observed in all ransomware breaches during the first quarter of 2022, considering both leak site data and data from cases handled by Unit 42 incident responders.
sentence.3033: According to data analysis of ransomware groups’ dark web leak sites, LockBit 2.0 was the most impactful RaaS for five consecutive months.
sentence.3034: As of May 25, LockBit 2.0 accounted for 46% of all ransomware-related breach events for 2022.
sentence.3035: And the LockBit 2.0 RaaS leak site has the most significant number of published victims, with over 850 in total.
sentence.3036: Additionally, LockBit 2.0 has affected many companies globally, with top victims based in the U.S., Italy and Germany.
sentence.3037: Its most highly targeted industry verticals include professional services, construction, wholesale and retail, and manufacturing.
sentence.3038: Palo Alto Networks customers receive protections against LockBit 2.0 attacks from Cortex XDR, as well as from the WildFire cloud-delivered security subscription for the Next-Generation Firewall.
sentence.3039: (Please see the Conclusion section for more detail.)
sentence.3040: Table of Contents LockBit 2.0 OverviewVictimologyLeak Site DataUnit 42 Incident Response Data on LockBit 2.0LockBit 2.0 Tactics, Techniques and ProceduresLockBit 2.0 Technical DetailsLockBit 3.0Courses of ActionConclusionAppendix AAdditional Resources LockBit 2.0 Overview LockBit 2.0 is another example of RaaS that leverages double extortion techniques as part of the attack to pressure victims into paying the ransom.
sentence.3041: In some cases, LockBit 2.0 operators have performed DDoS attacks on the victims' infrastructure as well as using a leak site.
sentence.3042: This practice is known as triple extortion, a tactic observed in groups like BlackCat, Avaddon and SunCrypt in the past.
sentence.3043: Like other ransomware families such as BlackByte, LockBit 2.0 avoids systems that use Eastern European languages, including many written with Cyrillic alphabets.
sentence.3044: Unlike other RaaS programs that don't require the affiliates to be super technical or savvy, LockBit 2.0 operators allegedly only work with experienced penetration testers, especially those experienced with tools like Metasploit and Cobalt Strike.
sentence.3045: Affiliates are tasked with gaining initial access to the victim network, allowing LockBit 2.0 to conduct the rest of the attack.
sentence.3046: LockBit 2.0 has been observed changing infected computers’ backgrounds to a ransomware note.
sentence.3047: The ransomware note was also used to recruit insiders from victim organizations.
sentence.3048: The notes claimed the threat actors would pay “millions of dollars” to insiders who provided access to corporate networks or facilitated a ransomware infection by opening a phishing email and<FILE_PATH> launching a payload manually.
sentence.3049: The threat actors also expressed interest in other access methods such as <PROTOCOL>, VPN and corporate email <DATA_OBJECT>.
sentence.3050: In exchange, they offer a cut of the paid ransom.
sentence.3052: The operators work with initial access brokers to save time and allow for a larger profit potential.
sentence.3053: While typically seeking victims of opportunity, LockBit 2.0 does appear to have victim limitations.
sentence.3054: The group announced that they would not target healthcare facilities, social services, educational institutions, charitable organizations and other organizations that “contribute to the survival of the human race”.
sentence.3055: However, despite these claims, there have been instances of affiliates undermining these guidelines by still opting to attack industry verticals such as healthcare and education.
sentence.3056: Organizations in Europe and the U.S. are hit more often by LockBit 2.0 than those in other countries, likely due to the high profitability and insurance payouts.
sentence.3057: Leak Site Data During the first calendar year quarter of 2022, LockBit 2.0 persisted as the most impactful and the most deployed ransomware variant we observed in all ransomware breaches shared on leak sites.
sentence.3059: Ransomware leak site data from the first calendar year quarter of <DOMAIN> to leak site data analysis, LockBit 2.0 was the most impactful RaaS for five consecutive months.
sentence.3060: As of May 25, LockBit 2.0 accounted for 46% of all ransomware-related breach events for 2022 shared on leak sites.
sentence.3061: Additionally, the LockBit 2.0 RaaS leak site has the most significant number of published victims, with over 850 in total.
sentence.3062: The site itself typically features information such as victim domains, a time tracker and measures of how much data was compromised. Figure 2.

sentence.3073: Unit 42 Incident Response Data on LockBit 2.0 Cases handled by Unit 42 security consultants involving LockBit 2.0 since its appearance in June 2021 demonstrate shorter dwell times and less flexibility in negotiation in the beginning of FY 2022 (measured October-September) in comparison to the end of FY 2021.

sentence.3085: LockBit 2.0 Tactics, Techniques and Procedures Technically speaking, we have observed LockBit 2.0 affiliates leveraging the following tactics, techniques and procedures: TA0001 Initial Access T1078 Valid Accounts <DATA_OBJECT> that have either been reused across multiple platforms or have previously been exposed.
sentence.3086: Additionally, this includes VPN accounts – not just domain and local accounts.

sentence.3092: LockBit 2.0 can be executed via scheduled tasks.

sentence.3100: Valid Accounts Compromised accounts may be used to maintain access to the network.
sentence.3103: In rare cases, LockBit 2.0 has been observed to create accounts for persistence with simple names, such as “a.” T1505.003 Server Software Component With the upsurgence of ProxyShell, webshells have become more common entry points.

sentence.3130: LockBit 2.0 Technical Details LockBit 2.0 was developed using the Assembly and Origin C programming languages and leverages advanced encryption standard (<ENC_ALGO>) and elliptic-curve cryptography (ECC) algorithms to encrypt victim data.
sentence.3131: It can affect both Windows and Linux OS, as the operator released a Linux version of LockBit 2.0 to target VMware ESXi hypervisor systems in October 2021, coded exclusively in the C programming language.
sentence.3132: The LockBit group claimed that LockBit 2.0 is “the fastest encryption software all over the world” and provided a comparative table showing the encryption speed of various ransomware samples.
sentence.3136: LockBit 2.0 also contains a self-spreading feature, clears logs and can print the ransom note on network printers until the paper runs out.
sentence.3137: A management panel that affiliates can use to manage victims and affiliate accounts, generate new ransomware builds and generate the decryptor if the demanded ransom is paid also exists.
sentence.3141: LockBit 2.0 operators also released an information-stealer dubbed StealBit, which was developed to support affiliates of the LockBit 2.0 RaaS when exfiltrating data from breached companies.
sentence.3142: StealBit contains the following capabilities: Operates as a <DATA_OBJECT> grabber and dumps<FILE_PATH> victim data to the LockBit victim-shaming site.
sentence.3143: No reliance on third-party cloud <DATA_OBJECT>-sharing services, where data can be easily removed if the victim submitted a complaint.
sentence.3144: The download speed is limited only by internet connection bandwidth, so it is possible to clone folders from corporate networks and upload them to the LockBit victim shaming blog quickly.
sentence.3145: The operator of LockBit 2.0 has provided a comparative table speed showing the information stealer compared to other tools. Figure 10.

sentence.3148: After the bug’s disclosure, LockBit forum members discussed how the bug will not exist in LockBit’s next iteration.
sentence.3149: Moreover, on March 17, LockBit forum members mentioned the release of LockBit’s next version in one or two weeks.
sentence.3150: On March 25, VX underground posted a tweet with details of this new version, dubbed LockBit Black. Figure 11.

sentence.3177: Conclusion LockBit 2.0 and its evolution over time is a perfect example to illustrate the persistence, increasing complexity and impact brought by the ransomware landscape as a whole.
sentence.3178: With claims of this RaaS offering the fastest encryption on the ransomware market, coupled with the fact that it has been delivered in high volume by experienced affiliates, this RaaS poses a significant threat.
sentence.3179: LockBit’s continuation with operations and its next iteration coming up on the horizon means that organizations and their security teams need to stay vigilant in the ever-evolving threat landscape.
sentence.3180: Palo Alto Networks detects and prevents LockBit 2.0 ransomware in the following ways: WildFire:
sentence.3181: All known samples are identified as malware.
sentence.3182: Cortex XDR: Identifies indicators associated with LockBit 2.0.
sentence.3183: Anti-Ransomware Module to detect LockBit 2.0 encryption behaviors on Windows.
sentence.3184: Local Analysis detection for LockBit 2.0 binaries on Windows.
sentence.3186: <PROTOCOL> Signatures detect the known C2 domains, which are also categorized as malware in Advanced URL Filtering.

sentence.3192: In August 2021, a Russian blogger published a 22-minute interview with an alleged representative of the group behind LockBit 2.0 called “LockBitSupp” on a YouTube channel called “Russian-language open source intelligence (OSINT).”
sentence.3193: The same Russian blogger previously published interviews with a representative of the group behind the REvil ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS), hackers and security experts.
sentence.3194: Some key takeaways from the claims made in the interview were: The LockBit 2.0 threat actor claimed the group’s RaaS was unlikely to be rebranded since the team allegedly was a business that was honest with their customers – suggesting a supposed contrast between LockBit 2.0 and Avaddon, DarkSide and REvil affiliates.
sentence.3195: The LockBit 2.0 ransomware disregarded keyboard layout, but it allegedly would not run on a host where the system language was set to any of the languages spoken in the Commonwealth of Independent States region.
sentence.3196: The group did not devise attacks on companies of their choice; they simply worked with initial access to any corporate network they obtained elsewhere, since this was more profitable and saved time.
sentence.3197: The team selected targets for ransomware attacks based on the company’s finances — the bigger, the better.
sentence.3198: The location also did not matter.
sentence.3199: However, team members allegedly did not attack healthcare facilities, social services, educational institutions and charitable organizations or any other organization that “contributed to the survival of the human race.”
sentence.3200: [Note that Unit 42 case data does include indications that threat actors using LockBit 2.0 have targeted healthcare organizations at times.]
sentence.3201: The threat actor claimed that the largest number of victims who paid ransom were company representatives who did not care about creating backup copies and did not protect their sensitive data.
sentence.3202: According to the threat actor’s claims, companies that violated regulations about collecting and handling customer or user personal information were among those eager to pay.
sentence.3203: The threat actor claimed that there generally were only a few companies who refused to pay ransom on principle, while most of the victims evaluated profit and loss to decide whether or not to pay a ransom.
sentence.3204: LockBit 2.0 operators allegedly almost always offered discounts to their victims since the goal was to streamline attacks.
sentence.3205: The threat actor claimed that the COVID-19 pandemic facilitated ransomware attacks significantly, saying it was easy to compromise home computers of employees who work remotely and use them as a springboard to access other networked systems.
sentence.3206: Companies in Europe and the U.S. were hit with ransomware much more often than companies based in other countries allegedly because of high profit and insurance and not because of language barriers.
sentence.3207: Ransomware operators usually recruit negotiators, who coerce victims to pay ransom, since professional penetration testers allegedly lack the time for chatter.
