sentence.3210: title: SOC Team Essentials | How to Investigate and Track the 8220 Gang Cloud Threat url: <URL> 8220 Gang is a low-skill crimeware actor known for infecting cloud hosts through n-day vulnerabilities and remote access brute forcing.
sentence.3211: We have previously detailed how 8220 expanded its botnet and rotated its infrastructure.
sentence.3212: Since our last write up in October, the group has again switched to new infrastructure and samples, providing us with an opportunity to share an educational walkthrough of the process of investigating cybercrime activity that may be useful to new or lesser experienced SOC teams, analysts and researchers.
sentence.3213: In this post, we use 8220 Gang activity as a lens through which to explain the process of investigating a threat, researching the threat activity as a whole, and gaining a perspective into attacker objectives, ultimately concluding with a wider understanding of related threat intelligence.
sentence.3214: Refresher on 8220 Gang 8220 Gang (pronounced eighty-two twenty), also known as 8220 Mining Group, was first publicly reported by Talos in 2018.
sentence.3215: Victims of 8220 Gang are typically, but not exclusively, users of cloud networks operating vulnerable and misconfigured Linux applications and services.
sentence.3216: Attacks make use of <PROTOCOL> brute forcing post-infection to automate local and global spreading attempts.
sentence.3217: Victims using cloud infrastructure (AWS, Azure, GCP, Aliyun, QCloud) are often infected via publicly accessible hosts running Docker, Confluence, Apache WebLogic, and Redis.
sentence.3218: Victims are not targeted geographically but simply identified by their internet accessibility.
sentence.3219: Initial Discovery Our walkthrough starts with the initial discovery of an interesting script found on a compromised AWS machine with publicly available <PROTOCOL> service secured with weak <DATA_OBJECT>.
sentence.3220: For readers not running a honeypot, this initial discovery could have also been observed in the monitoring of new <DATA_OBJECT> uploaded to <DATA_OBJECT> scanning services like VirusTotal or MalShare.
sentence.3221: For those looking to monitor this group, international <PROTOCOL> honeypots plus VirusTotal YARA rules offer a reliable method of catching new activity as it occurs.
sentence.3222: The script in question has the <ENC_ALGO> <FILE_HASH>. 8220 Infection Script Snippet We can see it is quite simple in design and built around the process of downloading and setting persistence of some other <DATA_OBJECT>.
sentence.3223: With a few string pivots inside VT, or even a few Google searches, we can quickly discover the core functionality of the script has been widely reported on as it has been reused by many amateur cryptocurrency mining groups and opportunistic profit-seeking attackers.
sentence.3224: Pivoting on part of the script’s content in VirusTotal Intelligence One example of such reporting is our July 2022 post on 8220 Gang expanding their botnet to roughly 30,000 hosts.
sentence.3225: However, this time the attacker-specific infrastructure is different, and we have not determined if it has delivered similar malware.
sentence.3226: Remember, this “infection script” is used by many attackers, and it alone is a very weak source of attribution. 8220 Infection Script Analysis The script goes through a set of instructions, often at multiple levels of encoded commands, aimed at the delivery of setting persistence on the victim machine by downloading itself from malicious servers.
sentence.3227: The multiple levels of <ENC_ALGO> encoding attempt to hide the fact that it is also downloading a specific payload as well.
sentence.3228: This is first observed under the createservices function.
sentence.3229: Infection Script createservices Function One difference that’s quickly apparent to past reporting on the script is that the attacker began adding the lwp-download command as a failover for wget and curl to enable downloading commands.
sentence.3230: We initially observed this activity on January 6th, and since then the actor has continued to standardize it in their infection scripts today.
sentence.3231: Sysdig also noted this activity in a recent blog.
sentence.3232: Infection Script use of lwp-download The key take away from analyzing these infection scripts is noting unique additions, like lwp–download, combined with the destination of download requests.
sentence.3233: By clustering infection scripts based on function names and order, if the functions are called, and what infrastructure is associated, we can weed out the non-8220 Gang samples.
sentence.3234: Additionally, we can link this further based on the encoding quantity and repetition to past 8220 Gang samples.
sentence.3235: For example, in our infection scripts createservices makes use of three <ENC_ALGO> encoded echo commands.
sentence.3236: The first command can be decoded into a new script which pings associated attacker infrastructure and then starts a “payload” command. Infection Script’s encoded payload
sentence.3237: The payload contains two additional <ENC_ALGO> encoded scripts to set permissions, download, and configure miner and IRC bot infections.
sentence.3239: Post-Infection Activity & Sample Pivots The post infection activity for this and other recent 8220 infection scripts evolve slightly, but generally proceed with infecting the victim with an updated PwnRig cryptocurrency miner and IRC bot.
sentence.3240: In the infection scripts we observed in this campaign, the group continued to use old bash IRC bot “Tsunami”.
sentence.3241: The sample delivered remains unchanged; however, the network it communicates with evolves over campaigns.
sentence.3242: The infection script here delivered <FILE_HASH> – the Tsunami sample.
sentence.3243: More useful for tracking 8220 Gang are the samples of PwnRig – the custom version of the open source XMRig cryptocurrency miner – that they drop.
sentence.3244: In this campaign, the script downloads the UPX packed sample <FILE_HASH>, which unpacks to <FILE_HASH>.
sentence.3245: A characteristic of 8220 Gang is their repeated use of fake miner pool domains themed around the FBI.
sentence.3246: Here, we see this theme again through the use of the malicious domain <DOMAIN>.
sentence.3247: Infrastructure Analysis Tracking 8220 Gang is aided somewhat by their failures in infrastructure OPSEC.
sentence.3248: Since the beginning of what the industry calls “8220 Gang” the primary method of attribution has been reused infrastructure and identification of newly associated infrastructure.
sentence.3249: While this technique alone does not link the actor with certainty, it remains reliable when combined with the previously noted linkability around malware samples delivered.
sentence.3250: During our initial investigation in January, the group was using <IPv4>, and <DOMAIN> for malware download location post-infection such as in their infection script.
sentence.3251: Anyone looking into this group should pivot on all subdomains associated with the actor-controlled domain, in addition to all <PROTOCOL> history of malicious IPs to identify a wider set of the malicious activity.
sentence.3252: For example, the recent <DOMAIN> host resolved to <IPv4> during the initial deployment of the script.
sentence.3253: More activity of 8220 Gang scripts can be found calling directly to this IP rather than the domain.
sentence.3254: The same goes for <IPv4>, which is called by IP in the script, and which at the time resolved to <DOMAIN>, a widely reported known 8220 Gang domain.
sentence.3255: Overall, the group is clumsy and unsophisticated in their infrastructure management, providing a good opportunity for those willing to track the mess or cut their teeth in threat actor investigation.
sentence.3256: Our graphic from a previous campaign explains the overlap, which can still be found in this most recent activity.
sentence.3257: Visual Context of 8220 Gang Infrastructure Roles Conclusion Tracking and researching 8220 Gang, which has exhibited a lack of operational security, requires a simple understanding of their use of malicious scripts, malware samples, and malicious infrastructure.
sentence.3258: A successful approach to tracking this group can involve monitoring and analyzing malware samples, identifying patterns in their malicious scripts, and mapping out their infrastructure. sentence.3260: title: Fantasy – a new Agrius wiper deployed through a supply‑chain attack url: <URL> ESET researchers analyzed a supply-chain attack abusing an Israeli software developer to deploy Fantasy, Agrius’s new wiper, with victims including the diamond industry ESET researchers discovered a new wiper and its execution tool, both attributed to the Agrius APT group, while analyzing a supply-chain attack abusing an Israeli software developer.
sentence.3261: The group is known for its destructive operations.
sentence.3262: In February 2022, Agrius began targeting Israeli HR and IT consulting firms, and users of an Israeli software suite used in the diamond industry.
sentence.3263: We believe that Agrius operators conducted a supply-chain attack abusing the Israeli software developer to deploy their new wiper, Fantasy, and a new lateral movement and Fantasy execution tool, Sandals.
sentence.3264: The Fantasy wiper is built on the foundations of the previously reported Apostle wiper but does not attempt to masquerade as ransomware, as Apostle originally did.
sentence.3265: Instead, it goes right to work wiping data.
sentence.3266: Victims were observed in South Africa – where reconnaissance began several weeks before Fantasy was deployed – Israel, and Hong Kong.
sentence.3267: Key points of this blogpost: Agrius conducted a supply-chain attack abusing an Israeli software suite used in the diamond industry.
sentence.3268: The group then deployed a new wiper we named Fantasy.
sentence.3269: Most of its code base comes from Apostle, Agrius’s previous wiper.
sentence.3270: Along with Fantasy, Agrius also deployed a new lateral movement and Fantasy execution tool that we have named Sandals.
sentence.3271: Victims include Israeli HR firms, IT consulting companies, and a diamond wholesaler; a South African organization working in the diamond industry; and a jeweler in Hong Kong.
sentence.3272: Group overview Agrius is a newer Iran-aligned group targeting victims in Israel and the United Arab Emirates since 2020.
sentence.3273: The group initially deployed a wiper, Apostle, disguised as ransomware, but later modified Apostle into fully fledged ransomware.
sentence.3274: Agrius exploits known vulnerabilities in internet-facing applications to install webshells, then conducts internal reconnaissance before moving laterally and then deploying its malicious payloads.
sentence.3275: Campaign overview On February 20th, 2022 at an organization in the diamond industry in South Africa, Agrius deployed credential harvesting tools, probably in preparation for this campaign.
sentence.3276: Then, on March 12th, 2022, Agrius launched the wiping attack by deploying Fantasy and Sandals, first to the victim in South Africa and then to victims in Israel and lastly to a victim in Hong Kong.
sentence.3277: Victims in Israel include an IT support services company, a diamond wholesaler, and an HR consulting firm.
sentence.3278: South African victims are from a single organization in the diamond industry, with the Hong Kong victim being a jeweler.
sentence.3281: The campaign lasted less than three hours and within that timeframe ESET customers were already protected with detections identifying Fantasy as a wiper, and blocking its execution.
sentence.3282: We observed the software developer pushing out clean updates within a matter of hours of the attack.
sentence.3283: We reached out to the software developer to notify them about a potential compromise, but our enquiries went unanswered.
sentence.3284: Preparing for departure The first tools deployed by Agrius operators to victim systems, through means unknown, were: MiniDump, “a C# implementation of mimikatz<FILE_PATH> minidump functionality to get <DATA_OBJECT> from LSASS dumps” SecretsDump, a Python script that “performs various techniques to dump hashes from [a] remote machine without executing any agent there” Host2IP, a custom C#<FILE_PATH> tool that resolves a hostname to an IP address.
sentence.3285: Usernames, passwords, and hostnames collected by these tools are required for Sandals to successfully spread and execute the Fantasy wiper.
sentence.3286: Agrius operators deployed MiniDump and SecretsDump to this campaign’s first victim on February 20th, 2022, but waited until March 12th, 2022 to deploy Host2IP, Fantasy, and Sandals (consecutively).
sentence.3288: Sandals is a 32-bit Windows executable written in C#<FILE_PATH>
sentence.3289: We chose the name because Sandals is an anagram of some of the command line arguments it accepts.
sentence.3290: It is used to connect to systems in the same network via <PROTOCOL>, to write a batch <DATA_OBJECT> to disk that executes the Fantasy wiper, and then run that batch <DATA_OBJECT> via PsExec with this command line string:
sentence.3293: -s “C:\<path>\<GUID>.bat” The PsExec options have the following meanings: -d – Don’t wait for process to terminate (non-interactive).
sentence.3294: <FILE_PATH> – Suppress display of the license dialog.
sentence.3296: Run the remote process in the SYSTEM account.
sentence.3297: Sandals does not write the Fantasy wiper to remote systems.
sentence.3298: We believe that the Fantasy wiper is deployed via a supply-chain attack using the software developer’s software update mechanism.

sentence.3412: title: AA22-320A: Iranian Government-Sponsored APT Actors Compromise Federal Network, Deploy Crypto Miner, Credential Harvester url: <URL> Original release date: November 16, 2022 | Last revised: November 25, 2022SummaryFrom mid-June through mid-July 2022, CISA conducted an incident response engagement at a Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) organization where CISA observed suspected advanced persistent threat (APT) activity.
sentence.3413: In the course of incident response activities, CISA determined that cyber threat actors exploited the Log4Shell vulnerability in an unpatched VMware Horizon server, installed XMRig crypto mining software, moved laterally to the domain controller (DC), compromised <DATA_OBJECT>, and then implanted Ngrok reverse proxies on several hosts to maintain persistence.
sentence.3414: CISA and the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) assess that the FCEB network was compromised by Iranian government-sponsored APT actors.
sentence.3415: CISA and FBI are releasing this Cybersecurity Advisory (CSA) providing the suspected Iranian government-sponsored actors’ tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) and indicators of compromise (IOCs) to help network defenders detect and protect against related compromises.
sentence.3416: CISA and FBI encourage all organizations with affected VMware systems that did not immediately apply available patches or workarounds to assume compromise and initiate threat hunting activities.
sentence.3417: If suspected initial access or compromise is detected based on IOCs or TTPs described in this CSA, CISA and FBI encourage organizations to assume lateral movement by threat actors, investigate connected systems (including the DC), and audit privileged accounts.
sentence.3418: All organizations, regardless of identified evidence of compromise, should apply the recommendations in the Mitigations section of this CSA to protect against similar malicious cyber activity.
sentence.3419: For more information on Iranian government-sponsored Iranian malicious cyber activity, see CISA’s Iran Cyber Threat Overview and Advisories webpage and FBI’s Iran Threats webpage.

sentence.3425: Overview In April 2022, CISA conducted retrospective analysis using EINSTEIN—an FCEB-wide intrusion detection system (IDS) operated and monitored by CISA—and identified suspected APT activity on an FCEB organization’s network.
sentence.3426: CISA observed bi-directional traffic between the network and a known malicious IP address associated with exploitation of the Log4Shell vulnerability (<CVE>) in VMware Horizon servers.
sentence.3427: In coordination with the FCEB organization, CISA initiated threat hunting incident response activities; however, prior to deploying an incident response team, CISA observed additional suspected APT activity.
sentence.3428: Specifically, CISA observed <PROTOCOL> activity from IP address to the organization’s VMware server.
sentence.3429: Based on trusted third-party reporting, is a Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (<PROTOCOL>) server associated with threat actors exploiting Log4Shell.
sentence.3430: Following <PROTOCOL> activity, CISA observed a suspected <PROTOCOL> callback on port 443 to this IP address.
sentence.3431: CISA also observed a <PROTOCOL> query for that resolved back to when the victim server was returning this Log4Shell <PROTOCOL> callback to the actors’ server.
sentence.3432: CISA assessed that this traffic indicated a confirmed compromise based on the successful callback to the indicator and informed the organization of these findings; the organization investigated the activity and found signs of compromise.
sentence.3433: As trusted-third party reporting associated Log4Shell activity from with lateral movement and targeting of DCs, CISA suspected the threat actors had moved laterally and compromised the organization’s DC. From mid-June through mid-July 2022, CISA conducted an onsite incident response engagement and determined that the organization was compromised as early as February 2022, by likely Iranian government-sponsored APT actors who installed XMRig crypto mining software.
sentence.3434: The threat actors also moved laterally to the domain controller, compromised <DATA_OBJECT>, and implanted Ngrok reverse proxies.
sentence.3435: Threat Actor Activity In February 2022, the threat actors exploited Log4Shell [T1190] for initial access [TA0001] to the organization’s unpatched VMware Horizon server.
sentence.3436: As part of their initial exploitation, CISA observed a connection to known malicious IP address lasting 17.6 seconds.

sentence.3769: title: #StopRansomware: Royal Ransomware url: <URL> SUMMARY Note: This joint Cybersecurity Advisory (CSA) is part of an ongoing #StopRansomware effort to publish advisories for network defenders that detail various ransomware variants and ransomware threat actors.
sentence.3770: These #StopRansomware advisories include recently and historically observed tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) and indicators of compromise (IOCs) to help organizations protect against ransomware.
sentence.3771: Visit <DOMAIN> to see all #StopRansomware advisories and to learn more about other ransomware threats and no-cost resources.
sentence.3772: Actions to take today to mitigate cyber threats from ransomware: Prioritize remediating known exploited vulnerabilities.
sentence.3773: Train users to recognize and report phishing attempts.
sentence.3775: The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) are releasing this joint CSA to disseminate known Royal ransomware IOCs and TTPs identified through FBI threat response activities as recently as January 2023.
sentence.3776: Since approximately September 2022, cyber criminals have compromised U.S. and international organizations with a Royal ransomware variant.
sentence.3777: FBI and CISA believe this variant, which uses its own custom-made <DATA_OBJECT> encryption program, evolved from earlier iterations that used “Zeon” as a loader.
sentence.3778: After gaining access to victims’ networks, Royal actors disable antivirus software and exfiltrate large amounts of data before ultimately deploying the ransomware and encrypting the systems.
sentence.3779: Royal actors have made ransom demands ranging from approximately $1 million to $11 million USD in Bitcoin.
sentence.3780: In observed incidents, Royal actors do not include ransom amounts and payment instructions as part of the initial ransom note.
sentence.3781: Instead, the note, which appears after encryption, requires victims to directly interact with the threat actor via a .onion URL (reachable through the Tor browser).
sentence.3782: Royal actors have targeted numerous critical infrastructure sectors including, but not limited to, Manufacturing, Communications, Healthcare and Public Healthcare (HPH), and Education.
sentence.3783: FBI and CISA encourage organizations to implement the recommendations in the Mitigations section of this CSA to reduce the likelihood and impact of ransomware incidents.
sentence.3784: Download the PDF version of this report: #StopRansomware: Royal Ransomware (PDF, 586.96 KB )
sentence.3785: For a downloadable copy of IOCs, see AA23-061A STIX XML (XML, 114.26 KB ) TECHNICAL DETAILS Note: This advisory uses the MITRE ATT&CK:registered: for Enterprise framework, version 12.
sentence.3786: See MITRE ATT&CK for Enterprise for all referenced tactics and techniques.
sentence.3787: Royal ransomware uses a unique partial encryption approach that allows the threat actor to choose a specific percentage of data in a <DATA_OBJECT> to encrypt.
sentence.3788: This approach allows the actor to lower the encryption percentage for larger <DATA_OBJECT>, which helps evade detection.[1]
sentence.3789: In addition to encrypting <DATA_OBJECT>, Royal actors also engage in double extortion tactics in which they threaten to publicly release the encrypted data if the victim does not pay the ransom.
sentence.3790: Initial Access Royal actors gain initial access to victim networks in a number of ways including: Phishing.
sentence.3791: According to third-party reporting, Royal actors most commonly (in 66.7% of incidents) gain initial access to victim networks via successful phishing emails [T1566].
sentence.3792: According to open-source reporting, victims have unknowingly installed malware that delivers Royal ransomware after receiving phishing emails containing malicious PDF documents [T1566.001], and malvertising [T1566.002].[2] Remote Desktop Protocol (<PROTOCOL>).
sentence.3793: The second most common vector Royal actors use (in 13.3% of incidents) for initial access is <PROTOCOL> compromise.
sentence.3795: FBI has also observed Royal actors gain initial access through exploiting public-facing applications [T1190]. Brokers.
sentence.3796: Reports from trusted third-party sources indicate that Royal actors may leverage brokers to gain initial access and source traffic by harvesting virtual private network (VPN) <DATA_OBJECT> from stealer logs.
sentence.3797: Command and Control Once Royal actors gain access to the network, they communicate with command and control (C2) infrastructure and download multiple tools [T1105].
sentence.3798: Legitimate Windows software is repurposed by Royal operators to strengthen their foothold in the victim’s network.
sentence.3799: Ransomware operators often use open-source projects to aid their intrusion activities; Royal operators have recently been observed using Chisel, a tunneling tool transported over <PROTOCOL> and secured via <PROTOCOL> [T1572], to communicate with their C2 infrastructure.
sentence.3800: FBI has observed multiple Qakbot C2s used in Royal ransomware attacks, but has not yet determined if Royal ransomware exclusively uses Qakbot C2s.
sentence.3801: Lateral Movement and Persistence Royal actors often use <PROTOCOL> to move laterally across the network
sentence.3803: Microsoft Sysinternals tool PsExec has also been used to aid lateral movement.
sentence.3804: FBI has observed Royal actors using remote monitoring and management (RMM) software, such as AnyDesk, LogMeIn, and Atera, for persistence in the victim’s network
sentence.3806: In some instances, the actors moved laterally to the domain controller.
sentence.3807: In one confirmed case, the actors used a legitimate admin account to remotely log on to the domain controller [T1078].
sentence.3808: Once on the domain controller, the threat actor deactivated antivirus protocols
sentence.3810: [T1484.001]. Exfiltration Royal actors exfiltrate data from victim networks by repurposing legitimate cyber pentesting tools, such as Cobalt Strike, and malware tools and derivatives, such as Ursnif<FILE_PATH>, for data aggregation and exfiltration.
sentence.3811: According to third-party reporting, Royal actors’ first hop in exfiltration and other operations is usually a U.S. IP address.
sentence.3812: Note: In reference to Cobalt Strike and other tools mentioned above, a tool repository used by Royal was identified at IP: <IPv4> in December 2022.
sentence.3813: Encryption Before starting the encryption process, Royal actors: Use Windows Restart Manager to determine whether targeted <DATA_OBJECT> are currently in use or blocked by other applications [T1486].[1] Use Windows Volume Shadow Copy service (<FILENAME>) to delete shadow copies to prevent system recovery.[1] FBI has found numerous batch (.bat) <DATA_OBJECT> on impacted systems which are typically transferred as an encrypted 7zip <DATA_OBJECT>.
sentence.3814: Batch <DATA_OBJECT> create a new admin user [T1078.002], force a group policy update, set pertinent <DATA_OBJECT> keys to auto-extract
sentence.3816: and execute the ransomware, monitor the encryption process, and delete <DATA_OBJECT> upon completion—including Application, System, and Security event logs [T1070.001].
sentence.3817: Malicious <DATA_OBJECT> have been found in victim networks in the following directories: <FILE_PATH> <FILE_PATH>
sentence.3818: title: Tomiris called, they want their Turla malware back url: <URL> We continued to track Tomiris as a separate threat actor over three new attack campaigns between 2021 and 2023, and our telemetry allowed us to shed light on the group.
sentence.3819: In this blog post, we’re excited to share what we now know of Tomiris with the broader community, and discuss further evidence of a possible connection to Turla.
